W1-001.title: An admin can block or delete their own (or the last admin's) account with no guard, permanently locking the whole site out of admin
W1-001.expected: The panel refuses (or at least loudly warns about) blocking/deleting yourself, and refuses blocking/deleting the last remaining admin, exactly as adminSetRole already refuses demoting the last admin ("This is the only admin. Make somebody else one first.").
W1-001.actual: adminBlockUser and adminDeleteUser have no self-check and no last-admin check. The owner's own row is reachable at /admin/people/<own-id> and PersonDetail renders Block, Delete and Merge for it unconditionally (no current-admin id is even passed to the component). Blocking yourself takes effect on the very next request: the session callback in src/lib/auth.ts:277 invalidates any session whose row reads isBlocked, and authorize() (auth.ts:155) refuses a blocked account at login, so the sole admin can never unblock himself. The block dialog's copy makes it worse: "You can undo this from the same button" (person-detail.tsx:373) is false for self-block.
W1-001.evidence: adminBlockUser body is only: `const actor = await requireAdminActor(); ... await prisma.user.update({ where: { id: userId }, data: { isBlocked: block, credentialVersion: { increment: 1 } } });` — no comparison of userId against actor.actorId and no count of remaining admins. adminDeleteUser likewise goes straight to `purgeUserAccount(userId)`. Contrast adminSetRole (people/actions.ts:216-225) which counts admins and refuses the last demotion, and whose comment explains the stake: "demoting the only admin locks everybody out of moderation permanently, and the only way back would be editing the database by hand" — the identical lockout exists via block and delete and is unguarded. Recovery script scripts/dev/set-password.mjs --admin restores role but nothing documents clearing isBlocked, and delete is unrecoverable.
W1-001.fixDirection: In adminBlockUser and adminDeleteUser, after requireAdminActor: (1) if userId === actor.actorId, refuse with copy like "You cannot block your own account from here."; (2) for block=true and for delete, if the target row has role admin and prisma.user.count({where:{role:"admin", isBlocked:false}}) <= 1, refuse like adminSetRole does. Also hide/disable Block, Delete and Merge on your own detail page (pass the acting admin's id into PersonDetail) and fix the block dialog copy for the other-admin case.
W1-001.reproPlan: code-argument-only (a live proof would block/delete a real admin on the shared production database).
W1-001.gateOrTest: Extend src/lib/security-regressions.test.mjs (or a new unit test) asserting adminBlockUser/adminDeleteUser return an error for self-target and for the last unblocked admin; write-path-reviewer on admin-actions.ts.

W1-002.title: Analytics Rhythms heatmap converts timezones the wrong way: every visit is bucketed 11 hours off the IST hour it claims
W1-002.expected: The 7x24 heatmap and its "Busiest: <day> around <hour> IST" line show visits at their Indian wall-clock hour, since Visit.endedAt stores a UTC wall time in a `timestamp without time zone` column.
W1-002.actual: The query applies `"endedAt" AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'` directly to a timestamp-without-time-zone. In Postgres that means "interpret this wall time AS Kolkata local", producing an instant 5h30 EARLIER in UTC; EXTRACT then reads it in the session timezone (UTC on Supabase). A 19:30-IST visit (stored 14:00 UTC wall) buckets at hour 8 instead of 19 — 11 hours off, with DOW shifting wrongly near midnight too. The peak hour the page tells the owner to schedule Catch-up email against is fiction.
W1-002.evidence: admin-analytics.ts:584-585: `SELECT EXTRACT(DOW FROM "endedAt" AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::int AS dow, EXTRACT(HOUR FROM "endedAt" AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')::int AS hour`. schema.prisma Visit model: `endedAt DateTime @default(now())` with no @db.Timestamptz, i.e. `timestamp(3) without time zone` holding UTC wall time (bugs.md #6 documents exactly this column class). Postgres semantics: `timestamp AT TIME ZONE zone` -> timestamptz (interprets AS that zone); the correct incantation for a UTC wall time is `("endedAt" AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'`. The component then prints "Busiest: {day} around {hour} IST. Worth matching the Catch-up email to it." (heatmap.tsx:75-87) — an explicit recommendation drawn from wrong buckets. This is the 6h IST class the audit brief predicts, in the one query that tried to handle it.
W1-002.fixDirection: Change both EXTRACT expressions to `("endedAt" AT TIME ZONE 'UTC') AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'`. While there, apply the same double-conversion to any future raw-SQL IST bucketing; note loadRhythm is the only AT TIME ZONE use in the repo today (verified by grep).
W1-002.reproPlan: Read-only SQL proves it without touching app data: `SELECT EXTRACT(HOUR FROM TIMESTAMP '2026-08-21 14:00:00' AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')` returns 8 on a UTC-session connection where the member's IST hour is 19. Alternatively load /admin/analytics?view=rhythms and compare a known recent visit's IST time to its cell.
W1-002.gateOrTest: A unit test on the corrected SQL expression via a raw query fixture, or pin loadRhythm output for a synthetic Visit row at a known UTC instant.

W1-003.title: Worklist 'flagged' and 'asked to be verified' queues sort and timestamp on User.updatedAt, which the 15-minute presence stamp rewrites — order is wrong and timestamps read 'just now' forever
W1-003.expected: "X asked to be verified" is ordered by when they asked (the comment says orderBy updatedAt asc = waited longest first) and carries the time of the request; flagged rows likewise carry when they were flagged.
W1-003.actual: User has `updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt` (schema line 94), and Prisma bumps @updatedAt on every update/updateMany — including touchLastSeen's `prisma.user.updateMany({... data: { lastSeenAt: now }})` (last-seen.ts:167-173) which fires from the (main) layout every 15 minutes of activity, plus any profile edit or admin-note save. So: (1) the pendingVerify queue's "oldest first" is actually "least recently active first" — an active member who asked days ago sorts below an inactive member who asked an hour ago; (2) the mixed Overview worklist sorts newest-`at` first, so any flagged or pending member who is currently browsing permanently squats at the top with a timestamp that reads "just now"/"3m ago" no matter when the flag or request happened.
W1-003.evidence: admin-worklist-query.ts:63-78: flagged `orderBy: { updatedAt: "desc" }` and pendingVerify `orderBy: { updatedAt: "asc" }`, then rows map `at: u.updatedAt.toISOString()` (139, 147); loadWorklist ends `items.sort((a, b) => b.at.localeCompare(a.at))` (177). last-seen.ts:167-173 writes User every LAST_SEEN_STALE_MS=15min. There is no verifyRequestedAt/flaggedAt column, so updatedAt is the only field available and it is actively churned.
W1-003.fixDirection: Add a real timestamp for each state change: e.g. `verifyRequestedAt DateTime?` set when verifyState flips to "pending" and `flaggedAt DateTime?` when it flips to "flagged" (dated idempotent migration in prisma/migrations-manual/ per house rules), then order and display on those. Cheaper stopgap: exclude lastSeenAt writes from bumping updatedAt is not possible with @updatedAt, so the column route is the honest fix.
W1-003.reproPlan: Read-only: open /admin with a member in verifyState "pending" who is actively browsing; their worklist row shows a fresh "time ago" each reload. Or compare AuditLog/roster timestamps against the shown 'at'.
W1-003.gateOrTest: Unit test on loadWorklist fixtures: a pending user whose lastSeenAt-driven updatedAt is newer must not outrank an older request once the dedicated column exists.

W1-004.title: Report dismiss/resolve have no status precondition: double-click or two admins produce duplicate and even contradictory messages to the reporter
W1-004.expected: Settling a report is once-only: the first admin's action wins, the second attempt is a no-op ("already settled"), and the reporter gets exactly one closing message.
W1-004.actual: adminDismissReport and adminResolveReport update `where: { id: reportId }` with no `status: "pending"` guard, then unconditionally post a thread note + notification via noteOnReportThread. Two admins triaging the same pending report (the exact worklist-claim race), or one admin double-clicking before React re-renders the disabled state (report-list.tsx act() sets state, so a second click in the same tick passes `busy === r.id` false), sends the reporter two notes. Worse, one admin clicking "Nothing wrong here" while another clicks resolve sends BOTH "decided to leave it as it is" AND "has dealt with it", with final status = last write.
W1-004.evidence: admin-actions.ts:171-174 `await prisma.report.update({ where: { id: reportId }, data: { status: "dismissed" } }); await noteOnReportThread(reportId, "An admin read this and decided to leave it as it is...")` — no precondition, and noteOnReportThread (admin-threads-server.ts:67-83) creates an adminMessage + notification every call. Same shape at 186-202 for resolve. No unique constraint exists to backstop the duplicate notification (Notification has no @@unique).
W1-004.fixDirection: Use updateMany with a precondition: `const r = await prisma.report.updateMany({ where: { id, status: "pending" }, data: { status } }); if (r.count === 0) return { error: "Already settled." }` and only call noteOnReportThread when count === 1. Same conditional-claim pattern claimAndSend already uses in email-queue.ts:160.
W1-004.reproPlan: code-argument-only (would write duplicate notifications to a real reporter's account on the shared DB).
W1-004.gateOrTest: Unit test: two concurrent adminDismissReport calls on one pending report yield exactly one adminMessage row.

W1-005.title: Every admin client wrapper awaits server actions without try/catch, and several actions throw (not return) on concurrently-deleted rows — one thrown P2025 wedges the UI in a permanent busy state
W1-005.expected: If a row was deleted by another admin (or the network blips) between page render and click, the action surfaces "that's gone" and the UI recovers.
W1-005.actual: The shared pattern is `setBusy(x); const result = await fn(); setBusy(false/null);` with no try/finally — in person-detail run() (128-139), the three card save()s (466-476, 543-553, 588-598), MailCard retry (641-651), content-list act() (104-113), report-list act() (56-65), ConfirmDialog run() (61-72, where close() also refuses while busy, so the dialog cannot even be dismissed), ModerationDialog handleConfirm (38-49), mail-rows act() (72-81), thread-view setStatus (43-53). Meanwhile approvePhoto (`prisma.photo.update` with no existence check, collection/actions.ts:525), adminHidePost (admin-actions.ts:157), adminVerifyUser (:99), adminSetPhotoTrusted, adminUpdatePerson and declinePhoto's `photo.delete` all THROW P2025 when the target vanished — a scenario two admins working the same photo queue or people list produce naturally. The await rejects, setBusy(false) never runs, the button says "Saving..."/"Working..." forever, and the admin sees no error (unhandled rejection in an event handler shows nothing in production). Related swallow: report-list's "Hide the post" composite (152-155) ignores adminHidePost's returned {error} and resolves the report anyway.
W1-005.evidence: person-detail.tsx:128-133: `async function run(fn, done) { setBusy(true); const result = await fn(); setBusy(false); ... }` — a rejection skips line 3. confirm-dialog.tsx:55-58: `function close() { if (busy) return; ... }` — a stuck busy makes the dialog unclosable. collection/actions.ts:521-528: `await prisma.photo.update({ where: { id: photoId }, ... })` with no findUnique guard, so the second admin's Approve after a concurrent Decline (row deleted at :549) throws.
W1-005.fixDirection: Wrap each wrapper's await in try/finally (finally: setBusy/setSaving reset; catch: toast a generic "That didn't go through — reload and try again"). Server-side, make the racy actions return {error} instead of throwing: precheck existence or catch P2002/P2025 (approvePhoto, adminHidePost, adminVerifyUser, adminUpdatePerson, adminSetPhotoTrusted, declinePhoto). In report-list's composite, check adminHidePost's result before resolving the report.
W1-005.reproPlan: Two tabs on the same photo in /admin/content?type=pending: Decline in tab A, then Approve in tab B — tab B's buttons stay disabled with no toast. Safe only against a test photo; otherwise code-argument-only.
W1-005.gateOrTest: Unit tests that the racy actions return {error} for a missing id; a Playwright spec pinning that a failed action re-enables its button.

W1-006.title: Person-detail 'Given' sums contributions without the livemode filter, so a developer's Razorpay test payment shows as real money on a member's admin record
W1-006.expected: Every money figure filters `livemode: true` — the spec calls this load-bearing (docs/spec/admin.md 9.7: "the ledger must honour the same split or the two surfaces disagree about how much money exists"), and /admin/support, /admin (overview) and loadSupport all do it.
W1-006.actual: The person page aggregates `where: { userId: id, status: "paid" }` with no livemode, and the Tally renders it as "Given ₹N". A local-dev test order against a real member's account (the databases are shared) inflates that member's giving on the page an admin reads as fact, and disagrees with the Support ledger one click away.
W1-006.evidence: people/[id]/page.tsx:64-68: `prisma.contribution.aggregate({ _sum: { amount: true }, _count: true, where: { userId: id, status: "paid" } })` — compare support/page.tsx:46 `where: { status: "paid", livemode: true }` and admin/page.tsx:77 `where: { status: "paid", livemode: true, paidAt: { gte: monthStart } }`.
W1-006.fixDirection: Add `livemode: true` to the person-page aggregate (both _sum and _count). If test gifts should still be visible on the record, count them separately and mark them Test like the ledger does.
W1-006.reproPlan: Read-only: pick a member with a livemode:false contribution row (if any exist) and compare their /admin/people/[id] 'Given' tally with their rows on /admin/support.
W1-006.gateOrTest: Unit test on the query where-shape, or a lint-style grep gate: any contribution aggregate on amount must carry livemode.

W1-007.title: adminMergeUsers fails wholesale with an opaque error when both accounts answered the same Catch-up prompt (CatchupEntry unique not in the dropped set)
W1-007.expected: Merging a duplicate account handles every unique-keyed collision: the comment's own rule is that everything carrying a `@@unique([userId, thingId])` is dropped rather than moved precisely because "moving them throws the moment both accounts touched the same post".
W1-007.actual: CatchupEntry carries `@@unique([promptId, authorId])` (schema:789) yet is in the MOVED set: `prisma.catchupEntry.updateMany({ where: { authorId: sourceId }, data: { authorId: targetId } })` (actions.ts:297). One human who answered the same prompt from both accounts — the definitional duplicate-account behavior — makes the updateMany violate the constraint, the whole transaction rolls back, and the admin gets only "Could not merge those accounts. Nothing was changed. Check the server log." with no path forward inside the panel. (CatchupPrompt has no such unique; posts/comments/photos/contributions are safe.)
W1-007.evidence: actions.ts:290-316 lists catchupEntry.updateMany among "Kept" while the "Dropped" rationale (258-264) is exactly about @@unique collisions; schema.prisma:784-789: CatchupEntry relations plus `@@unique([promptId, authorId])`. The catch at 317-320 collapses every failure into one generic string.
W1-007.fixDirection: Before the transaction, find the source's entry promptIds that the target already answered (`prisma.catchupEntry.findMany({ where: { authorId: targetId, promptId: { in: sourcePromptIds } } })`) and delete those source entries inside the transaction (dropping the duplicate answer, consistent with the likes rationale) — or move them with per-row conflict handling. Also surface P2002 distinctly so a future collision names the table.
W1-007.reproPlan: code-argument-only (a live proof merges real accounts).
W1-007.gateOrTest: Unit test: merge two fixture users who both answered one prompt; assert success and that the target keeps its own answer.

W1-008.title: purgeUserAccount deletes R2 objects one-by-one after the row cascade: an image-heavy member (or a multi-account sweep night) can blow the function time ceiling and permanently orphan the remainder
W1-008.expected: Deletion of a member with hundreds of images finishes inside a serverless invocation, or the cleanup continues after the response; nothing can leave publicly-fetchable bytes with no row pointing at them (the audit-H9 guarantee this module exists to keep).
W1-008.actual: After the DB transaction commits, `for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); deleted += 1; }` issues one sequential DeleteObject per URL. A Collection contributor at 2,000-user scale can own hundreds of objects (each photo is thumb+url+original = 3 objects); at ~50-150ms per R2 round trip, 400+ objects approaches or exceeds the 60s Vercel ceiling. Because the user row and every pointing row are ALREADY deleted (the transaction ran first, by design), a timeout mid-loop strands the uncollected remainder exactly in the unfindable-forever state H9 closed. The nightly sweep compounds it: runRetentionSweep purges every due account serially in one GET (retention.ts:115-127) with no maxDuration export on the route.
W1-008.evidence: account-purge.ts:99-113: transaction (report clear + user.delete) commits, then the serial loop; delImageByKey (storage.ts:218-228) is one DeleteObjectCommand per call and swallows failures, so nothing even records which objects were reached. sweep route has no `export const maxDuration`.
W1-008.fixDirection: Batch the deletes: S3/R2 DeleteObjects accepts 1,000 keys per request — one call replaces the loop (add a delImagesByKeys to storage.ts); or chunked Promise.all of 20. Export maxDuration on the sweep route and cap accounts purged per run (carry the rest to tomorrow's sweep, which the design already tolerates). Optionally persist the collected URL list before deleting rows so an interrupted cleanup is resumable.
W1-008.reproPlan: code-argument-only; arithmetic from a member's Photo count (3 objects per photo) x observed delImage latency suffices.
W1-008.gateOrTest: Unit test that purge uses the batch delete path; ops note in docs/OPERATIONS.md tying sweep batch size to the duration limit.

W1-009.title: Server-rendered admin dates and month windows are computed in UTC for an IST reader: events between 00:00 and 05:30 IST display the previous day, and 'this month' totals roll over 5h30 late
W1-009.expected: Dates the owner reads (Joined, Confirmed, Sent, Due, ledger dates) and calendar windows ("Given this month", "New members each month", distinct active days) reflect the Indian calendar day, the way /admin/mail already formats its budget-reset clock with `timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata"` (mail/page.tsx:94-100).
W1-009.actual: formatDisplayDate (utils.ts:151-157) and formatTimeAgo's >4-week fallback call toLocaleDateString with NO timeZone, so on Vercel (UTC) every event stamped between 18:30 and 24:00 UTC — i.e. 00:00-05:30 IST, prime late-night India hours — renders as the previous day everywhere in admin (person-detail Joined/Confirmed/verified dates, mail history, support ledger, catch-up "Due" dates). The overview's and support page's monthStart (`new Date(now); setDate(1); setHours(0,0,0,0)` on a UTC server) means "Given this month" still shows last month until 05:30 IST on the 1st, and a gift paid 00:30 IST on the 1st counts into the old month; loadGrowth's `date_trunc('month', "createdAt")` buckets signups the same way, and the `date_trunc('day', "startedAt")` distinct-day counts (loyal/returning/daysActive) split or merge IST days at 05:30.
W1-009.evidence: utils.ts:151-157: `return new Date(date).toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { day: "numeric", month: "short", year: "numeric" })` — no timeZone. admin/page.tsx:63-65 and support/page.tsx:38-40: monthStart from server-local midnight. admin-analytics.ts:811 and :443/:622/:956: UTC date_trunc. Counter-example in the same territory proving the intended standard: mail/page.tsx:94-100 formats with `timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata"`.
W1-009.fixDirection: Add `timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata"` to formatDisplayDate and formatTimeAgo's date fallback (one change fixes every admin call site; the audience is IST by product definition). Compute monthStart as IST midnight (e.g. shift now by +5:30, truncate, shift back) in overview and support. For the raw SQL month/day buckets use the corrected `AT TIME ZONE 'UTC' AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata'` double conversion before truncating.
W1-009.reproPlan: Read-only: find any row with a UTC timestamp between 18:30 and 24:00 (e.g. an OutboundEmail.sentAt) and compare the rendered date in admin with its IST date.
W1-009.gateOrTest: Unit test on formatDisplayDate for an 18:45-UTC instant asserting the IST date; visual-suite masking unaffected.

W1-010.title: Visit, SearchLog and ContentView — the identifiable presence telemetry — have no retention window and grow unbounded, while analytics runs full-table scans over them on every load
W1-010.expected: Every personal-data table has an expiry (the retention module's stated principle: "personal data stops accumulating forever"), and analytics queries stay bounded as data grows toward 2,000 users.
W1-010.actual: KEEP_DAYS (retention.ts:23-40) covers adminMessages, reports, contributions, notifications, security logs and outboundEmails — but not Visit, SearchLog or ContentView, the per-person, identifiable tables added 2026-08-19 (after the retention decisions were recorded). prune.mjs only prunes notifications. At 2,000 members these grow on the order of hundreds of thousands of rows a year (one Visit row per session, one SearchLog row per search), and the Faces/Compare analytics views run raw full-table scans with joins and `mode() WITHIN GROUP` over ALL of them with no time bound (loadFaces heartsGiven/loyal/longest/deepest at 609-684; loadMemberMetrics CTE at 939-1017 — its own comment concedes "the moment that stops being true, this becomes a materialised table"). Result: a privacy-posture gap now, and admin analytics pages that degrade toward multi-second loads within a year at target scale.
W1-010.evidence: retention.ts KEEP_DAYS object lists exactly six keys, none of them Visit/SearchLog/ContentView; grep across src+scripts finds no visit.deleteMany/searchLog.deleteMany/contentView.deleteMany outside generated client docs. loadFaces: `FROM "Visit" v JOIN "User" u ... GROUP BY u."name"` with no WHERE clause on four of its eight queries.
W1-010.fixDirection: Add Visit/SearchLog/ContentView windows to KEEP_DAYS (the analytics reads need at most 90 days for rhythm/arrivals and 30 for presence; Faces' all-time superlatives should either accept a 1-year window or read MetricSnapshot) and extend runRetentionSweep with the three deleteMany steps. Record the windows in docs/SECURITY.md's retention table first, per the module's own rule.
W1-010.reproPlan: code-argument-only; row-count arithmetic and the absent deleteMany calls are the whole proof.
W1-010.gateOrTest: Extend whatever asserts the retention table's coverage (or add a unit test enumerating KEEP_DAYS against the schema's telemetry models).

W1-011.title: adminSetRole's last-admin check is a read-then-write outside the transaction: two concurrent demotions can still leave zero admins
W1-011.expected: The "never remove the last admin" invariant holds under concurrency.
W1-011.actual: With two admins, if each demotes the other at the same time, both `prisma.user.count({ where: { role: "admin" } })` reads return 2, both pass the `admins <= 1` check, and both updates run — zero admins. TOCTOU: the check (216-225) and the update (227) are separate statements with no transaction or conditional write.
W1-011.evidence: `const admins = await prisma.user.count({ where: { role: "admin" } }); ... if (target?.role === "admin" && admins <= 1) { return ... } await prisma.user.update({ where: { id: userId }, data: { role } });` — nothing serializes the two demotions. Recovery does exist (`node scripts/dev/set-password.mjs <email> --admin`, documented in auth.ts:303-314), which caps the severity.
W1-011.fixDirection: Make the demotion conditional in one statement, e.g. a raw `UPDATE "User" SET role='member' WHERE id=$1 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM "User" WHERE role='admin') > 1` via $queryRaw, or wrap count+update in a serializable transaction / take an advisory-free approach with `updateMany({ where: { id, role: "admin" } })` plus a post-update count that restores on zero.
W1-011.reproPlan: code-argument-only (requires two live admin sessions racing on production).
W1-011.gateOrTest: Unit test simulating interleaved demotions against a two-admin fixture.

W1-012.title: adminUpdatePlaces and the member's own updateUserPlaces are identical wipe-and-recreate transactions with no unique constraint: a concurrent save doubles the member's places
W1-012.expected: Two surfaces editing one member's cities (admin fixing them while the member edits their own settings — the exact two-surfaces-one-row case the audit brief names) converge on one coherent set.
W1-012.actual: Both run `$transaction([ userPlace.deleteMany({where:{userId}}), ...creates, user.update(currentCity) ])`. Under READ COMMITTED, B's deleteMany snapshot cannot see rows A creates after B's delete begins, so interleaved saves commit BOTH sets: duplicate rows, two rows at position 0, doubled map pins, and currentCity from whichever committed last. UserPlace has no @@unique([userId, position]) (schema 659-677 shows only indexes) to make the second insert fail instead.
W1-012.evidence: people/actions.ts:150-169 and settings/actions.ts:162-181 are byte-for-byte the same transaction shape; schema UserPlace model: `@@index([userId])`, `@@index([city])`, no unique.
W1-012.fixDirection: Add `@@unique([userId, position])` (idempotent manual migration) so the loser's transaction aborts cleanly and the client retries; or make both writers upsert against that key. The window is narrow but the constraint also documents the invariant.
W1-012.reproPlan: code-argument-only (would need two racing sessions writing a real member's places).
W1-012.gateOrTest: Schema assertion in a unit test that UserPlace carries the unique; write-path-reviewer on both actions.

W1-013.title: purgeUserAccount collects image URLs before the delete transaction: anything the member uploads in between is cascaded away as rows but its R2 bytes are never collected — orphaned unfindably
W1-013.expected: Everything the deleted member's rows pointed at is enumerated for byte deletion (the delete-vs-post-create race the brief names).
W1-013.actual: `const urls = await collectImageUrls(userId);` runs, then the transaction deletes and cascades. A post, Collection photo or avatar change landing between the two (an admin deleting a member who is mid-session uploading) has its rows cascade-deleted while its R2 objects were never in `urls` — publicly fetchable forever with nothing left to find them by, the exact H9 failure mode reintroduced through a window of a few hundred milliseconds.
W1-013.evidence: account-purge.ts:88-102: collect at line 89, `prisma.$transaction([...user.delete...])` at 99-102, with no re-collection or upload freeze in between; nothing bumps credentialVersion before collecting, so the member's session is fully live during the window.
W1-013.fixDirection: Narrow the window: bump credentialVersion (ending their sessions) FIRST, then collect, then delete — an in-flight upload can still slip through, so alternatively collect inside the transaction (reads see a consistent snapshot) or re-collect-and-diff after commit while the Photo/Post rows are gone (requires collecting keys from R2 by ownerPrefix `avatars/<id>/`, `uploads/<id>/`, `collection/<id>/` instead of from rows — prefix listing survives the cascade and is the robust fix).
W1-013.gateOrTest: Unit test on ordering (session-revocation before collection), or switch to prefix-based enumeration and pin that.

W1-014.title: retryMail accepts rows in status 'sending': a stale failed-list plus an impatient second retry can double-send a real email
W1-014.expected: Retry applies only to rows that are actually dead (status failed), matching what the UI offers it for.
W1-014.actual: The guard is `if (row.status === "sent") return { error }` — 'queued' and 'sending' pass. Sequence: admin retries a failed row (now queued), a drain claims it (sending, mid-Resend-call), the admin's still-stale page shows Try again and they click again — retryMail resets it to `{ status: "queued", attempts: 0, claimedAt: null }` while the in-flight claimAndSend later completes its send and its bookkeeping; the next drain sends the SAME message a second time. claimAndSend's conditional claim (email-queue.ts:160-164) protects queued->sending, but nothing protects a sending row from being force-reset underneath it.
W1-014.evidence: mail/actions.ts:28-38: findUnique status, reject only "sent", then unconditional update to queued. The row read and the reset are also a read-then-write pair.
W1-014.fixDirection: Use a conditional write: `updateMany({ where: { id, status: "failed" }, data: {...} })` and return "Only a message that gave up can be retried" on count 0 — the same shape dismissMail already half-follows and claimAndSend fully follows.
W1-014.reproPlan: code-argument-only (a live proof emails a real member twice).

W1-022.title: People 'Show more' silently ends when the cursor row was deleted: the rest of the list becomes unreachable until reload
W1-022.expected: Pagination survives a row deletion mid-scroll (the taxonomy's "cursor at deleted row" case), since this very surface is where admins delete users.
W1-022.actual: loadPeoplePage paginates with `cursor: { id: cursor }, skip: 1`; Prisma's documented behavior when the cursor row no longer exists is to return no results. If the last row of the loaded page is deleted (by this admin in another tab, or another admin) before "Show more" is clicked, the action returns `{ rows: [], nextCursor: null }`, the button disappears, and everyone after that point is silently unreachable until a full reload — no error, no retry.
W1-022.evidence: admin-people-query.ts:60-66: `...(cursor ? { cursor: { id: cursor }, skip: 1 } : {})`; people-list.tsx:104-117: showMore sets `setCursor(result.nextCursor)` (null) and renders nothing when rows are empty-appended.
W1-022.fixDirection: Switch to a value cursor instead of a row cursor: the sort is (createdAt desc, id desc), so pass the last row's createdAt+id and use a WHERE tuple comparison (`OR [createdAt lt X, {createdAt: X, id: {lt}}]`) which needs no existing row — the loadPosts keyset pattern this file cites. Alternatively detect the empty-with-cursor case and retry from the previous surviving row.
W1-022.reproPlan: code-argument-only (deleting a user on production to prove pagination is not acceptable).
W1-022.gateOrTest: Unit test: page 1 of fixtures, delete the boundary row, assert page 2 still returns the remainder.

W1-023.title: Server-rendered dates show the UTC calendar day, not IST: every date between midnight and 05:30 IST renders one day early
W1-023.expected: A letter posted at 00:30 IST on 15 July shows "15 July" everywhere; all absolute dates agree across surfaces for the IST-based membership.
W1-023.actual: Server components format dates with the server's timezone (UTC on Vercel). Any timestamp between 18:30 and 23:59 UTC — i.e. anything a member does between midnight and 05:30 IST, a prime posting window — renders as the previous day on every server-rendered surface. Worse, the SAME timestamp renders differently on different surfaces: post-card.tsx and collection-client.tsx are "use client" (browser = IST, correct day) while the letters index, the letter reader byline, and the admin tables are server components (UTC, wrong day), so one letter can show "14 Jul" in the letters index and "15 Jul" on the feed card simultaneously.
W1-023.evidence: src/lib/utils.ts:151-157: `export function formatDisplayDate(date: Date | string): string { return new Date(date).toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { day: "numeric", month: "short", year: "numeric" }) }` — no `timeZone` option, so it resolves to the runtime's zone. Called from server components: letters/page.tsx:163 `metaLine(batchLine(l.author), formatDisplayDate(l.createdAt))`, letters/[id]/page.tsx:188 `date={formatDisplayDate(letter.createdAt)}`, admin/support/page.tsx:222, admin/catchups/page.tsx:136-138, admin/people/person-detail.tsx (multiple). The letter reader also inline-formats server-side at letters/[id]/page.tsx:165-169: `new Date(letter.createdAt).toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { day: "numeric", month: "long", year: "numeric" })` — again no timeZone. Meanwhile src/components/posts/post-card.tsx:1 is `"use client"` and calls `formatDisplayDate(post.createdAt)` at line 108 in the browser (IST for members), proving the cross-surface disagreement. `formatTimeAgo`'s >4-week fallback (utils.ts:21) has the same gap but runs client-side in the bell, so it is mostly unaffected. Vercel servers run UTC; members are IST (+5:30) — the brief's exact 6h class.
W1-023.fixDirection: Add `timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata"` to formatDisplayDate and to the inline toLocaleDateString calls in server components (letters/[id]/page.tsx:165, and audit every server-side toLocaleDateString/toLocaleString in src/app and src/components without a "use client" directive). The site's audience is IST by definition (same rule wordle.ts:18-21 already applies with `istDateKey` using `timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata"` — follow that precedent). Alternatively move date formatting into client components, but the one-line timeZone option is smaller and keeps RSC rendering.
W1-023.gateOrTest: New unit test beside the existing 14 (npm run check): assert formatDisplayDate(new Date("2026-07-14T19:00:00Z")) === "15 Jul 2026" (19:00 UTC = 00:30 IST next day). It fails today, passes after the fix.
W1-023.reproPlan: Read-only: in chrome-devtools, load /letters signed in and evaluate the rendered byline for any letter whose createdAt falls in the 18:30-24:00 UTC window (query not needed — compare the same letter's date on /feed vs /letters).

W1-024.title: NotificationBell: three unguarded server-action awaits — a single transient failure permanently kills infinite scroll, makes notification clicks silently do nothing, or wedges "Loading..."
W1-024.expected: A failed fetch of the next notifications page retries on the next scroll; clicking a notification always navigates to its target; a failed first-page load shows something actionable.
W1-024.actual: (1) handleLoadMore sets loadingMoreRef.current = true, awaits getNotifications, and only resets the flag on the success path — no try/finally. One rejection (flaky mobile network, DB hiccup) leaves the flag true forever: every later sentinel intersection returns at the `if (loadingMoreRef.current || !hasMore) return;` guard, the skeleton shimmer row stays visible, and the list can never load more until a full page reload. (2) handleClickNotification does `await markNotificationRead(notif.id)` BEFORE `router.push(notif.link)`; if the action rejects, the push never runs — the member taps a notification and nothing happens, no toast, just an unhandled rejection in the console. This rejection is not only network: `prisma.notification.update({ where: { id, userId } })` (actions.ts:77-80) throws P2025 when the row is gone — e.g. a tab holding rows past position 100 while another first-page open ran the KEEP=100 prune (actions.ts:44-57 deletes everything older than the 100th-newest). Even on success, navigation is serialized behind a full server-action round trip to Mumbai, so every notification tap pays extra latency for a bookkeeping write. (3) handleOpen has no catch: a rejection leaves loaded=false and the panel shows "Loading..." until closed and reopened.
W1-024.evidence: notification-bell.tsx:147-158: `async function handleLoadMore() { if (loadingMoreRef.current || !hasMore) return; loadingMoreRef.current = true; const data = await getNotifications({ cursor: nextCursor }); ... loadingMoreRef.current = false; }` — the reset is unreachable on throw. Lines 160-171: `if (!notif.read) { await markNotificationRead(notif.id); ... } if (notif.link) { router.push(notif.link); }`. Lines 134-145 handleOpen: `const data = await getNotifications(); setNotifications(...); setLoaded(true);` with `void handleOpen()` at line 121 — rejection is unhandled. actions.ts:77-80: `await prisma.notification.update({ where: { id: notificationId, userId: session.user.id }, data: { read: true } })` — Prisma update throws P2025 on zero matching rows; there is no P2002/P2025 handling anywhere in the file.
W1-024.fixDirection: handleLoadMore: wrap in try/finally so loadingMoreRef always resets. handleClickNotification: navigate first (or in parallel) and mark-read optimistically — `router.push` should not be gated on the write; catch the action failure and revert the optimistic decrement (or just toast). markNotificationRead server-side: use updateMany (no-throw on zero rows) instead of update, keeping the userId scope. handleOpen: catch, and render a small "Couldn't load — tap to retry" row instead of eternal "Loading...".
W1-024.gateOrTest: Unit test for the actions file: markNotificationRead with a non-existent id resolves (updateMany) rather than throwing. For the client, a component test simulating a rejected getNotifications and asserting a second load attempt still fires is the pin; at minimum the try/finally is trivially inspectable in /check's tsc pass.
W1-024.reproPlan: Read-only-ish: in chrome-devtools, open the bell, use network emulation (offline) mid-scroll of the panel, restore network, observe the sentinel shimmer never resolves; click an unread notification while offline and observe no navigation and no error surface.

W1-025.title: Unread badge can only ever fall, never rise: initialUnreadCount is captured once into state with no prop re-sync, making the bell's shake-on-new-notification animation unreachable dead code and the badge stale for the whole session
W1-025.expected: The bell badge reflects arriving notifications during a session (the shake effect at lines 109-115 exists specifically to fire "when the unread count RISES"), and the count shown after navigation matches what the member just did in the panel.
W1-025.actual: `const [unreadCount, setUnreadCount] = useState(initialUnreadCount)` (line 98) never re-syncs when the prop later changes, and the only setUnreadCount calls are `Math.max(0, c - 1)` (line 166) and `setUnreadCount(0)` (line 176) — both decrements. So within any mounted bell instance the count monotonically falls: (a) notifications arriving during a session never surface on the badge (the header-variant dot at line 205 renders only when unreadCount > 0, so a member browsing all day sees no indicator at all until a hard reload, even though opening the panel would show unread rows); (b) the shake effect (lines 109-115, `if (unreadCount > prevUnread.current) setShakeKey(...)`) can never fire — confirmed dead code, which is strong evidence the prop was expected to flow through; (c) two bell instances don't share state: on mobile, mark-all-read in /feed's header bell (its own instance) then navigating to /letters mounts the sidebar band bell fresh from the Sidebar's `unreadCount` prop (sidebar.tsx:740), which is whatever the (main) layout last rendered — under App Router partial rendering the shared layout is not re-executed on soft navigation, so the cleared badge can resurrect with the pre-read count until a refetch that includes the layout happens.
W1-025.evidence: notification-bell.tsx:97-98: `const [notifications, setNotifications] = useState<Notification[]>([]); const [unreadCount, setUnreadCount] = useState(initialUnreadCount);` — no useEffect or render-adjust syncing from initialUnreadCount afterwards. Lines 109-115: `useEffect(() => { if (unreadCount > prevUnread.current) { setShakeKey((k) => k + 1); } prevUnread.current = unreadCount; }, [unreadCount]);` — grep confirms setUnreadCount appears only at lines 166 (`setUnreadCount((c) => Math.max(0, c - 1))`) and 176 (`setUnreadCount(0)`); nothing ever increases it. handleOpen (134-145) refreshes the LIST every open but never recomputes unreadCount from the fresh data, so badge and list visibly disagree after another device/tab reads or receives notifications. markAllNotificationsRead's `revalidatePath("/")` (actions.ts:95) targets only the root page path, not the layout, so it does not push a corrected count either.
W1-025.fixDirection: Three coordinated small changes: (1) sync state to the prop with the sanctioned adjust-during-render pattern (track prevInitial; when initialUnreadCount changes, setUnreadCount to it) — this also resurrects the shake; (2) have getNotifications return the fresh unread total and set it in handleOpen so badge and list always agree; (3) use `revalidatePath("/", "layout")` (or a targeted tag) in the two mark-read actions so the layout's count refetches. A later polling/refresh mechanism is optional; these three make the existing plumbing self-consistent.
W1-025.gateOrTest: The tour-provider-style .test.mjs harness can pin the pure part: extracting the shake-decision into a function tested for the rising case. Live pin: e2e spec asserting the badge equals the panel's unread rows after open.
W1-025.reproPlan: Live: sign in as admin in chrome-devtools with 0 unread; from a second session trigger a like on the admin's post; navigate between pages in tab 1 — badge stays absent; open the panel — unread row is there, badge still absent. Mobile-width repro of the resurrection: mark all read via /feed header bell, navigate to /letters, read the band bell badge.

W1-026.title: Fire-and-forget DB writes in server components without after(): recordView (4 pages) and logSearch (feed) can be killed by serverless suspend, silently losing the analytics they exist to record
W1-026.expected: View counters and search logs are recorded reliably — either awaited off the critical path or scheduled via after()/waitUntil, the pattern this codebase itself already established (drainMailQueue runs inside after() in (main)/layout.tsx:63 precisely because "it must run AFTER the response"; touchLastSeen is awaited inside the layout's Promise.all).
W1-026.actual: `void recordView(session.user.id, "letter", letter.id)` (letters/[id]/page.tsx:85, and the same shape at collection/[id]/page.tsx:58, profile/[id]/page.tsx:117, catchups/round/[editionId]/page.tsx:194) and `void logSearch({ scope: "feed", query: q, userId })` (feed/page.tsx:31) detach a Postgres round trip from the render. On Vercel the function may be suspended as soon as the response finishes streaming; a detached promise that has not yet resolved is not guaranteed to run. The writes therefore succeed or vanish depending on timing — the owner's "most viewed" analytics and search log undercount non-deterministically, and because recordView/logSearch swallow errors in production (content-view.ts:34-38, search-log.ts) there is no signal it is happening.
W1-026.evidence: letters/[id]/page.tsx:85: `void recordView(session.user.id, "letter", letter.id);` — inside the RSC render, no after(). content-view.ts:28-33 shows it is a real network write: `await prisma.contentView.upsert({...})`. feed/page.tsx:29-31: `if (q) { const s = await auth(); void logSearch({ scope: "feed", query: q, userId: s?.user?.id }); }`. Contrast with the codebase's own correct pattern, (main)/layout.tsx:63-69: `after(async () => { try { await drainMailQueue(); } catch (err) {...} });` with the comment explaining post-response work must use after(). The four recordView call sites and the feed logSearch call are the only detached DB writes in server components (grep verified).
W1-026.fixDirection: Wrap each in `after(() => recordView(...))` / `after(() => logSearch(...))` (import from next/server, already used in the same tree), preserving the never-throws contract inside. Do not await them serially in render — the point of the current shape (not delaying the page) is right; only the scheduling primitive is wrong.
W1-026.gateOrTest: grep-style regression check in the security-regressions/unit test suite: assert no `void recordView(`/`void logSearch(` outside an after() callback (a simple source scan test in the existing .mjs test pattern).
W1-026.reproPlan: code-argument-only (the loss is a serverless-runtime timing property; locally the dev server never suspends, so it cannot be demonstrated read-only).

W1-027.title: One error boundary for the whole app: any thrown error in any (main) widget or page unmounts the entire shell (sidebar, nav, bell) into a bare full-screen error; no route-group error.tsx, no global-error.tsx
W1-027.expected: An error in one page or one widget (e.g. FeedRail's query failing) degrades that region: the shell and navigation survive, and the member can move to another page. The taxonomy's question — "one thrown error in a widget: does the whole shell die?" — should answer no.
W1-027.actual: find over src/app returns exactly one error boundary: src/app/error.tsx. There is no error.tsx in (main), (auth), admin, or any nested segment, and there are no <ErrorBoundary>-style client boundaries around widgets (FeedRail, the notification panel, etc.). So a render-time throw anywhere under (main) — a page's Prisma query rejecting after the shell streamed, a widget's bad data — replaces EVERYTHING including the sidebar with the root boundary's full-screen `min-h-screen` card (error.tsx:16). The member loses navigation entirely; their only affordance is "Try again" re-running the same failing tree. Separately, there is no global-error.tsx, so an error thrown by the root layout itself falls through to Next's unstyled default page (low likelihood today — the root layout only awaits getThemeCookie — but zero-cost to cover).
W1-027.evidence: find output (verified): error boundaries = `src/app/error.tsx` only, against ~46 (main) pages. error.tsx:16: `<div className="flex min-h-screen flex-col items-center justify-center bg-background px-4 text-center">` — a viewport-filling replacement, no shell. (main)/layout.tsx:35-41 throws to this same boundary if the notification count query rejects (DB down), which is acceptable for a layout-level failure, but page-level failures (e.g. letters/[id] canViewCityScope query rejecting at line 106 of that page) take the shell down with them for no reason.
W1-027.fixDirection: Add src/app/(main)/error.tsx rendering the same copy inside the content column — because it sits below (main)/layout.tsx, the AppShell/sidebar stay mounted and the member keeps navigation. Optionally one more in admin. Add a minimal global-error.tsx (own <html><body>) for root-layout failures. Widget-level boundaries (FeedRail) are a nice-to-have after that.
W1-027.gateOrTest: e2e: a lab-only route that throws on demand, asserting `aside` (the sidebar rail) is still present when the error card shows. Simpler pin: the lab registry audit could assert (main)/error.tsx exists.
W1-027.reproPlan: Live-safe: temporarily unreachable read-only — instead verify by navigating to a route and using next-devtools get_errors after inducing a client-side throw in a widget via evaluate_script (React DevTools error injection); or accept the structural argument (single boundary file is a fact of the tree).

W1-028.title: Five async DB-backed routes ship no loading.tsx, so navigating to them gives zero feedback for the full auth+DB round trip — including the letter reader, the app's core reading surface
W1-028.expected: House rule (CLAUDE.md): "Any new async route ships a loading.tsx using the warm shimmer." Clicking a letter shows the shimmer immediately while the server renders.
W1-028.actual: find over src/app shows loading.tsx everywhere EXCEPT these async pages: letters/[id] (page runs auth + post.findUnique + optional groupMember.findUnique + canViewCityScope, all sequential — lines 66-106 — plus generateMetadata's own duplicate set), collection/[id] (auth + photo.findUnique in both generateMetadata and page), notice/[id] (auth + notification.findUnique), support (auth + contribution aggregates), admin/audit (prisma queries; every OTHER admin section has loading.tsx — audit is the one omission). W1-029.title: MascotFlightLayer: a second launch while a flight is live shares abortRef/rafRef/ranId with the first — the first flight's failsafe then aborts and unmounts the second mid-air, deleting the bird in front of the viewer
W1-029.expected: Launching a new flight cancels the previous one cleanly; only one runFlight loop ever drives the portal.
W1-029.actual: onLaunch → `setActive({ ...launch, id: Date.now() })` (line 203) remounts the Hoopoe (key change) and queues a new runFlight, but NOTHING cancels the previous runFlight: its rAF chain keeps stepping (it holds its own closure; the shared `rafRef` only tracks the newest frame id), and because the old rig was stopped at remount, its awaited rig verbs (`await api.perch()`, line 493) never settle — motion v12's .stop() never resolves .finished (documented in this very file's comments, lines 195-201). Flight 1 therefore hangs until ITS failsafe (line 292-297) fires, which sets the SHARED `abortRef.current = true`, cancels the SHARED rafRef (flight 2's current frame), calls signalHandoff, and `setActive(null)` — unmounting the portal while flight 2 is mid-cruise. The visible result is the second bird vanishing abruptly mid-air. Entry path: the landing's own double-click is guarded (`if (phase === "exiting") return`, landing-hero.tsx:211), but browser-Back to the landing during the first flight's 2.5s no-perch hover window (destination never mounted because the user backed out) and clicking the other CTA reproduces it within the 5.8s failsafe window.
W1-029.evidence: Line 203: `return onLaunch((launch) => setActive({ ...launch, id: Date.now() }));` — no cancellation of a live flight. Lines 258-261: `async function runFlight(api, flight) { if (ranId.current === flight.id) return; ranId.current = flight.id; abortRef.current = false;` — flight 2 resets the shared abort flag while flight 1 still reads it. Lines 292-297 (flight 1's failsafe, still armed): `abortRef.current = true; signalHandoff(); cancelAnimationFrame(rafRef.current); setActive(null);` — rafRef at that moment holds flight 2's frame id, and setActive(null) removes flight 2's portal. Flight 1's `finally` (573-577) also does `cancelAnimationFrame(rafRef.current)`.
W1-029.fixDirection: Give each runFlight its own abort token (the not-found.tsx flight-token pattern in the same codebase is the worked example) instead of the shared refs, and have the onLaunch handler cancel the current token before setActive; clear the previous failsafe on new launch. Alternatively, ignore launches while active is non-null (one flight at a time is already the bus's stated contract, mascot-flight.ts:15-18).
W1-029.gateOrTest: scripts/qa/hoopoe-landing-check.mjs already samples the flyer's transform per frame; extend it with a back-nav + second-CTA scenario asserting the [data-mascot-flyer] element survives to handoff.
W1-029.reproPlan: Live: chrome-devtools on the landing at desktop width — click Sign in, immediately history.back(), click Join within ~3s, watch the second bird vanish when the first flight's 5.8s failsafe fires.

W1-032.title: ImageViewer's Download button silently degrades to open-in-new-tab in production because the R2 public host fetch is cross-origin and bucket CORS was never configured
W1-032.expected: "Download photo" saves the file, on the deployment members actually use.

Project memory records the R2 bucket CORS configuration as blocked/never applied (the presign work hit the same wall). Without it, fetch rejects every time and the catch (line 192-194) falls back to `window.open(current.src, "_blank", "noopener,noreferrer")` — a new tab showing the image, which on iOS Safari especially is a confusing dead-end compared to a save. In local dev images are same-origin (/uploads), so the button works there and the degradation is invisible to development. Note also that even the anchor-download fallback path cannot work cross-origin (the download attribute is ignored for cross-origin URLs), so the new-tab behavior is total in prod until CORS is set.
W1-032.evidence: image-viewer.tsx:180-195: `async function download() { ... try { const res = await fetch(current.src); const blob = await res.blob(); ... a.download = name; a.click(); ... } catch { window.open(current.src, "_blank", "noopener,noreferrer"); } }`. Suspected (not confirmed) because bucket CORS state is infrastructure, not code.
W1-032.fixDirection: Either configure R2 bucket CORS to allow GET from the site origin (also unblocks the tracked presign-upload work), or proxy the download through a small same-origin route (`/api/media/download?key=` streaming from R2 with Content-Disposition: attachment), which additionally fixes the filename and avoids exposing the r2.dev host. The in-code fallback is fine to keep.
W1-032.gateOrTest: After fix: an e2e step on the production URL clicking Download and asserting a download event rather than a popup (or a curl check that the pub URL answers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin).
W1-032.reproPlan: Live read-only on production: open any photo in the viewer, click Download, watch DevTools network for the CORS-failed fetch followed by the new tab.

W1-034.title: Email is stored and looked up with raw case at signup/login while the reset flow lowercases: mixed-case signups get false 'Invalid email or password' at login, can NEVER receive a password-reset mail, and one mailbox can register twice
W1-034.expected: One canonical form of an email address across signup, login, reset and duplicate-detection, so foo@x.com, Foo@x.com and 'Foo@x.com ' are the same account everywhere (orchestrator seed S-A1).
W1-034.actual: Signup stores the address exactly as typed (signupSchema: `email: z.email("Please enter a valid email")` — zod v4 z.email() validates format only, no trim/lowercase; the create writes `email: parsed.data.email` verbatim; User.email is a plain case-sensitive `String @unique`). Login looks up the RAW submitted string: authorize() does `const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email } })` while only the rate-limit key is normalized (`const acctKey = email.trim().toLowerCase()`). The reset flow normalizes the OTHER way: requestPasswordReset does `const raw = ((formData.get("email") as string) ?? "").trim().toLowerCase()` then `prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: raw } })`. Three concrete member-facing failures follow. (1) A member who signed up as Foo@x.com and later types foo@x.com (or vice versa — phone autofill and contact cards routinely change case) gets 'Invalid email or password' forever, because the Postgres lookup is case-sensitive. (2) Any member whose stored email contains an uppercase letter can NEVER receive a reset mail: the lowercased lookup misses their row, `if (!user?.password) return { ok: true }` answers the standard success screen, and nothing ever arrives — a silent, permanent lockout with no error anywhere (the anti-oracle design makes the failure invisible by construction). (3) Duplicate registration: registerUser's existing-account check (`findUnique({ where: { email: parsed.data.email } })`) and the DB unique constraint are both case-sensitive, so Foo@x.com registers cleanly beside an existing foo@x.com — two accounts, one mailbox, both confirmable (verify links go to the same inbox). Secondary inconsistencies confirm the drift: LoginAttempt rows are lowercased (`input.email.trim().toLowerCase().slice(0, 200)`), roster matching lowercases (`where: { email: user.email.toLowerCase() }`), the human-pass HMAC lowercases (`email.toLowerCase()` in signHumanPass) — the auth lookups are the only case-sensitive ones left. The login input is a controlled component storing `e.target.value` raw; no client normalizes.
W1-034.evidence: src/lib/auth.ts:62 `const acctKey = email.trim().toLowerCase();` vs src/lib/auth.ts:102-104 `const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email }, });` — the same function normalizes for rate limiting but not for the account lookup. src/components/auth/email-actions.ts:160-166 `const raw = ((formData.get("email") as string) ?? "").trim().toLowerCase(); ... const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: raw }, ...})` — reset lookup is lowercase-only, so a stored 'Foo@x.com' can never match. src/components/auth/actions.ts:103-105 `const existing = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: parsed.data.email } });` and :149 `email: parsed.data.email,` — signup stores and dedupes raw. src/lib/validators.ts:18 `email: z.email("Please enter a valid email"),` — no transform, no max length. prisma/schema.prisma:13 `email String @unique` — case-sensitive text unique. src/lib/login-attempt.ts:49 `email: input.email.trim().toLowerCase().slice(0, 200)` — proves the codebase's own canonical form is trim+lowercase everywhere except the two auth lookups.
W1-034.reproPlan: Read-only SQL against the shared DB proves whether members are ALREADY affected: SELECT count(*) FROM "User" WHERE email <> lower(email); any nonzero count is a member who today cannot reset their password. A full live proof (register Foo@…, sign out, sign in as foo@…) writes a row, so use a throwaway test address and delete via the admin surface afterwards, or accept the code argument.
W1-034.fixDirection: Pick trim().toLowerCase() as the canonical form (the codebase already uses it in four places). Apply it (a) in signupSchema via z.email().trim().toLowerCase() or in registerUser before the existing-check and create; (b) in authorize() — look up by acctKey, which already exists; (c) leave requestPasswordReset as is; (d) add a max length (e.g. .max(200)) to the signup email to match displayEmail's cap. Then backfill: UPDATE "User" SET email = lower(email) WHERE email <> lower(email) — but FIRST check for case-variant duplicate pairs (SELECT lower(email) FROM "User" GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1) and merge those by hand before the update, or the unique constraint aborts the backfill. Also mirror the normalization in dev-login's lookup for tooling consistency.
W1-034.gateOrTest: Unit test in the -rule style: a signup/login/reset round-trip helper asserting all three paths resolve 'FoO@x.com ' to the same row; plus a security-regressions-style static check that no prisma.user lookup uses an unnormalized email. A Playwright spec pinning signup-then-relogin with changed case.

W1-035.title: Onboarding photo step posts the raw picked file (up to 15MB) through a server action; Vercel's ~4.5MB platform body cap kills typical phone photos with an opaque error at the first-run moment
W1-035.expected: A new member picking a normal phone photo (5–12MB is typical for modern phones) during the onboarding wizard has it uploaded, or is downscaled/cropped client-side first so the bytes on the wire fit — exactly what the profile page's avatar path and the feed's /api/upload path already do.
W1-035.actual: PhotoStep validates only `if (file.size > 15 * 1024 * 1024)` and then ships the original bytes straight into the updateAvatar server action: `const fd = new FormData(); fd.set("file", file); const result = await updateAvatar(fd);`. There is no crop dialog and no downscaleImage call on this path (AttachImageDialog explicitly has 'no opinion about size/format limits'). On Vercel, request bodies above ~4.5MB are rejected by the PLATFORM (413 FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE) before the function runs — the `serverActions: { bodySizeLimit: "25mb" }` in next.config.ts only lifts Next's own guard and cannot raise Vercel's cap. So any photo between ~4.5MB and 15MB passes every client check, then dies at the edge; the action never executes, the client's `result.error` handling never gets a structured error, and the member sees a generic failure on the very first flow they touch. The project has already diagnosed this exact hazard twice elsewhere: image-downscale.ts's header comment ('a route handler's request body is hard-capped at about 4.5MB... a normal phone photo (often 5 to 12MB) sailed past the client check and then died at Vercel's edge with an opaque failure') and letterhead-profile.tsx ('a 6MB phone photo could die on Vercel's ~4.5MB serverless body cap'), whose avatar path was fixed with a client-side crop that produces a small webp blob. The onboarding step reuses the same server action but never received the same client-side fix.
W1-035.evidence: src/components/onboarding/steps/photo-step.tsx:42-49 `if (file.size > 15 * 1024 * 1024) { toast.error("Photo must be under 15MB"); return; } setBusy(true); const fd = new FormData(); fd.set("file", file); const result = await updateAvatar(fd);` — raw file, no downscale, no crop. src/components/settings/actions.ts:20 `const MAX_AVATAR_INPUT = 15 * 1024 * 1024; // 15MB input` — the server-side cap promises 15MB but can never see more than ~4.5MB on Vercel. next.config.ts:111-112 `serverActions: { bodySizeLimit: "25mb" }` — configures Next, not the platform. src/components/profile/letterhead-profile.tsx:363-365 comment: 'the old path shipped the ORIGINAL bytes... a 6MB phone photo could die on Vercel's ~4.5MB serverless body cap' — the same team's own statement of the failure mode this step still has.
W1-035.reproPlan: Local dev won't reproduce (no platform cap); code-argument-only, or a one-off probe on a preview/prod deployment with a throwaway account and a 6MB JPEG at the onboarding photo step, observing the 413 in the network tab.
W1-035.fixDirection: Run the picked file through the existing downscaleImage() (2048px webp, already in src/lib/image-downscale.ts) before fd.set in PhotoStep — one import and one line — or route the step through the same crop dialog letterhead-profile uses. Optionally also lower MAX_AVATAR_INPUT/client caps to something the platform can actually carry (~4MB) so the error copy stops promising 15MB.
W1-035.gateOrTest: A unit test asserting PhotoStep's pick handler produces a payload under 4MB for an oversized input (jsdom + a stubbed downscale), or at minimum a grep-style regression test that every `fd.set("file", ...)` call site references downscaleImage or a crop dialog.

W1-036.title: Auth is fail-closed on every Cloudflare failure except the narrowest one: a missing Turnstile token is always refused, so a blocked/failed widget script (or a Cloudflare outage, or siteverify answering 200 {success:false,'internal-error'}) locks members out of sign-in, signup and reset — and the widget's own comment believes the opposite
W1-036.expected: The stated posture (turnstile.ts header: 'a bot check that takes sign-in down with it whenever a third party blinks would be a worse bug than the bots') — a Cloudflare failure degrades to open, and the two files agree on what happens when the widget cannot produce a token.
W1-036.actual: The fail-open branch only covers the case where a token EXISTS but the siteverify fetch throws/times out (turnstile.ts:102-105). Two other Cloudflare failure modes fail closed. (1) No token: turnstile.ts:86 `if (!token) return false;`. The widget produces null whenever the challenge script cannot load or errors (`s.onerror`/`error-callback` set dead=true; getToken 12s timeout resolves null) — which is what happens under an ad/privacy blocker, a corporate proxy that blocks challenges.cloudflare.com, or a Cloudflare outage (the widget network being down is the COMMON outage shape; siteverify-reachable-but-widget-down and vice versa rarely split). The login/signup/forgot clients then submit without a token and authorize()/verifyHumanFromForm refuse with the bot-check error. For a member whose network blocks the script this is permanent: they can never sign in, sign up, or request a reset, and the human-pass cookie cannot help (it is only minted by signup/reset, which are themselves behind the same wall). (2) siteverify reachable but degraded: Cloudflare returns HTTP 200 with `{"success": false, "error-codes": ["internal-error"]}` during partial outages (their docs say to retry it); turnstile.ts:100-101 `const data = (await res.json())...; return data.success === true;` treats that as a forged token and refuses. The contradiction is documented in the code itself: turnstile-widget.tsx:18-21 claims 'the form submits without a token: the server is the judge anyway, and its own posture... matches — a broken third party never bricks sign-in', while turnstile.ts:19 says 'A request with NO token is refused in both environments alike.' One of the two beliefs is wrong, and the shipped behavior is the fail-closed one.
W1-036.evidence: src/lib/turnstile.ts:86 `if (!token) return false;` (unconditional). src/lib/turnstile.ts:100-101 `const data = (await res.json()) as { success?: boolean }; return data.success === true;` — no res.ok check, no error-codes handling, so 'internal-error' (Cloudflare's own transient-failure signal, delivered as HTTP 200) reads as a bot. src/components/auth/turnstile-widget.tsx:18-21 comment: 'If the script cannot load or the challenge errors, getToken() settles to null and the form submits without a token: the server is the judge anyway, and its own posture (refuse a bad token, fail open only when Cloudflare itself is down) matches — a broken third party never bricks sign-in.' — the server does not match. src/components/auth/turnstile-widget.tsx:107-110 `"error-callback": () => { dead.current = true; waiters.current.splice(0).forEach((w) => w(null)); }` — every widget failure funnels to a null token.
W1-036.reproPlan: Locally: block challenges.cloudflare.com in DevTools network conditions on a TURNSTILE_DEV_REAL=1 dev server (or read-only argue from code, since dev pins the always-pass test key); the widget errors, getToken resolves null, and sign-in answers the bot-check refusal. No production write needed.
W1-036.fixDirection: Decide the posture deliberately and make the files agree. If availability wins (the stated intent): treat a missing token as fail-open WHEN the account-level protections still stand (rate limits still count, password still checked) — e.g. accept token-less requests but consume rate-limit budget, or retry/pass on siteverify 'internal-error' codes. If security wins: fix the widget comment, and give the member an actionable error ('our human-check service could not load; disable content blockers or try later') instead of the generic bot-check sentence. At minimum, handle the documented 'internal-error' code as retry/fail-open in verifyTurnstile.
W1-036.gateOrTest: Unit test on verifyTurnstile with a mocked fetch returning 200 {success:false,'error-codes':['internal-error']} pinning the chosen posture; a second test for the null-token path documenting the decision.

W1-037.title: recordLoginAttempt (and the AuthToken expiry sweep) are fire-and-forget prisma writes with no after()/waitUntil, so on Vercel the insert races the lambda freeze and the sign-in analytics the owner will lean on at launch are silently lossy
W1-037.expected: Work that must survive the response on serverless is wrapped in after()/waitUntil (the codebase already knows this: requestPasswordReset's enqueue was moved into after() as audit L3, and the consume() calls in authorize are explicitly 'Awaited so a serverless instance cannot freeze before the count lands').
W1-037.actual: recordLoginAttempt fires `void prisma.loginAttempt.create({...}).catch(...)` and returns void by design ('Deliberately not awaited... A statistics row must never be able to delay, or fail, a sign-in'). On Vercel, once authorize() returns/throws and NextAuth sends the response, the instance freezes; an in-flight insert may complete only if the instance thaws for a later request, or never if it is reaped. The rate-limited and bot-check branches are worst: `recordLoginAttempt({ email, ok: false, reason: "rate-limited" }); throw new RateLimitedLogin();` — the throw ends the request in the same tick the insert starts. These rows are the entire data source for the admin analytics 'who cannot sign in' panel, which the code's own comments call 'the one place the owner would ever notice somebody locked out who should not be' — under launch load that panel will silently undercount by whatever fraction of inserts lose the race, which is undetectable from inside the product. Same class, same file family: mintToken's opportunistic sweep `void prisma.authToken.deleteMany({ where: { expiresAt: { lt: ... } } }).catch(...)` — minting runs inside the mail drain's after() callback, which awaits drainMailQueue but not this orphan promise, so the sweep's completion also races the freeze; since it is the ONLY cleanup for AuthToken ('a project that has no cron' — note retention.ts sweeps LoginAttempt/AuditLog/OutboundEmail but NOT AuthToken), dead token rows will mostly accumulate in production (small rows, slow growth — a hygiene failure rather than a scale one at 2,000 users).
W1-037.evidence: src/lib/login-attempt.ts:46-54 `void prisma.loginAttempt.create({ data: {...} }).catch((err) => {...})` — no await, no after(). src/lib/auth.ts:72-74 `if (!ipOk || !acctOk) { recordLoginAttempt({ email, ok: false, reason: "rate-limited" }); throw new RateLimitedLogin(); }` — insert launched and abandoned in the same statement as the throw. Contrast src/lib/auth.ts:96-98 'Awaited so a serverless instance cannot freeze before the count lands' — the adjacent rate-limit spend acknowledges the exact failure mode this write is exposed to. src/lib/auth-tokens.ts:107-118 `void prisma.authToken.deleteMany({ where: { expiresAt: { lt: new Date(Date.now() - 7 * 24 * 60 * 60_000) } } }).catch(...)` — same fire-and-forget; src/lib/retention.ts KEEP_DAYS covers loginAttempts/auditLogs/outboundEmails but has no AuthToken step.
W1-037.reproPlan: Code-argument-only (freeze behavior is a platform property; local dev keeps the process alive and will always show the row landing). A production-side read-only check after launch week: compare LoginAttempt counts against Vercel request logs for /api/auth/callback/credentials.
W1-037.fixDirection: In recordLoginAttempt, attempt `after(() => prisma.loginAttempt.create(...))` (authorize runs inside the NextAuth route handler's request scope, so after() is available; keep the current void-promise as the fallback for non-request contexts, mirroring scheduleDrain's try/catch pattern in email-queue.ts:364-377). Alternatively await the insert behind a short timeout — a single ~10ms insert cannot meaningfully delay sign-in and the .catch already protects the return value. For the AuthToken sweep: either await it inside mintToken (it already runs post-response inside the drain's after()), or add an authToken step to runRetentionSweep, which is the project's real home for table hygiene.
W1-037.gateOrTest: The security-regressions/gate-coverage test family: a static check that `void prisma.` never appears outside an after() wrapper, or a unit test on recordLoginAttempt asserting it registers with after() when a request scope exists.

W1-038.title: joinBatchGroup is find-then-create with no unique constraint on Group.name: two same-batch alumni signing up concurrently create two 'Batch of {year}' groups, silently splitting the batch for group-scoped posts and Catch-ups
W1-038.expected: Exactly one 'Batch of {year}' group per batch, however many members of that batch register simultaneously — per the taxonomy, an 'only one per X' rule is real only if a DB unique constraint enforces it (6c/6d check-then-insert TOCTOU).
W1-038.actual: registerUser → joinBatchGroup does `let group = await prisma.group.findFirst({ where: { name } }); if (!group) { group = await prisma.group.create({...}) }`. Group.name is `name String` with no @@unique, so two concurrent registrations from one batch (the launch-day scenario the mail queue was explicitly built for: 'more than 100 signups on the first day') can both read 'no group' and both create one — permanently duplicating the batch container with nothing to stop it and nothing to detect it. The code's own comment concedes the gap ('Group.name is not unique in the schema, so match by exact name'). Groups are retired as UI but remain load-bearing: group membership gates post visibility (feed actions read `prisma.groupMember.findMany({ where: { userId } })` and filter posts by `OR: [{ groupId: null }, { groupId: { in: groupIds } }]`) and Catch-ups hang off Group rows (Catchup has a 1:1 `catchup Catchup?` relation on Group). With a split batch, members auto-joined to duplicate A cannot see group posts or batch Catch-ups attached to duplicate B, and later members from the same batch land in whichever duplicate findFirst returns first (no orderBy, so it is not even deterministic which one accretes members). There is no admin surface for merging groups, so the split is permanent without SQL.
W1-038.evidence: src/components/auth/actions.ts:215-230 `let group = await prisma.group.findFirst({ where: { name }, select: { id: true } }); if (!group) { group = await prisma.group.create({ data: { name, ... } }) }` — classic read-then-create race. prisma/schema.prisma:191-208 Group model: `name String` with only `@@index([visibility, createdAt])`, no unique on name. src/app/(main)/feed/actions.ts:955-972 membership-derived `groupIds` gating `OR: [{ groupId: null }, { groupId: { in: groupIds } }]` — the concrete surface where a member in the wrong duplicate loses visibility.
W1-038.reproPlan: Code-argument-only for the race itself (a live proof needs two concurrent real signups against the shared production DB). A read-only check for whether it has ALREADY happened: SELECT name, count(*) FROM "Group" WHERE name LIKE 'Batch of %' GROUP BY name HAVING count(*) > 1.
W1-038.fixDirection: Add a unique constraint that pins the invariant — either `@@unique([name])` (batch groups are the only auto-created names; verify no legit duplicate names exist first with the read above) or a dedicated nullable `batchYear Int? @unique` column on Group for batch containers — then replace findFirst/create with a single upsert on that key, and keep a P2002 catch that re-reads the winner. The GroupMember upsert half is already race-safe.
W1-038.gateOrTest: Unit test on joinBatchGroup simulating the race (two calls with the create mocked to interleave, asserting one group id), plus the schema constraint itself, which makes the DB the test.

W1-039.title: Legacy /onboarding page's updateProfile server action writes seven profile columns with zero validation — no length caps, no schema, no normalization — bypassing every rule profileSchema enforces on the same columns
W1-039.expected: Every write path to a profile column enforces the same rules (the codebase's own standard: contactMethodsSchema exists precisely because 'this is the second write path to them, so it gets the same gate' — audit M18 closed exactly this class on updateContactMethods).
W1-039.actual: src/app/(auth)/onboarding/actions.ts exports updateProfile, which takes FormData and writes `bio, currentCity, workplace, jobTitle, phone, instagram, linkedin` with only `if (value && value.trim()) data[field] = value.trim()` — no Zod, no length limits, no normalizePhone, no titleCase. The live /onboarding page (still routed, still imports and calls it) enforces `maxLength={1000}` only in the client textarea; a direct POST to the action (every 'use server' export is a public HTTP endpoint) stores arbitrarily large strings — a multi-megabyte bio (bounded only by the 25mb bodySizeLimit locally / 4.5MB on Vercel) lands in User.bio and is then fetched and rendered on every surface that selects bio, degrading profile and directory reads for everyone who views that member. It also skips the normalization contract: a phone stored here is un-normalized ('(080) 4123 5678' instead of digits), workplace/city skip titleCase, so the directory's assumption that 'every stored number reads the same way' quietly breaks. The 2026-08-20 mass-assignment hardening covered src/components/settings/actions.ts but this parallel legacy action was missed; the gate-coverage test passes it because it does contain `await auth()` — the sweep proves shape, not validation, exactly as its own comment warns.
W1-039.evidence: src/app/(auth)/onboarding/actions.ts:12-27 `const data: Record<string, string | null> = {}; const fields = ["bio", "currentCity", "workplace", "jobTitle", "phone", "instagram", "linkedin"]; for (const field of fields) { const value = formData.get(field) as string | null; if (value && value.trim()) { data[field] = value.trim(); } } if (Object.keys(data).length > 0) { await prisma.user.update({ where: { id: session.user.id }, data }); }` — the entire action; no schema import anywhere in the file. Contrast src/lib/validators.ts:53-67 profileSchema capping the same columns (`bio: z.string().max(1000)`, `currentCity: z.string().max(100)`, `phone: z.string().max(24)`, etc.). src/app/(auth)/onboarding/page.tsx:16,26 shows the action is live (`import { updateProfile } from "./actions"; ... await updateProfile(formData);`).
W1-039.reproPlan: Code-argument-only, or on local dev (shared DB — use your own test account): POST the action with a 100KB bio via the /onboarding form with the client maxLength removed in DevTools; confirm the column stores it. Clean up by re-saving a normal bio.
W1-039.fixDirection: Either delete the legacy /onboarding route + action outright (the /welcome wizard with saveOnboardingRegister supersedes it — confirm nothing else links to /onboarding, note proxy.ts DEMO_CLOSED_PATHS lists it) or validate through profileSchema (or a pick() of it) and run phone through normalizePhone / free-text through titleCase like every sibling action does. Deleting is the better move: one fewer write path to keep in sync.
W1-039.gateOrTest: If kept: extend gate-coverage-style static checks so every action writing User profile columns references a validator schema. If deleted: the lab-registry/route audit in npm run check plus a security-regressions test pinning the file gone.

W1-040.title: A database error during sign-in surfaces as 'Invalid email or password.', sending members with correct passwords into a doomed reset loop during any DB blip
W1-040.expected: 6k: DB slow/down mid-request — the member sees something actionable ('something went wrong on our side, try again in a minute'), not an accusation that their credentials are wrong.
W1-040.actual: When any awaited call in authorize() throws for infrastructure reasons (the findUnique, bcrypt on a malformed row, the deletion-cancel update), the error is not a CredentialsSignin subclass, so NextAuth surfaces a generic error result with no recognised code. The login client maps every unrecognised code to the credentials sentence: `setError(code === "rate-limited" ? RATE_LIMITED : code === "bot-check" ? BOT_CHECK_FAILED : "Invalid email or password.")`. During a Supabase hiccup every member signing in is told their password is wrong; the natural next step (forgot-password) also fails or silently no-ops against the same down DB, compounding confusion at exactly the moment support load spikes. The client's try/catch 'Something went wrong' branch never fires because signIn({redirect:false}) resolves with an error field rather than throwing.
