W1-077.evidence: actions.ts:271-272: `const limited = await rateLimit("uploads", session.user.id); if (!limited.ok) return { error: limited.error };` — returns with the staged key intact (contrast the quota path at 282-287, which does `await delImageByKey(input.key)`). actions.ts:289-297: `const parsed = photoSchema.safeParse({...}); if (!parsed.success) return { error: parsed.error.issues[0].message };` — same, no cleanup. finalize/route.ts:60-63: `const limited = await rateLimit("uploads", session.user.id); if (!limited.ok) return NextResponse.json({ error: limited.error }, { status: 429 });` — before keys are even parsed, so the staged post originals stay. The rate-limit case is reachable in normal use: each photo costs 2 tokens (presign + contribute) from the 40/hour "uploads" bucket (rate-limit.ts:69 `uploads: { tokens: 40, window: "1 h" }`), so a member whose presign takes the last token PUTs 20MB and then gets 429'd, orphaning it. Objects are up to MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES (20MB) each.
W1-077.fixDirection: Two halves: (1) add `await delImageByKey(input.key)` to every refusal path in contributePhotoDirect after the key-shape/ownership check passes (rate-limit, gate, Zod), and delete validated keys when finalize refuses; (2) add a reaper — either an R2 lifecycle rule on the `staging/` prefix and on `collection/**/-o.*` objects older than ~24h (dashboard, owner action), or a daily cron that lists those prefixes and deletes objects older than a day. The lifecycle rule is the robust answer since it also covers crashes and abandoned tabs that no server code can see.
W1-077.gateOrTest: Unit test asserting contributePhotoDirect's rate-limited and Zod-failure branches call delImageByKey (mock storage); an ops checklist entry pinning the R2 lifecycle rule.
W1-077.reproPlan: code-argument-only (proving it live would write real objects into the shared production bucket).

W1-078.title: CollectionClient never handles a failed loadPhotos call: transient DB/network failure leaves an infinite skeleton or a stuck "Loading..." button, and a stale Load more response appends into a newer filtered list
W1-078.expected: If the photos fetch fails, the member sees something actionable (an error state or a retry); changing a filter while Load more is in flight discards the stale response.
W1-078.actual: (1) The initial effect does `fetchPage(0).then((data) => { ... setLoading(false); })` with no `.catch`: a rejected server-action call (DB blip through pgbouncer, dropped connection) leaves `loading` true forever — the page shows the skeleton indefinitely with an unhandled rejection in the console. (2) `handleLoadMore` has no try/catch: a rejection leaves `loadingMore` true, so the button reads "Loading..." and is disabled forever. (3) `handleLoadMore` has no cancellation/sequence guard: tap Load more on a slow connection, then change a filter — the effect refetches page 0 and replaces `photos`, then the in-flight load-more resolves and runs `setPhotos((prev) => [...prev, ...data.photos])`, appending page 2 of the OLD, unfiltered result set into the new filtered list (wrong photos shown under the active filter, wrong total, possible duplicate keys).
W1-078.evidence: Lines 146-161: `useEffect(() => { let cancelled = false; setLoading(true); setPage(0); fetchPage(0).then((data) => { if (cancelled) return; ... setLoading(false); }); return () => { cancelled = true; }; }, [fetchPage]);` — the `cancelled` flag guards only the effect's own fetch, and there is no rejection handler anywhere. Lines 163-172: `async function handleLoadMore() { const next = page + 1; setLoadingMore(true); const data = await fetchPage(next); setPhotos((prev) => [...prev, ...data.photos]); ... }` — no try/finally, no check that the filters that produced `data` are still current.
W1-078.fixDirection: Add .catch/finally to both fetch paths (surface a toast + a retry affordance, always clear loading flags), and carry a request-sequence number (or reuse the `cancelled` pattern via a ref incremented on every filter change) that handleLoadMore checks before appending.
W1-078.gateOrTest: Component test: mock loadPhotos to reject → assert skeleton is replaced by an error/retry state and loadingMore resets; mock a delayed page-2 response racing a filter change → assert it is discarded.
W1-078.reproPlan: Live proof read-only: open /collection with devtools offline mode toggled after page load, click Load more → observe the stuck button; or throttle to Slow 3G, click Load more, immediately change the When filter → observe unfiltered photos appended.

W1-079.title: togglePhotoLove is a check-then-act race with no P2002/P2025/P2003 handling, and the client button neither serializes clicks nor catches a thrown action, leaving the heart in a wrong state
W1-079.expected: Double-clicking the heart lands on a consistent final state; a lost race resolves silently; an invalid photoId returns a clean error.
W1-079.actual: actions.ts:508-518 does `const existing = await prisma.photoLove.findUnique(...); if (existing) { await prisma.photoLove.delete({ where: { id: existing.id } }); } else { await prisma.photoLove.create(...); }`. Two rapid clicks (LoveButton's handleClick calls onToggle with no pending guard, love-button.tsx:74-80, and PhotoLoveButton.handle has no in-flight lock) run two overlapping actions: both can read `existing = null` → the second `create` throws P2002 (schema @@unique([userId, photoId])); or both read the same row → the second `delete` throws P2025. A crafted/stale photoId (photo just declined) makes `create` throw a foreign-key error. None of these are caught, so the action rejects; on the client, photo-love-button.tsx:24 `const result = await togglePhotoLove(photoId);` has no try/catch, so the rollback branch (`if (result.error)`) never runs — the optimistic setLoved/setCount state is left disagreeing with the database until a reload, plus an unhandled rejection.
W1-079.evidence: Quoted above; additionally the action does not verify the photo exists/is visible before writing (no findUnique on Photo), unlike toggleLike for posts which calls `canViewPost` first (feed/actions.ts:474-475), so the Collection heart is the one love path that can hit the FK error and also the one that lets a member love an unapproved photo by id.
W1-079.fixDirection: Make the toggle idempotent and error-tolerant: wrap in try/catch mapping P2002 to "already loved" (treat as success), P2025 to "already unloved", and return { error } for a missing photo (precheck `prisma.photo.findUnique({ select: { approved, isHidden } })` like canViewPost). On the client, wrap the await in try/catch performing the same rollback, and/or ignore clicks while a call is in flight.
W1-079.gateOrTest: Unit test firing two concurrent togglePhotoLove calls for the same (user, photo) asserting both resolve without throwing and the table ends with exactly 0 or 1 row; a test asserting a bogus photoId yields { error } not a throw.
W1-079.reproPlan: Live proof on a test account: rapid-double-click a photo heart with the network throttled and watch the console for the unhandled rejection and the count desync after reload.

W1-080.title: Animated GIFs are silently flattened to a static first frame by every server encode path, while the client-side downscaler deliberately passes GIFs through untouched "to preserve the animation"
W1-080.expected: Either animated GIFs post as animations, or they are refused/explained; the pipeline should not half-support them.
W1-080.actual: GIF is an accepted input everywhere (upload-shared.ts:83 sniffImageType returns "gif"; presign EXT_BY_TYPE includes "image/gif"), and image-downscale.ts:16-18 documents the pass-through: "GIF: re-rasterising would drop the animation." But every server path constructs the pipeline as `sharp(input, { limitInputPixels, sequentialRead, failOn })` (image.ts:27-39) WITHOUT `animated: true` (or `pages: -1`), so libvips decodes only the first frame, and `.webp({ quality: 80 })` encodes a single-frame WebP (upload/route.ts:119-126, finalize/route.ts:111-115, collection actions.ts:346-359). Net: a member attaches an animated GIF, the composer preview (object URL of the original) animates, the published post shows a frozen frame.
W1-080.evidence: image.ts:26-40: `return sharp(input, { limitInputPixels: MAX_INPUT_PIXELS, sequentialRead: true, failOn: "error" });` — no `animated` option; sharp's documented default is first-frame-only for multi-page input. upload-shared.ts:83: `if (b.length >= 6 && b[0] === 0x47 && b[1] === 0x49 && b[2] === 0x46) return "gif";` — GIFs pass the sniff. presign/route.ts:33: `"image/gif": "gif"`.
W1-080.fixDirection: Owner decision, two clean options: (1) support animation: pass `animated: true` to sharp for GIF-sniffed inputs and encode animated WebP (mind memory: limitInputPixels applies per-frame stack, so cap frames/pixels); or (2) drop the pretense: reject animated GIFs with a friendly "animations aren't supported" message at sniff time (a static GIF still passes), and delete the misleading pass-through comment in image-downscale.ts.
W1-080.gateOrTest: Unit test feeding a 2-frame GIF through the upload transform asserting either the output WebP has >1 frame (option 1) or the request is refused with the friendly message (option 2).
W1-080.reproPlan: code-argument-only for production (would write objects); locally provable by posting any animated GIF in dev and inspecting the stored WebP.

W1-081.title: Photo detail page renders the contribution date in server UTC, so any photo contributed 00:00-05:30 IST shows the previous day's date
W1-081.expected: A member in India who contributes a photo at 1am on Aug 21 sees "21 Aug 2026" beside their name on /collection/[id].
W1-081.actual: The date is computed in the server's timezone (UTC on Vercel): a 01:00 IST Aug 21 contribution is 19:30 UTC Aug 20, so the page shows "20 Aug 2026". Every contribution between midnight and 05:30 IST (a meaningful slice of evening-scrolling uploads) is off by one day. Note the asymmetry that proves the inconsistency: the grid's full-screen viewer formats the same timestamp CLIENT-side via formatDisplayDate (collection-client.tsx:77, a "use client" component, so IST) — the same photo can show different dates in the viewer vs its own permalink page.
W1-081.evidence: [id]/page.tsx:145-149 (a server component): `meta={new Date(photo.createdAt).toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { day: "numeric", month: "short", year: "numeric" })}` — no timeZone option, so it uses the server locale timezone (UTC). utils.ts:151-157 formatDisplayDate is the identical call but executed in the browser for the viewer path.
W1-081.fixDirection: Pass `timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata"` in the server-side call (or move the formatting into a client component / reuse formatDisplayDate client-side), and grep the repo for other server-component toLocaleDateString/toLocaleTimeString calls without an explicit timeZone — this is a class, not a one-off (the audit brief's other territories should cross-check).
W1-081.gateOrTest: Unit test on a date-formatting helper with a fixed 19:30Z timestamp asserting the rendered day is the IST day; lint-style grep gate for toLocaleDateString without timeZone in server components.
W1-081.reproPlan: Live proof read-only: find (or wait for) any photo whose createdAt falls between 18:30Z and 00:00Z and compare the permalink date against the viewer date on the same photo.

W1-082.title: Fallback (non-presigned) upload paths ship bodies far over Vercel's ~4.5MB request cap the codebase itself documents: avatar accepts 15MB originals and the contribute fallback sends up to 20MB, contradicting next.config's belief that 25MB bodies arrive
W1-082.expected: Every byte path that traverses a Vercel function stays under the platform request-body cap, or fails with the friendly size message.
W1-082.actual: The repo holds two contradictory beliefs. Belief A ("the cap is real"): avatar-crop-dialog.tsx:10-12 "comfortably under Vercel's ~4.5MB serverless body cap"; presign/route.ts:12 "Vercel caps serverless request bodies at ~4.5MB no matter what bodySizeLimit says"; upload-client.ts:13-15 "capped at ~4.5MB on Vercel". Belief B ("25MB bodies arrive"): next.config.ts:107-124 raises serverActions.bodySizeLimit and proxyClientMaxBodySize to "25mb" explicitly so "a 20MB photo" reaches contributePhoto, and attributes real-world 1-in-6 Collection failures to the 10MB proxy default — implying >4.5MB bodies were surviving the platform. If Belief A is right: updateAvatar's fallback (settings/actions.ts:215 `if (file.size > MAX_AVATAR_INPUT) return { error: "Photo must be under 15MB" }` — reached when the crop dialog cannot decode a file and hands the ORIGINAL to the plain path, per avatar-crop-dialog.tsx:19-22) and the contribute dialog's fallback (contribute-dialog.tsx:135-144 `fd.set("file", file)` with files up to 20MB, taken whenever presign/CORS hiccups per upload-client.ts) both die at the platform edge with an opaque 413 instead of the friendly messages the code promises. If Belief B is right, several load-bearing comments and the presign design rationale are stale and the real constraint is only the configured 25mb.
W1-082.evidence: Quoted above. The two beliefs cannot both be true, and each direction leaves a member-visible failure or a design built on a false premise.
W1-082.fixDirection: Orchestrator should settle it empirically once (see reproPlan), then either (A) cap the avatar fallback input and the contribute fallback at ~4MB with browser downscaling first (downscaleImage already exists and the composer's fallback uses it — contribute dialog's does not), or (B) correct the comments and simplify. Either way, wire downscaleImage into ContributeDialog's fallback branch: it costs nothing and makes the fallback survive under any cap.
W1-082.gateOrTest: A production smoke test (manual, post-deploy): upload a ~6MB photo with the presign path artificially disabled (devtools request blocking on /api/upload/presign) and record whether contributePhoto succeeds.
W1-082.reproPlan: Live proof on production with a test account: block /api/upload/presign in devtools, attempt a 6MB contribution; also attempt a 6MB undecodable-in-browser avatar. Observe 413 vs success.

W1-083.title: contributePhotoDirect re-encodes up to 100-megapixel originals at full resolution (two full decodes + q90 WebP encode) with no maxDuration configured: an at-limit legitimate scan can exceed the function ceiling, failing the upload and leaking the staged original
W1-083.expected: Any input the validators accept (<=20MB file, <=100MP pixels) processes within the function's time and memory budget, or is refused with a clear message and cleaned up.
W1-083.actual: The accepted envelope is generous: MAX_INPUT_PIXELS = 100_000_000 (image.ts:24) and MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES 20MB. contributePhotoDirect then (a) GETs up to 20MB from R2, (b) fully decodes for the display encode `sharpImage(original).rotate().resize(WEBP_MAX_DIM=16383, ...).webp({ quality: 90 }).toBuffer()` (actions.ts:345-350) — at 100MP that is a ~400MB RGBA working set and a very slow q90 encode — then (c) decodes the SAME original a second time for the 480px thumb (actions.ts:355-359), then (d) PUTs both outputs. No route/action in the repo sets maxDuration (grep: zero hits) and vercel.json sets none, so the platform default applies. If the default tier duration (10-60s depending on plan/Fluid settings) is exceeded, the invocation is killed: the member gets an opaque failure, the catch block's `delImageByKey(input.key)` never runs (the process is gone), and the EXIF-bearing staged original leaks (compounding the orphan finding). A 90MP flatbed scan of a heritage panorama is exactly the input this feature courts ("high-res in the Collection is the point", actions.ts:241).
W1-083.evidence: Quoted above; also the comment at actions.ts:341-344 shows the 16383 ceiling was added for WebP's dimension limit, not as a duration/memory bound — nothing bounds encode TIME below the 100MP pixel guard.
W1-083.fixDirection: Set an explicit generous `export const maxDuration` (e.g. 60-300s per plan) on the collection actions file and finalize route; reuse the decoded pipeline for the thumb (`.clone()` on one sharp instance, or resize the display buffer) to halve decode work; consider lowering MAX_INPUT_PIXELS to ~60MP or encoding q80 above a pixel threshold. Keep the staged-key cleanup robust via the lifecycle-rule fix from the orphan finding.
W1-083.gateOrTest: A load-shaped local benchmark committed as a script (not CI): time the current pipeline on a synthetic 95MP PNG; assert budget with margin. Plus the orphan-sweep gate covers the leak half.
W1-083.reproPlan: Live proof on a test account: contribute a synthetic large-dimension image (e.g. 12000x8000, under 20MB as PNG) in production and observe duration/outcome in Vercel logs. Safe: worst case is one failed upload and one orphan object.

W1-084.title: approvePhoto throws (unhandled P2025) when the photo was just declined by another admin, and the admin UI's act() helper then leaves the row stuck on its busy spinner
W1-084.expected: Two admins working the queue concurrently: the loser of an approve-vs-decline race sees "Photo not found" (like declinePhoto's own guard) and the row clears.
W1-084.actual: approvePhoto does a blind `await prisma.photo.update({ where: { id: photoId }, data: { approved: true, ... } })` (actions.ts:525-528) with no existence check and no P2025 handling — on a row declinePhoto just deleted (actions.ts:549 `await prisma.photo.delete(...)`), the update throws, the server action rejects, and content-list.tsx act() (lines 99-113: `setBusy(id); const result = await fn(); setBusy(null); ...`) has no try/finally, so `setBusy(null)` never runs: the Approve/Decline buttons for that row stay disabled on "…" until a page reload, with an unhandled rejection. declinePhoto shows the intended pattern (findUnique → `if (!photo) return { error: "Photo not found" }`), approvePhoto just lacks it.
W1-084.evidence: Quoted above; adminRemovePhoto also races declinePhoto the same way but both of its Prisma calls follow a findUnique-null-check, leaving only the narrow window between check and update — approvePhoto has no check at all.
W1-084.fixDirection: In approvePhoto: findUnique first and return { error: "Photo not found" } on null, or wrap the update in try/catch mapping P2025 to that error. In content-list act(): wrap `await fn()` in try/finally (finally: setBusy(null)) and toast a generic failure on throw — this hardens every admin action routed through it, not just photos.
W1-084.gateOrTest: Unit test: approvePhoto on a nonexistent id resolves to { error } rather than rejecting.
W1-084.reproPlan: Live proof on production is safe-ish but needs two admin sessions racing; code-argument-only is sufficient — the throw path is unconditional for a deleted id.

W1-085.title: deletePost deletes image bytes BEFORE the row delete, inverting the codebase's own stated ordering invariant: a failed row delete leaves a live post with permanently broken images
W1-085.expected: Per account-purge.ts:80-86's explicit rule — "bytes are deleted only AFTER the row delete succeeds, because if the delete throws and rolls back, the member still exists and their images must keep rendering" — the same holds for a single post.
W1-085.evidence: Quoted above; deletePostImages (line 32-35) = `await Promise.all(parseImageUrls(images).map((img) => delImage(img)))` runs to completion before the row delete is attempted.
W1-085.fixDirection: Swap the order: delete the row first, then best-effort delImage the collected URLs (they were selected at line 317-320 before deletion, so nothing is lost). One-line move.
W1-085.gateOrTest: Unit test with a mocked prisma.post.delete that throws: assert delImage was NOT called.
W1-085.reproPlan: code-argument-only (forcing a DB failure mid-delete in production is not acceptable).

W1-086.title: Photo.uploaderId and PhotoLove.photoId have no index: every /collection visit and every contribution runs sequential scans on the hot per-user queries
W1-086.expected: The queries the page runs on every load are index-backed (charter: @@index coverage vs actual query shapes).
W1-086.actual: Photo has only `@@index([approved, isHidden, createdAt])` and `@@index([era])` (schema.prisma:176-177); Postgres does not auto-index FK columns. But myPendingPhotos runs `where: { uploaderId, approved: false, isHidden: false }` on EVERY /collection page view (page.tsx:23-24), photoQuotaError runs `prisma.photo.count({ where: { uploaderId } })` on every contribution, and account purge/merge/export all filter by uploaderId — all sequential scans. PhotoLove has only `@@unique([userId, photoId])` (userId-prefixed), so `_count.loves` per photo and the loves-count sort resolve photoId lookups without an index. At the 2,000-user ceiling with a few thousand photos this is milliseconds — degradation, not breakage — but it is the one hot query shape with zero index support and costs two lines to fix.
W1-086.evidence: Quoted above from schema and actions.
W1-086.fixDirection: Add `@@index([uploaderId])` to Photo (or `[uploaderId, approved, isHidden]` to cover the pending query exactly) and `@@index([photoId])` to PhotoLove via the repo's manual-migration flow (prisma/migrations-manual/ + run-sql.mjs; never db push).
W1-086.gateOrTest: Schema review in the fix session; optionally EXPLAIN in Supabase console confirming index usage.
W1-086.reproPlan: Read-only EXPLAIN via Supabase dashboard if desired; code-argument-only otherwise.

W1-087.title: Two small date traps: photoYear's max is frozen at module load in UTC (New-Year IST rejections of a valid year), and eraFromYear buckets any 2030+ year to "unknown"
W1-087.expected: A year the contribute dialog offers is always accepted, and an exact year always maps to a real era bucket.
W1-087.actual: (1) validators.ts:184-189: `photoYear: z.number().int().min(1926, ...).max(new Date().getFullYear(), "That year hasn't happened yet")` — `new Date()` runs once at module initialization, in the server's UTC. The dialog's yearOptions() (contribute-dialog.tsx:39-47) computes currentYear() in the member's browser (IST). Every Jan 1 from 00:00 to 05:30 IST the browser offers the new year while the UTC server still rejects it; a warm serverless instance loaded before midnight keeps rejecting even longer. The member picking "2027" for a photo taken at the New Year gathering gets "That year hasn't happened yet." (2) collection.ts:57-62: `eraFromYear` builds `"${decade}s"` and falls back: `return (ERA_VALUES as readonly string[]).includes(bucket) ? bucket : "unknown"` — ERA_VALUES ends at "2020s" (collection.ts:28-38), so from Jan 2030 every exact-year contribution silently files under era "unknown" ("Undated" in the filter) despite the member giving a precise year.
W1-087.fixDirection: (1) Make the max a per-parse check: `.superRefine` or `.max(...)` replaced with a refine comparing against `new Date().getFullYear() + 1` (accepting IST's next-day year costs nothing — the value is a memory of the past). (2) Either generate ERA buckets programmatically through the current decade, or have eraFromYear return the computed bucket and append unseen buckets to the filter options from live data (the area facet already uses the live-values pattern).
W1-087.gateOrTest: Unit tests: photoSchema accepts currentYear during a mocked Dec-31-UTC/Jan-1-IST boundary; eraFromYear(2031) !== "unknown" after the fix.

W1-088.title: Blank-MIME image files (a mobile-browser quirk the codebase itself documents and accommodates elsewhere) dead-end: the contribute dialog refuses them at pick time and the composer's presign path throws a misleading "format isn't supported" without trying the sniff-based fallback
W1-088.expected: A real JPG whose File.type arrives blank (the exact case image-downscale.ts:27-33 handles by extension: `if (file.type === "" && /\.(jpe?g|png|webp)$/i.test(file.name)) return true;` and upload-shared.ts:32 acknowledges: "`type` is occasionally blank for these on some mobile browsers") still uploads — the server's magic-byte sniff, not the client MIME string, is the design's source of truth (M13).
W1-088.actual: Two dead ends: (1) ContributeDialog.pickFile line 85: `if (!f.type.startsWith("image/")) { toast.error("Please choose an image"); return; }` — a blank-type JPG cannot even be selected. (2) In the composer, handleImageFiles has no type gate, so the file reaches directUploadPut, which posts contentType "" to presign; presign/route.ts:75-86: `const ext = contentType ? EXT_BY_TYPE[contentType] : undefined; if (!ext) { return NextResponse.json({ error: "That photo format isn't supported. Export it as JPG or PNG..." }, { status: 400 }); }` — and upload-client.ts:45 treats every 400 as a definitive verdict: `if (status === 400 && presign.error) throw new Error(presign.error);`, so the /api/upload fallback — whose sniffImageType would have accepted the actual JPEG bytes — is never attempted. The member holds a valid photo and is told to export it as JPG.
W1-088.fixDirection: In both pickFile and presign, extend the type check with the extension fallback already written in isDownscalable (or better: infer contentType from extension client-side before presigning, e.g. map .jpg→image/jpeg when file.type is empty). Alternatively have directUploadPut return null (fallback) rather than throw when the 400 stems from a blank/unknown contentType rather than a known-bad one.
W1-088.gateOrTest: Unit test: directUploadPut-equivalent logic with a File of type "" and name "x.jpg" reaches the fallback rather than throwing.
W1-088.reproPlan: Hard to reproduce without the affected mobile browser; code-argument-only, anchored on the repo's own comments asserting the case occurs in the wild.

W1-089.title: Mail queue burns all 4 retry attempts within a single drain pass — any transient Resend failure permanently kills queued mail, including password resets
W1-089.expected: MAX_ATTEMPTS=4 spreads retries over time so a transient provider failure (a 30-second Resend 500 streak, or Resend's own ~2-req/s rate limit answering 429 under concurrent drains) is ridden out, and mail sends when the provider recovers.
W1-089.actual: The drain loop re-picks the SAME row immediately after a failed attempt, so all 4 attempts are spent within seconds of one drain pass; the row flips to terminal status 'failed' and is never retried when Resend recovers. There is no backoff column, no delay, and no next-attempt-at concept anywhere.
W1-089.evidence: drainMailQueue's loop (email-queue.ts:461-483) runs `for (let i = 0; i < BATCH; i++)` (BATCH=8) and each iteration does `findFirst({ where: { status: "queued", ..., attempts: { lt: MAX_ATTEMPTS } }, orderBy: [{ priority: "asc" }, { createdAt: "asc" }] })`. claimAndSend on failure sets `status: afterFailure` where `afterFailure = spent >= MAX_ATTEMPTS ? "failed" : "queued"` (lines 173-174, 222-226) — a requeued row keeps its createdAt, so the next iteration's findFirst returns the identical row (same priority, still oldest). Four consecutive iterations exhaust attempts 1→4 and the fourth writes terminal `status: "failed"`. Nothing ever retries a 'failed' row: the drain filter is `status: "queued"`. Amplifiers: (a) every authenticated page view schedules a drain (`after(drainMailQueue)` in (main)/layout.tsx:63-69) and every enqueue schedules another (scheduleDrain, email-queue.ts:350), so on launch day many drains run concurrently, each claiming different rows and collectively exceeding Resend's ~2 req/s → 429s that count as failed attempts; (b) dailyBudget (lines 452-475) is read non-atomically per drain, so N concurrent drains can each see remaining=1 and collectively overshoot the 5-message headroom (DAILY_CAP=95 vs 100), producing hard Resend rejections that also burn attempts. Member outcome: a password-reset requester (logged out, no banner to help them) waits at 'check your inbox' forever — the verify banner at least maps 'failed' to a resend offer, but resets have no equivalent surface.
W1-089.fixDirection: Add a `nextAttemptAt DateTime` (or reuse claimedAt) to OutboundEmail; on a failed send set it to now + backoff (e.g. 2^attempts minutes) and add `nextAttemptAt: { lte: now }` to the drain's findFirst so a failed row cannot be re-picked in the same pass. Distinguish transient provider failures (429/5xx/network) from permanent ones (invalid address) and only count permanent ones against MAX_ATTEMPTS, or raise MAX_ATTEMPTS with real backoff. Add a small jittered serialization (or a single-drainer advisory claim row) so concurrent page-view drains do not collectively exceed Resend's request rate; alternatively add an inter-send sleep inside the BATCH loop.
W1-089.gateOrTest: New unit test against email-queue drain logic (extract the pick/claim decision into a pure -rule file per repo convention): given a queued row that fails transiently, assert the same pass does not attempt it twice and that a 'failed' verdict requires attempts separated by backoff. Pin with a regression test in src/lib/security-regressions.test.mjs style.
W1-089.reproPlan: code-argument-only (simulating a Resend outage would require sending real mail or mutating the shared production queue).

W1-090.title: Client mutation/fetch handlers do not catch server-action rejections — a transient network/DB failure strands the UI: feed skeleton forever, bricked Post button, stuck save status
W1-090.expected: When a server action's POST fails in transit (mobile network blip — the membership is in India on mobile data — or DB down making the action throw server-side), the member sees an error with a retry, and pending state resets.
W1-090.actual: A rejected server-action promise is unhandled at these call sites, so the pending flag set before the await is never cleared and no message appears: the feed shows its loading skeleton indefinitely; the composer's Post button stays disabled with no toast; the catchup answer's save indicator sticks on 'saving'. Recovery requires a full page reload.
W1-090.evidence: post-feed.tsx initial load: `fetchPosts(null).then((data) => { ... setLoading(false); ... })` (lines 118-138) has NO .catch — `loading` starts true (line 57), so a rejection leaves the skeleton forever; React error boundaries do not catch async rejections. handleLoadMore (lines 152-159): `setLoadingMore(true); const data = await fetchPosts(cursor); ... setLoadingMore(false);` with no try/finally — a rejection strands `loadingMore=true` and the button renders disabled 'Loading...' permanently (lines 312-315). create-post-form handleSubmit (lines 497-596): `setSubmitting(true)` then bare `await createPost(formData)` / `await editPost(...)` / `await publishDraft(...)` with no try/catch/finally — a rejection never reaches `setSubmitting(false)` (line 595) and the submit button (`disabled={!content.trim() || submitting || savingDraft}`, line 1059/1087) is dead with zero feedback; contrast login-client.tsx handleSubmit which correctly wraps in try/catch/finally. answer-experience.tsx persist (lines 93-102): handles a RETURNED `{error}` but `await submitEntry(...)` rejection skips both the toast and `setSaveStatus("idle")`, stranding 'saving'. These actions all throw server-side on any Prisma failure (e.g. createPost's `prisma.post.create` at feed/actions.ts:153 has no try/catch), which the Next action transport surfaces as a client-side rejection.
W1-090.failure_scenario: A member on flaky 4G opens /feed; the loadPosts POST times out → skeleton shimmers forever with no error and no retry. Or: mid-post-submit the DB blips → the Post button greys out permanently, the member's text is still in the editor but nothing tells them what happened.
W1-090.fixDirection: Establish one pattern and apply it at every server-action await in client components: wrap in try/catch/finally, reset pending state in finally, and toast a generic 'That didn't go through — check your connection and try again' on rejection. For post-feed's initial load add .catch that sets an error state with a visible retry button instead of the skeleton. Grep target: every `await <action>(` inside src/components and src/app/**/*.tsx client files; the four sites above are confirmed, others likely follow the same shape.
W1-090.gateOrTest: Playwright spec: intercept/abort the action POST route and assert the feed shows an error+retry (geometry/text assertion per repo convention) rather than a skeleton after N seconds; same for the composer button re-enabling.
W1-090.reproPlan: Safe live proof: chrome-devtools MCP → load /feed signed in, use emulate/network offline just before scroll-triggered load-more (read-only), observe stuck 'Loading...' button and console unhandled rejection.

W1-091.title: Email case normalization is inconsistent across signup, login and reset — a member whose stored email contains an uppercase letter can never reset their password, silently
W1-091.expected: One address is one account regardless of typed case: signup, login and password reset all resolve 'John@Gmail.com' and 'john@gmail.com' to the same row.
W1-091.actual: Signup stores the email exactly as typed (no lowercasing anywhere in the pipeline); login looks the row up case-sensitively with the exact string typed; the forgot-password flow lowercases before lookup. So a mixed-case account (a) requires the identical casing to sign in, (b) NEVER matches in requestPasswordReset — which by anti-enumeration design returns the same { ok: true } and shows 'check your inbox', so no mail ever comes and no error is ever shown, and (c) the same mailbox can register twice under different casings (User.email unique is a plain case-sensitive Postgres unique).
W1-091.evidence: registerUser: `signupSchema` validates with `z.email(...)` only (validators.ts:18 — no .toLowerCase()/transform), and the row is created with `email: parsed.data.email` (actions.ts:149) after a case-sensitive `findUnique({ where: { email: parsed.data.email } })` (actions.ts:103). authorize(): `await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email } })` (auth.ts:102) with the raw credential string — only the rate-limit key is lowercased (`const acctKey = email.trim().toLowerCase()`, auth.ts:62). requestPasswordReset: `const raw = ((formData.get("email") as string) ?? "").trim().toLowerCase(); ... prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: raw } })` (email-actions.ts:160-167) and on miss silently `return { ok: true }` (line 172) — deliberate anti-oracle, which is exactly what makes this failure invisible. schema.prisma:13: `email String @unique` (no citext, no lower() expression index found in prisma/migrations-manual/). The human-pass is NOT affected (signHumanPass lowercases internally, human-pass-rule.ts:16), which shows the intended convention the other three paths missed.
W1-091.failure_scenario: An older alumnus types 'Ravi.Menon@gmail.com' on desktop at signup. Months later they forget their password, type 'ravi.menon@gmail.com' into /forgot-password, see 'check your inbox', and no mail ever arrives — repeatedly, forever. Support cannot see why without inspecting the row.
W1-091.fixDirection: Normalize (trim + toLowerCase) the email at all three write/lookup points: in signupSchema via z.transform, in authorize() before findUnique, and keep reset as-is. Then run a one-time read of `SELECT id, email FROM "User" WHERE email <> lower(email)` and migrate those rows to lowercase (checking for collisions first). Optionally add a lower(email) unique expression index in migrations-manual to enforce it at the DB.
W1-091.gateOrTest: Unit test in the .test.mjs suite on the normalization helper; a security-regressions-style pin asserting authorize and requestPasswordReset both lowercase before lookup.
W1-091.reproPlan: Read-only live proof of standing impact: run `SELECT count(*) FROM "User" WHERE email <> lower(email)` against the DB (read-only) — any nonzero count is a member already in the broken state.

W1-092.title: Letter autosave fails silently: on any error the desk keeps saying 'Saving...', nothing is surfaced, and a fresh (never-saved) letter has zero draft protection
W1-092.expected: The immersive letter desk (20,000-char compositions) either saves reliably or tells the writer loudly that saving has stopped; the owner's chaos question 'is the half-written letter lost?' should be answerable with 'no'.
W1-092.actual: Two gaps. (1) Resumed-draft autosave: `const result = await editPost(postId, fd); if (!result.error) onAutosaveState?.("saved")` — when result.error is set (e.g. 'Not authenticated' after the session was revoked, which the app's own credentialVersion mechanism does instantly on a password reset or deletion request from another device) NOTHING happens: no toast, no state change, the desk chrome stays on 'Saving...' (letter-desk.tsx:55) while every subsequent autosave also fails; a transport rejection additionally goes unhandled (no try/catch). The writer continues for an hour believing the letter is persisting; navigating away loses everything since the last good save. (2) A FRESH letter at /letters/new has no row, so no autosave, no localStorage fallback, and no beforeunload guard (grep for beforeunload across components/posts and components/letters returns nothing) — a crash, an accidental Back, or a session end discards the entire composition.
W1-092.evidence: create-post-form.tsx:218-227: `autosaveTimer.current = setTimeout(async () => { ... onAutosaveState?.("saving"); ... const result = await editPost(postId, fd); if (!result.error) onAutosaveState?.("saved"); }, 2500);` — the error branch is empty and the await is uncaught. letter-desk.tsx:54-56 renders `{saveState === "saving" ? "Saving..." : ...}` from exactly that callback. The session-revocation interaction is real and by design: auth.ts session callback returns invalid (→ auth() null → editPost returns { error: "Not authenticated" }) the moment credentialVersion changes (auth.ts:277-281), e.g. resetPassword's `credentialVersion: { increment: 1 }` (email-actions.ts:280).
W1-092.failure_scenario: A member's session is ended (password reset on their phone; or simply signs out in another tab) while a letter draft sits open on the laptop. Every autosave from then on returns 'Not authenticated'; the desk says 'Saving...' indefinitely; an hour of writing is gone when the tab closes.
W1-092.fixDirection: In the autosave callback: wrap in try/catch; on result.error or rejection set a third autosave state ('failed') that letter-desk renders loudly ('Not saving — check your connection / sign in again'), and toast once on first failure. Mirror the typed content into localStorage keyed by postId (and a 'new-letter' key for fresh compositions) as a crash net; offer restore on next mount. Consider a beforeunload prompt while unsaved changes exist.
W1-092.gateOrTest: Playwright: open a draft, block the action route, type, assert the failed-save state becomes visible within one autosave interval (expect.poll on the status text).
W1-092.reproPlan: Safe live proof on a test/admin account: open /letters/[id]/edit for a scratch draft, use chrome-devtools request blocking on the page's action endpoint, type, watch 'Saving...' persist with no error.

W1-093.title: Turnstile script blocked client-side means nobody can sign in from that browser — with a misleading 'refresh and try once more' message and a 12s stall per attempt
W1-093.expected: The widget's own header comment promises 'a broken third party never bricks sign-in': if the script cannot load, the form submits without a token and the server 'lets it pass if Turnstile itself is what broke'.
W1-093.actual: That promise only holds for a SERVER-side Cloudflare failure. When the CLIENT cannot load the script (corporate proxy, DNS filter, aggressive privacy extension blocking challenges.cloudflare.com), getToken() settles null, the form submits with no token, and the server hard-refuses: verifyTurnstile has `if (!token) return false` (turnstile.ts:86, and the file header states 'A request with NO token is refused in both environments alike'). The member gets BOT_CHECK_FAILED — 'We couldn't confirm you're human. Refresh the page and try once more.' — which is false advice: refreshing changes nothing, and the member is permanently locked out from that network/browser with no hint that their blocker is the cause. When the script load HANGS rather than erroring, each attempt first waits out the 12s getToken timeout (turnstile-widget.tsx:139-143).
W1-093.evidence: turnstile-widget.tsx comment lines 18-21: 'If the script cannot load or the challenge errors, getToken() settles to null and the form submits without a token: the server is the judge anyway, and its own posture ... matches — a broken third party never bricks sign-in.' vs turnstile.ts:86 `if (!token) return false;` and authorize() (auth.ts:83-94): `humanPassValid(...) || devBypassAllowed(...) || (await verifyTurnstile(credentials?.turnstileToken ...)); if (!human) { throw new BotCheckFailed(); }` — a no-token login from a script-blocked browser has none of the three. bot-check-message.ts:10-11 is the sentence shown.
W1-093.failure_scenario: An alumnus behind a corporate proxy that blocks challenges.cloudflare.com types correct credentials, waits 12 seconds, reads 'refresh and try once more', loops forever, concludes their account is broken.
W1-093.fixDirection: Owner decision needed on posture: either (a) accept the lockout but fix the copy for the no-token case — client knows the script failed (dead ref) and can show 'Your network or an extension is blocking our human-check (challenges.cloudflare.com). Allow it and retry' before submitting; or (b) treat a MISSING token differently from a failed verification server-side (e.g. allow missing-token logins under a stricter per-IP/account rate limit). At minimum align the widget comment with the real behavior and skip the 12s wait once loadScript has rejected.
W1-093.gateOrTest: e2e spec with request-blocking on the Turnstile script asserting the pre-submit guidance appears (once fixed); unit test pinning verifyTurnstile(null) behavior stays deliberate.
W1-093.reproPlan: Safe live proof: chrome-devtools MCP on /login with network request blocking for challenges.cloudflare.com/*, attempt sign-in with the dev account, observe the 12s stall then BOT_CHECK_FAILED.

W1-094.title: Account purge counts failed R2 deletes as deleted: an R2 outage (or function timeout) during purge silently orphans a deleted member's images at public URLs forever, with a false audit record
W1-094.expected: GDPR-motivated erasure (the file's own stated purpose) either deletes the R2 bytes or records that it could not, so the objects can be found and removed later.
W1-094.actual: The DB rows are deleted first (correct, argued in the file), then `for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); deleted += 1; }` — delImage → delImageByKey swallows every failure in a bare `catch { /* best-effort cleanup */ }` with not even a console line (storage.ts:225-227), and `deleted` increments unconditionally. If R2 returns 500/429 during the nightly purge, every object survives at its public pub-*.r2.dev URL, the rows that pointed at them are already cascaded away ('afterwards nothing can enumerate the objects' — the file's own words), and the audit entry writes 'N stored image(s) removed' (retention.ts:132) when zero were. A function timeout mid-loop (the sweep runs 7 deleteManys plus per-account purges with sequential per-object round trips, no maxDuration set anywhere) truncates the loop the same way.
W1-094.evidence: account-purge.ts:108-113: `let deleted = 0; for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); deleted += 1; } return { ok: true, imagesDeleted: deleted };` — the comment above it claims 'the audit entry the CALLER writes records how many objects were actually removed', which the code does not do. storage.ts:218-228: `export async function delImageByKey(key) { try { ... DeleteObjectCommand ... } catch { // best-effort cleanup } }` — no logging.
W1-094.failure_scenario: R2 has a bad ten minutes at 21:00 UTC on a night the sweep purges a member with 40 Collection photos. All 40 remain publicly fetchable forever; the audit log says '40 stored image(s) removed'; nobody can ever find them again.
W1-094.fixDirection: Make delImageByKey return success/failure (and log failures); in purgeUserAccount count only true deletions and, before the row delete, persist the collected URL list to a small PurgeQueue table (or the AuditLog detail) so a later retry can finish the job; have the retention sweep retry outstanding object deletions. Report imagesFailed alongside imagesDeleted in the audit detail.
W1-094.gateOrTest: Unit test on a refactored delImage that surfaces failure; a sweep-level test asserting a failed delete leaves a retryable record.
W1-094.reproPlan: code-argument-only (cannot safely exercise deletes against the production bucket).

W1-095.title: Orphaned R2 objects accumulate with no cleanup: abandoned staging uploads, partial finalize failures, validation-refused contributions, and DB-write-after-upload failures all leak publicly fetchable bytes
W1-095.expected: Objects written to R2 either end up referenced by a DB row or get cleaned up; at 2,000 users the bucket does not grow unbounded with unreachable (but publicly fetchable) member photos.
W1-095.actual: Several confirmed leak paths, and no lifecycle rule, reconciliation job, or cleanup sweep exists anywhere in the repo (no reference to staging cleanup in retention.ts, docs/spec/media.md, or any cron): (1) presigned PUT completes but the member closes the tab before finalize/contribute → object sits under staging/ or collection/ forever; (2) finalize's multi-file loop: for keys [A,B], A is processed and its display WebP written to uploads/ (route line 116), then B fails → the route returns 422 with no urls, A's WebP is orphaned, and the finally block deleted BOTH staged originals — so retry means full re-upload and the orphan stays; (3) contributePhotoDirect: the photoSchema validation failure at line 297 `return { error: parsed.error... }` does NOT delete the staged original (the quota branch at 282-287 does — the asymmetry is the bug); (4) any path where putImage succeeds and the subsequent prisma write fails (contributePhotoDirect's photo.create at line 377, updateAvatar's user.update at 246) orphans the fresh objects; (5) composer uploads whose post is never created.
W1-095.evidence: finalize/route.ts:83-125: per-key loop `urls.push(url)` then on a later key's failure `return NextResponse.json({ error ... }, { status: 422 })` inside the loop with `finally { await delImageByKey(key); }` — already-pushed urls are never cleaned and never returned. collection/actions.ts:289-297: `const parsed = photoSchema.safeParse({...}); if (!parsed.success) return { error: parsed.error.issues[0].message };` with no delImageByKey(input.key), unlike the quota branch directly above (lines 283-287). No cleanup exists: grep for 'staging' across retention.ts and the crons returns nothing.
W1-095.failure_scenario: Over months at 2k users, thousands of unreferenced objects accumulate — storage cost, and a privacy wrinkle: an abandoned staged original (full-resolution, EXIF/GPS intact — the re-encode that strips EXIF only happens on finalize) remains fetchable at a guessable-only-by-key public URL indefinitely.
W1-095.fixDirection: Two-pronged: (a) add an R2 lifecycle rule (dashboard, owner action) expiring staging/ objects after 24h — this catches most leaks structurally; (b) fix the code asymmetries: delete the staged key on ANY early return in contributePhotoDirect, and in finalize clean up already-processed WebPs when a later key fails (or return partial urls). Optionally add a weekly reconciliation listing bucket keys not referenced by any row (Photo, User.photoUrl, Post.images, CatchupEntry.images).
W1-095.gateOrTest: Unit test on the finalize loop's failure path asserting compensating deletes; an operational check in the admin worklist showing bucket-vs-rows drift if the reconciliation is built.
W1-095.reproPlan: Read-only live proof: list the bucket's staging/ prefix (read-only S3 ListObjects with existing creds) and check for objects older than a day.

W1-096.title: DB outage during login is reported as 'Invalid email or password', sending members into a doomed reset loop
W1-096.expected: An infrastructure failure at sign-in reads as 'something is wrong on our side, try again shortly' — the login client's own comment says telling someone their password is wrong when it isn't 'sends them into a doomed reset loop'.
W1-096.actual: authorize() throws raw Prisma errors (e.g. `prisma.user.findUnique` at auth.ts:102, pool timeout, connection refused) — these are not CredentialsSignin subclasses, so NextAuth surfaces a generic error result with no code; the client maps every non-'rate-limited'/non-'bot-check' error to the literal string 'Invalid email or password.' The member re-types the password, fails again, then requests a reset — which during the same DB outage also cannot work (and whose anti-oracle design shows success regardless).
W1-096.evidence: login-client.tsx:391-398: `const code = (result as { code?: string | null }).code; setError(code === "rate-limited" ? RATE_LIMITED : code === "bot-check" ? BOT_CHECK_FAILED : "Invalid email or password.");` — the fallback branch is reached for ANY error without those two codes, including NextAuth's wrapping of a thrown database error (CallbackRouteError/Configuration), not just a genuine credential refusal. auth.ts defines only the two CredentialsSignin subclasses (lines 21-26); every other throw in authorize is unclassified.
W1-096.failure_scenario: Supabase has a 2-minute blip at peak evening IST. Every member who tries to sign in is told their password is wrong; several start password resets; a few conclude their account was deleted.
W1-096.fixDirection: In login-client, distinguish the credential-refusal code path from the unknown-error path: NextAuth returns the error type in result.error — treat anything that is not the CredentialsSignin flavor (or: anything where code is absent AND error is not 'CredentialsSignin') as 'We're having trouble on our end. Please try again in a moment.' Optionally add a third CredentialsSignin subclass server-side wrapping infrastructure failures explicitly.
W1-096.gateOrTest: Unit-level test of the client mapping function (extract it); e2e with the auth route intercepted to return a 500 asserting the neutral message.
W1-096.reproPlan: Safe live proof: chrome-devtools on /login, block or 500 the /api/auth/callback/credentials request via request interception, submit dev credentials, read the rendered error text.

W1-097.title: Feed time filters ('Today', 'This week/month/year') use UTC day boundaries — wrong by 5.5 hours for the IST membership
W1-097.expected: A member in India filtering the feed to 'Today' sees posts since their midnight (IST).
W1-097.actual: getTimeFilterDate runs on the server (Vercel, TZ=UTC): `new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate())` is UTC midnight = 05:30 IST. 'Today' at 9am IST silently excludes everything posted between 00:00 and 05:30 IST; 'This week' starts Sunday-UTC (05:30 IST Sunday); 'This month'/'This year' shift the same way, and for the first 5.5 hours of the 1st the 'This month' filter still shows last month's boundary. The same server-local-midnight pattern (`setHours(0,0,0,0)`) appears in the admin dashboard month windows (admin/page.tsx:65, admin/support/page.tsx:40) — admin-only, but the same class.
W1-097.evidence: feed/actions.ts:747-759: `case "today": return new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate());` etc., invoked server-side from loadPosts (line 781) — server components/actions run in UTC on Vercel; members are IST (brief). This is precisely the tracked raw-SQL-timestamp-trap's 'deeper IST instances ARE in scope' class.
W1-097.failure_scenario: A member posts at 1:00am IST; at 8am IST another member filters 'Today' and the post is missing, though the feed unfiltered shows it timestamped 'today'.
W1-097.fixDirection: Compute the boundary in IST: either pass the client's UTC offset with the filter request (the composer already runs client-side), or hard-code Asia/Kolkata (the community is single-timezone by charter) via e.g. a small helper that shifts now by +5:30 before truncating to the day and shifts back. Apply the same helper to the admin month windows.
W1-097.gateOrTest: Unit test on an extracted istDayStart helper across the 00:00-05:30 IST window (repo already has the .test.mjs pattern).
W1-097.reproPlan: code-argument-only (a live proof needs a post created inside the 00:00-05:30 IST window).

W1-098.title: Concurrent same-batch signups can create duplicate 'Batch of {year}' groups (find-then-create with no unique constraint)
W1-098.expected: Exactly one batch group per year; every alumnus of that batch lands in it (batch groups back batch-targeted posts and Catch-ups).
W1-098.actual: joinBatchGroup does `findFirst({ where: { name } })` then `create(...)` with no unique constraint behind it — the code's own comment concedes 'Group.name is not unique in the schema'. Two alumni of the same batch signing up concurrently (launch day, an invite email blast to a batch WhatsApp group) both read null and both create, yielding two groups named 'Batch of 1994' with membership split between them; later signups join whichever findFirst returns first. GroupMember's (groupId,userId) unique protects only membership, not the group row.
W1-098.evidence: actions.ts:215-230: `let group = await prisma.group.findFirst({ where: { name }, select: { id: true } }); if (!group) { group = await prisma.group.create({...}) }`. schema.prisma:193: `name String` — no @@unique. Contrast: the same file's user-create race was explicitly fixed with a P2002 handler (actions.ts:144-169, 'audit L9'), showing the pattern was known but not applied here.
W1-098.failure_scenario: Launch morning: three 1998-batch alumni sign up within the same second from a shared reunion link. Two 'Batch of 1998' groups exist; batch-targeted posts and the batch Catch-up reach only half the batch, permanently, until an admin manually merges rows.
W1-098.fixDirection: Add a partial/derived uniqueness: either a dedicated batchYear column on Group with a unique index (cleanest), or a unique index on name for the 'Batch of %' namespace via migrations-manual, then convert joinBatchGroup to create-catch-P2002-then-findFirst (mirroring the registerUser pattern).
W1-098.gateOrTest: Unit test firing two concurrent joinBatchGroup calls against a test row (or pin via the P2002-handling code path); the migration itself is the real gate.
W1-098.reproPlan: code-argument-only (provoking it needs concurrent real signups against the shared DB).

W1-099.title: Production images are served straight from throttled pub-*.r2.dev through plain tags — Cloudflare rate-limits that hostname and does not intend it for production traffic
W1-099.expected: At 2,000 users, feed/collection/avatar image traffic is served from a host built for production volume (R2 custom domain behind Cloudflare's CDN, or Vercel image optimization absorbing origin fetches).
W1-099.actual: Post images render as `` (post-card.tsx:367, eslint-disabled next/no-img-element) where publicUrl is the raw `R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` — a pub-*.r2.dev URL per AGENTS.md ('served from a pub-*.r2.dev URL; a custom domain can be added before launch'). Cloudflare's documentation states r2.dev public development URLs are rate-limited and not recommended for production. Every member's browser fetches every image directly from that throttled host; nothing tracks the custom-domain switch as a launch blocker (bugs.md has no r2/custom-domain item — verified by grep).
W1-099.evidence: post-card.tsx:366-378: `{/* eslint-disable-next-line @next/next/no-img-element */} `. next.config.ts:167: 'Cloudflare R2 (pub-.r2.dev now; a custom domain can be added later)' — the remotePatterns entry shows next/image is configured for it, but the feed path bypasses next/image entirely. Suspected (not confirmed) because the actual throttle threshold is Cloudflare-side and undocumented numerically; the launch-scale risk is the claim.
W1-099.failure_scenario: Launch week: a few hundred members scroll the feed and collection; aggregate image requests to the single pub-*.r2.dev hostname cross Cloudflare's development-URL throttle; images across the site intermittently 429 and render broken, worst exactly when the most people are looking.
W1-099.fixDirection: Owner action before launch: attach a custom domain (e.g. media.rishivalley.space) to the rv-alumni-media bucket in the Cloudflare dashboard and set R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL to it (storage.ts already builds every URL from that one env var; existing DB rows carry the old host, so add the legacy pub-*.r2.dev host to keyForUrl/delImage handling or migrate stored URLs).
W1-099.gateOrTest: A check in npm run check or a boot log warning when R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL ends in .r2.dev in production; visual suite covers the render either way.
W1-099.reproPlan: Read-only: curl -I one stored image URL to confirm the serving host is pub-*.r2.dev.

W1-100.title: sendMail has no timeout, and verificationMailState performs an inline Resend send during layout render — a hung Resend connection stalls every page load for unconfirmed members
W1-100.expected: Page render never blocks on a third-party mail API; a wedged Resend connection times out in a bounded few seconds (the Turnstile client sets AbortSignal.timeout(5000) for exactly this reason — turnstile.ts:98).
W1-100.actual: `api.emails.send(...)` (email.ts:181-187) passes no timeout/AbortSignal, and the Resend SDK's fetch has no default timeout — a black-holed connection hangs until OS TCP timeouts (minutes) or the platform function ceiling. verificationMailState, awaited inside the (main) layout's render-blocking Promise.all (layout.tsx:35-52), calls claimAndSend → sendMail synchronously when the member has a queued verify row and budget exists (email-queue.ts:597-599, by design: 'it repairs'). So during a Resend hang, every page view by an unconfirmed member blocks on that call; and because each such page view is also a claim, four page views burn the row's four attempts (interlocks with the retry-burn finding).
W1-100.evidence: email.ts:181: `const { data, error } = await api.emails.send({ from: FROM, to: opts.to, ... });` — no signal, no timeout, unlike the fetch in turnstile.ts:89-99. layout.tsx:35: `const [unreadCount, mailState] = await Promise.all([ ..., session.user.emailConfirmed ? Promise.resolve(null) : verificationMailState(session.user.id), ...])` — render-blocking. email-queue.ts:597-599: `if (row.status === "queued") { const outcome = await claimAndSend(row); ... }`.
W1-100.failure_scenario: Resend degrades to hanging connections for ten minutes on launch morning. Every fresh (unconfirmed) signup's first pageview after signup hangs 30-120s on the shimmer, then errors; four pageviews later their verify row is terminally failed.
W1-100.fixDirection: Add AbortSignal.timeout(~8000) to the Resend send (treat abort as a transient failure); in verificationMailState consider moving the repair send into after() and returning 'imminent' for the current render, or keep the inline send but rely on the new timeout to bound render latency.
W1-100.gateOrTest: Unit test asserting sendMail rejects/settles within the timeout when the transport never responds (inject a stalled fetch).

W1-101.title: R2/network failures during upload are blamed on the member's photo ('try a different one'), the misleading generic branch of describeProcessingError
W1-101.expected: An infrastructure failure (R2 500/429, S3 SDK network error) tells the member the service is briefly unavailable and to retry the same photo.
W1-101.actual: Every upload path funnels ALL thrown errors — including putImage/getImageBuffer S3 failures — through describeProcessingError, whose fallback is 'Could not process the photo. Please try a different one, or a JPG or PNG export of it.' During an R2 incident the member re-exports and re-picks photos that were never the problem.
W1-101.evidence: upload-shared.ts:96-108: only 'unsupported image format' and 'premature end|truncated|invalid' are special-cased; everything else → the photo-blaming fallback. finalize/route.ts:118-120 catches around a block containing `getImageBuffer(key)` and `putImage(...)` and returns `describeProcessingError(error)`; same shape at upload/route.ts:130-135 and collection/actions.ts:369-371.
W1-101.failure_scenario: R2 returns 500s for five minutes; a member trying to attach a photo to a post is told three different photos of theirs are unprocessable.
W1-101.fixDirection: In describeProcessingError (or at the call sites), detect S3/aws-sdk error shapes (err.name of S3ServiceException subclasses, $metadata.httpStatusCode, ECONNRESET/ETIMEDOUT) and return 'Our photo storage is briefly unavailable — please try again in a minute.'
W1-101.gateOrTest: Unit test feeding a mock S3ServiceException and asserting the storage-blame sentence.

W1-102.title: GitHub Actions disables scheduled workflows after 60 days of repository inactivity — the nightly retention sweep and 60-day account purge will silently stop once development quiets down
W1-102.expected: The retention sweep (and with it the GDPR account purge) keeps running unattended for the life of the site.
W1-102.actual: GitHub automatically disables cron-scheduled workflows in repositories with no commit activity for 60 days (documented GitHub behavior; an email warning is easy to miss). This project's deploys are git-push driven, so post-launch quiet periods are exactly the plan; after 60 quiet days the sweep stops, retention windows silently stop being enforced, and members' 60-day deletion requests are never purged — precisely the 'cron missed for N days' chaos case, but permanent. Suspected because it depends on future repo activity, not on code.
W1-102.evidence: retention.yml runs `on: schedule: - cron: '0 21 * * *'` from this repo; nothing monitors that it ran (the route writes a 'retention.sweep' audit entry, but nothing alerts on its ABSENCE — retention.ts:151-155 only records successes).
W1-102.failure_scenario: Six months post-launch, no commits for two months: purge-due accounts sit undeleted indefinitely; nobody notices because the failure mode is a job not running.
W1-102.fixDirection: Add a keepalive (the workflow can re-enable itself via a scheduled commit or use the GH API to keep-alive), or move the sweep to the app's existing lazy-tick pattern as a backstop (e.g. the admin dashboard checks the last 'retention.sweep' audit row's age and runs/flags it when stale), or surface 'last sweep ran N days ago' in /admin as a red state.
W1-102.gateOrTest: An /admin worklist item when the newest retention.sweep audit entry is older than 48h.
W1-102.reproPlan: Read-only: `gh api repos/:owner/:repo/actions/workflows` shows workflow state; currently active — the risk is future.

W1-103.title: Place gazetteer search does a full 234,934-row sequential scan on every keystroke of 4+ characters: the altNames ILIKE arm in an OR defeats both expression indexes, and ~15-25 members typing in the onboarding city picker saturate the Supavisor pooler for the whole site
W1-103.expected: Type-ahead city search stays on the two `lower(...) text_pattern_ops` expression indexes at every query length, so each keystroke costs single-digit milliseconds and the shared pooler never notices it.
W1-103.actual: For queries of 4+ characters (i.e. most of every city name typed: "chen", "chenn", "chennai") the WHERE clause becomes `indexable-arm OR indexable-arm OR altNames ILIKE '%q%'`. Postgres can only use a BitmapOr when EVERY arm of an OR is indexable; `"altNames"` has no index of any kind (schema.prisma:636 is a bare `String?`, no migration creates one — verified across all of prisma/migrations-manual/), so the planner falls back to a sequential scan of the full 234,934-row Place table, evaluating `lower()` twice plus an ILIKE over a long comma-joined text column per row, per keystroke, per member.
W1-103.evidence: src/app/api/places/search/route.ts:99-109: `const altNamesClause = raw.length >= 4 ? Prisma.sql`OR "altNames" ILIKE ${containsPattern} ESCAPE '\\'` : Prisma.empty;` folded into `WHERE lower("asciiName") LIKE lower(${prefixPattern}) ESCAPE '\\' OR lower("name") LIKE lower(${prefixPattern}) ESCAPE '\\' ${altNamesClause}`. The only indexes on Place are `CREATE INDEX ... ON "Place" (lower("asciiName") text_pattern_ops)` and the same for name (2026-07-18-round6.sql:30-31) — grep for `pg_trgm|GIN|altNames` across prisma/migrations-manual/*.sql finds no altNames index. The route's own comment admits the arm "degrades to a sequential scan" but treats the 4-char gate as the mitigation; 4+ chars is the COMMON case for a real city name, not the rare one. The arithmetic: Supabase Free plan (docs/OPERATIONS.md:57 "Supabase's free plan has no automatic backups") means Nano compute with Supavisor's default transaction-mode pool_size of ~15 server connections. A 234k-row seq scan with per-row lower()+ILIKE on shared nano CPU is realistically 80-200ms. Ceiling = 15 slots / 0.15s ≈ 100 scans/s. A member typing fires ~3 requests/s (the rate limit at line 84 deliberately allows 120/min); so ~15-25 members simultaneously typing in the LocationPicker — exactly the launch-day onboarding shape, and src/lib/email-queue.ts:18-20 records the owner "expects more than 100 signups on the first day" — occupies every server connection, and EVERY other query in the app (feed, login, notification counts) queues behind the scans at the pooler. Combined with the missing timeouts (next finding) the queue manifests as site-wide hangs, not errors.
W1-103.fixDirection: Two independent fixes, either sufficient: (1) add `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm; CREATE INDEX ON "Place" USING gin ("altNames" gin_trgm_ops);` in a dated migrations-manual file and keep the query as-is (BitmapOr then works for all three arms); or (2) restructure so the OR never mixes indexable and non-indexable arms — run the two prefix arms first (indexed), and only if they return fewer than LIMIT 8 rows run the altNames contains query as a separate statement (or UNION ALL with per-arm LIMIT). Option 2 also cuts the common-case cost to zero extra. Keep the existing ORDER BY semantics (exact match, then own-name prefix, then population).
W1-103.gateOrTest: After the fix, run `EXPLAIN SELECT id FROM "Place" WHERE lower("asciiName") LIKE 'chen%' OR lower("name") LIKE 'chen%' OR "altNames" ILIKE '%chen%'` via scripts/dev/run-sql.mjs and pin that the plan contains no `Seq Scan on "Place"`; add that EXPLAIN assertion as a script check so a future query edit cannot silently regress it.
W1-103.reproPlan: Read-only: run the EXPLAIN above through scripts/dev/run-sql.mjs (SELECT-only) and observe `Seq Scan on Place` with a 4+ char pattern vs `BitmapOr` with a 3-char pattern; optionally time 20 parallel curl requests to /api/places/search?q=chennai against the dev server and watch other routes' latency climb.

W1-104.title: Supabase Free plan cannot carry the 2,000-member ceiling: database egress alone lands multiples over the 5GB/month cap, on top of the already-documented no-backups and Nano-compute constraints
W1-104.expected: The database plan has quota headroom for the stated 2,000-user maximum: query-result egress, compute, and connection caps all clear the projected load.
W1-104.actual: The project is on the Supabase Free plan (docs/OPERATIONS.md:57 states it outright), whose bundled egress is 5GB/month across database + storage. Every authenticated pageview moves roughly 20-60KB of query results out of Supabase (feed/letters post bodies, directory rows, plus the ~13-16 statements per pageview the (main) layout and drain pass run — see coverage notes). At even a conservative 400 daily-active members x 20 pageviews x 30KB, that is ~240MB/day ≈ 7GB/month; at the owner's 2,000-member ceiling with launch-week engagement it is 20-90GB/month. Past the cap Supabase issues over-usage warnings and can restrict the project — i.e. the site degrades precisely when it succeeds. Free also pins Nano compute, which is the denominator in the gazetteer-scan finding, and OPERATIONS.md already documents the no-backup consequence separately.
W1-104.evidence: docs/OPERATIONS.md:57: "Supabase's free plan has **no automatic backups and no point-in-time recovery**" — the plan is Free, stated in the repo's own ops doc. Per-pageview volume is code-verified: src/app/(main)/layout.tsx:35-52 runs `prisma.notification.count`, `advanceDueCatchups(session.user.id)` (a CatchupEdition findMany minimum), `touchLastSeen` (Visit upsert + User updateMany), plus the page's own list queries, plus the `after(drainMailQueue)` pass (5 more statements); feed/letters pages then transfer full post/letter text columns per row. The 5GB/month Free-tier egress figure is a Supabase plan quota, external to the repo — hence status suspected — but the multiplication needs only the repo-side facts above to show the cap is exceeded at any realistic fraction of 2,000 members. R2 already carries image bytes (zero egress), so this is text/query egress alone.
W1-104.fixDirection: This is an ops decision for the owner, pre-launch: upgrade the Supabase project to Pro ($25/mo, 250GB egress, real backups, Micro+ compute) before public release — it simultaneously retires this finding, doubles down on the backup gap OPERATIONS.md already flags, and raises the compute floor under the gazetteer-scan finding. Secondary code lever if egress must shrink: trim over-fetching in list views (select only the columns rendered) — but the plan upgrade is the real fix.
W1-104.gateOrTest: Ops checklist item, not a code gate: after upgrade, verify plan and compute tier in the Supabase dashboard; optionally record the decision in docs/OPERATIONS.md next to the backup paragraph.
W1-104.reproPlan: Read-only: Supabase dashboard usage page shows current egress run-rate; multiply by the member-growth factor. No app interaction needed.

W1-105.title: No timeout at any layer for ordinary queries: pool checkout queues forever (pg default), no connect/statement/query timeout is configured, so a slow or wedged database turns into multi-minute blank-page hangs and platform 504s instead of the app's error page — and each hung request holds pool and concurrency slots, compounding the incident
W1-105.expected: When the database is slow, saturated, or a query wedges, a member's request fails fast into src/app/error.tsx ("something went wrong, retry") within a few seconds, and the stuck request releases its connection so the incident does not snowball.
W1-105.actual: The adapter is constructed as `new PrismaPg({ connectionString })` (src/lib/prisma.ts:16) — no `connectionTimeoutMillis`, no `statement_timeout`, no `query_timeout`, no `max`. The installed pg-pool (node_modules/pg-pool/index.js) defaults `connectionTimeoutMillis` to unset, and its connect() path at lines 205-207 reads `if (!this.options.connectionTimeoutMillis) { this._pendingQueue.push(new PendingItem(response.callback)); return result; }` — the checkout waits in the pending queue with NO timer, forever. The (main) layout awaits its Promise.all BEFORE returning any JSX, above every loading.tsx boundary, so a hung checkout or hung statement means the member sees a blank page (not even the shimmer) until Vercel kills the function at the plan's max duration (minutes under Fluid compute) and returns a bare platform 504 — never the app's error.tsx. Meanwhile that request holds its Fluid concurrency slot and any already-checked-out connections, so under a DB brown-out the backlog compounds. Only interactive transactions have a bound (Prisma JS runtime defaults verified in node_modules/@prisma/client/runtime/client.js: `maxWait??2e3, timeout: ...??5e3`); the ~99% of traffic that is plain queries has none. Note the fast-failure path DOES work when the DB refuses connections outright (ECONNREFUSED -> DriverAdapterError -> error.tsx); it is specifically slowness/saturation that hangs.
W1-105.evidence: src/lib/prisma.ts:16: `const adapter = new PrismaPg({ connectionString });` — the config object is passed verbatim to `new pg.Pool(config)` (node_modules/@prisma/adapter-pg/dist/index.js:779-788). pg-pool defaults verified in node_modules/pg-pool/index.js: line 89 `this.options.max = this.options.max || this.options.poolSize || 10`, line 99 `this.options.idleTimeoutMillis = 10000`, lines 205-207 queue-without-timer as quoted above. src/app/(main)/layout.tsx:35 `const [unreadCount, mailState] = await Promise.all([...])` sits above the per-page loading.tsx boundaries, so its hang blanks the whole response.
W1-105.fixDirection: Pass explicit limits into the one PrismaPg construction site: `new PrismaPg({ connectionString, connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000, statement_timeout: 15_000, query_timeout: 20_000 })` (pg forwards statement_timeout per-connection and enforces query_timeout client-side; both are pgbouncer-transaction-mode safe because pg applies statement_timeout via the startup/SET on the checked-out client per query — verify with one EXPLAIN-style smoke test through the 6543 pooler, and if SET-based statement_timeout proves unreliable through Supavisor, keep query_timeout + connectionTimeoutMillis, which are purely client-side). With a checkout timeout, exhaustion surfaces as `Error('timeout exceeded when trying to connect')` -> DriverAdapterError -> the server component throws -> src/app/error.tsx renders — the actionable path. Consider `max` left at 10 (the arithmetic in this audit shows 10/instance is ample).
W1-105.gateOrTest: A unit test in the security-regressions style that imports src/lib/prisma.ts's adapter options (export the options object) and asserts connectionTimeoutMillis/query_timeout are set, so a future refactor cannot silently drop them.
W1-105.reproPlan: code-argument-only (a live proof would require degrading the shared production database, which is off the table). The pg-pool queue-without-timer lines plus the layout's await placement are sufficient.

W1-106.title: Layout render blocks on an untimed Resend network call for unconfirmed members: a Resend brown-out (accepting connections but not answering) hangs every page view of every unconfirmed member for minutes, and the 2-minute stale-claim recycler makes it recur
W1-106.expected: The verification banner's self-heal ("send the queued row before answering") costs one bounded network call: if Resend does not answer within a few seconds, the layout renders with state "imminent" and the member gets their page.
W1-106.actual: src/app/(main)/layout.tsx:44-46 awaits `verificationMailState(session.user.id)` inside the render-blocking Promise.all for every member with `emailConfirmed` false. email-queue.ts:597-599: `if (row.status === "queued") { const outcome = await claimAndSend(row); ... }` — claimAndSend calls `sendMail`, and email.ts:181 `await api.emails.send({...})` has no AbortSignal, no timeout, no race. The Resend SDK's underlying undici fetch waits up to the default headers timeout (~300s). So when Resend is slow-but-up: the member's page render hangs behind the send; the row was already flipped to "sending" by the claim, so concurrent views take the fast `imminent` path for 2 minutes — then STALE_CLAIM_MS (email-queue.ts:101, `2 * 60_000`) recycles it to "queued" and the NEXT page view hangs again. Every unconfirmed member with a pending verify row loops through hang -> 2min grace -> hang for the duration of the provider incident. This is exactly taxonomy 6k "email provider down mid-signup", and signup week is when the maximum number of members are unconfirmed. The design intent ("Cost: one Resend call inside one page load, once" — email-queue.ts:561-562) assumed the call is bounded; it is not.
W1-106.evidence: email.ts:181-187: `const { data, error } = await api.emails.send({ from: FROM, to: opts.to, subject: opts.subject, html: opts.html, text: opts.text });` — no signal/timeout anywhere in the file (grep for `timeout|AbortSignal|signal` matches nothing). Contrast turnstile.ts:98 which does exactly the right thing for the same class of call: `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`. layout.tsx:44-46: `session.user.emailConfirmed ? Promise.resolve(null) : verificationMailState(session.user.id)` inside the awaited Promise.all.
W1-106.fixDirection: Bound sendMail the way turnstile is bounded: wrap the Resend call in `Promise.race` with a 5-8s timer (or pass fetch options if the SDK version supports a signal), returning `{ ok: false, error: "timeout" }` so claimAndSend's existing requeue path handles it. Independently, consider moving the layout's self-heal send behind `after()` (report the pre-send state synchronously as "imminent", repair post-response) so the render path never contains a mail-provider round trip at all — the banner's honesty invariant survives because the very next view reads the repaired row.
W1-106.gateOrTest: Unit test for sendMail with an injected hanging fetch/SDK double asserting it settles within N seconds with ok:false; the existing email-flow unit tests are the natural home.
W1-106.reproPlan: code-argument-only in production terms; locally provable by pointing RESEND_API_KEY at a black-holing mock (dev-only env) and loading a page as an unconfirmed user — but the quoted code suffices.

W1-107.title: Collection upload fallback path dies at Vercel's 4.5MB request-body cap for any photo between 4.5MB and the advertised 20MB limit, with only a vague toast — and the fallback is the path every member is on while the R2 bucket CORS rule remains unconfigured
W1-107.expected: A member contributing a 12MB phone photo either uploads it via the presigned direct PUT (bytes never touch Vercel) or, on the fallback path, gets the friendly "over the 20MB limit"-style message the action was built to give.
W1-107.actual: contributePhoto is a Server Action accepting `formData.get("file")` up to `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES = 20MB` (upload-shared.ts:9), and next.config.ts raises the Next-level caps to 25mb (serverActions.bodySizeLimit and proxyClientMaxBodySize). But Vercel's platform caps serverless request bodies at 4.5MB regardless of framework config, returning a 413 FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE before the action executes — the 25mb settings only govern local/self-hosted. The dialog knows this and prefers the presigned path (contribute-dialog.tsx:119-125: "Vercel's ~4.5MB request cap never sees the bytes"), but when `directUploadPut` returns null (its documented cases: "local dev without R2, or an origin the bucket's CORS rule does not name") it silently falls back to the Server Action (line 144). Project memory records the bucket CORS configuration as blocked on an admin-scoped token — if that is still true in production, EVERY member is on the fallback, and every photo over ~4.5MB fails with the generic catch toast ("The photo may be too large, or the connection dropped"), which matches the owner's previously reported "fails maybe 1-in-6" symptom. Modern phone photos are routinely 5-12MB.
