Try again in a moment?")`. A member attaching a phone photo of a problem (5-12MB typical) retries forever. This is the support channel — the place members go when something is already wrong.

W1-165.title: For unconfirmed members, every authenticated page render blocks on a synchronous Resend API call with no timeout — a slow or down email provider turns their whole app into hung pages
W1-165.expected: A page render should not be held hostage by a third-party mail API; provider slowness should degrade to the 'imminent' banner state, not to a hanging page.
W1-165.actual: layout.tsx:44-46 awaits `verificationMailState(session.user.id)` inside the render-blocking Promise.all for every unconfirmed member. email-queue.ts:597-599: when their verify row is queued and budget remains, it calls `await claimAndSend(row)` synchronously — which awaits `sendMail` → `api.emails.send(...)` (email.ts:181), a network call with no AbortController/timeout anywhere in the chain. The design intent ("one Resend call inside one page load, once") holds only while Resend answers promptly; if Resend hangs (chaos row: email provider down mid-signup — exactly when unconfirmed members exist in numbers, i.e. launch day), each such member's page views hang until the provider responds or the function duration ceiling 504s the page. The daily budget check does not protect against latency, only volume.
W1-165.evidence: layout.tsx:44-46: `session.user.emailConfirmed ? Promise.resolve(null) : verificationMailState(session.user.id)` inside `await Promise.all([...])`. email-queue.ts:594-599: "Budget is available, so nothing may sit queued: send it now." `const outcome = await claimAndSend(row);`. email.ts:180-187: `await api.emails.send({...})` with no timeout configured; the Resend SDK does not impose one by default.
W1-165.fixDirection: Race the in-render send against a short timeout (~2-3s) and fall through to the honest 'imminent' state on expiry (the row stays claimed/queued and the after() drain retries it); or move the repair-send itself into after() and have the banner poll. Additionally give sendMail an AbortController timeout so no caller can hang on the provider.
W1-165.gateOrTest: Unit test on verificationMailState with a sendMail stub that never resolves, asserting the function returns 'imminent' within the timeout budget.
W1-165.reproPlan: code-argument-only (requires making Resend hang; not reproducible safely against production).

W1-166.title: Abandoned presigned uploads leak R2 objects forever: a browser that PUTs to staging/ or collection/*-o.* but never calls finalize leaves up to 20MB per object with no lifecycle rule and no cleanup job
W1-166.expected: Staged originals that are never finalized (tab closed between PUT and finalize, network drop, browser crash) are eventually reclaimed — via an R2 lifecycle rule on the staging/ prefix or a periodic sweep.
W1-166.actual: The presign route mints keys under `staging/<uid>/...` (posts) and `collection/<uid>/...-o.*` (collection) and the browser PUTs directly to R2. Cleanup of the staged original happens only inside the finalize route's `finally { await delImageByKey(key); }` (finalize/route.ts:121-124) and contributePhotoDirect's success/error paths — i.e. only when the SECOND request actually arrives. Nothing else ever touches these prefixes: the retention sweep (retention.ts) is DB-rows-only, grep for 'staging' across src finds no sweep, and no doc records an R2 lifecycle rule (docs/OPERATIONS.md and docs/SECURITY.md have no mention). Each abandoned attempt strands up to 20MB; the uploads rate limit allows 40/hour/user, so flaky mobile sessions across 2,000 members accumulate real storage cost with no way to distinguish live from dead objects except age — which nothing checks.
W1-166.evidence: presign/route.ts:104-106 builds the staged key; finalize/route.ts:122-123 comment "The staged original's job is done either way" — but only executes when finalize is called. retention.ts contains only prisma deleteMany + purgeUserAccount; no S3 client import. keyForUrl/KNOWN_ROOTS include "staging" (storage.ts:63) yet no code path lists or expires that prefix.
W1-166.fixDirection: Add an R2 lifecycle rule (dashboard) expiring objects under staging/ after ~2 days and *-o.* collection originals after ~2 days (finalize deletes them in seconds when the flow completes); or add a step to the nightly retention sweep that lists the staging/ prefix and deletes objects older than 48h. Document it in docs/OPERATIONS.md either way.
W1-166.gateOrTest: Operational check in docs/OPERATIONS.md; optionally an admin panel counter of staging-prefix object count/age so growth is visible.
W1-166.reproPlan: Read-only live proof: presign an upload with a test account, PUT the object, never call finalize, confirm the object still exists at its public URL days later (HEAD request).

W1-167.title: Worst-case image finalize work (3×20MB originals; full-resolution q90 WebP encode up to 100MP) can exceed the function duration ceiling, and no route or vercel.json sets maxDuration so the deploy rides an unverified platform default
W1-167.expected: The heaviest legitimate upload (a large heritage scan near the 20MB/100MP limits, or three near-max post images in one finalize call) completes within the function's duration limit, or the limit is explicitly configured with headroom.
W1-167.actual: finalize/route.ts processes up to 3 keys sequentially, each: R2 HEAD + GET of ≤20MB + sharp decode (≤100MP allowed by MAX_INPUT_PIXELS, image.ts:24) + 1920px WebP encode + PUT + DELETE. contributePhotoDirect is heavier per image: a full-resolution encode at quality 90 capped only at WebP's 16383px dimension (actions.ts:345-350) — a ~90-100MP PNG scan is decoded twice (display + thumb) and q90-encoded at full size, which on one vCPU is plausibly 60-150s of CPU plus two 20MB transfers. Nothing in the repo sets maxDuration (no `export const maxDuration`, no functions block in vercel.json), so the ceiling is whatever the Vercel project's default is — 300s with Fluid compute, 60s on the legacy Hobby serverless default; the repo gives no evidence which applies. At 60s the collection path fails for exactly the archival scans the feature exists for; even at 300s the 3-file finalize plus a slow R2 day is uncomfortable. On timeout the member gets an opaque 504 after a long wait, and the staged original is left orphaned (ties to the staging-leak finding; the delete in `finally` never runs on a hard timeout).
W1-167.evidence: actions.ts:345-350: `const WEBP_MAX_DIM = 16383; const display = await sharpImage(original).rotate().resize(WEBP_MAX_DIM, WEBP_MAX_DIM, { fit: "inside", withoutEnlargement: true }).webp({ quality: 90 })...` followed by a second full decode for the thumb (line 355). image.ts:24 `MAX_INPUT_PIXELS = 100_000_000` — a 100MP encode at q90 is minutes-scale on serverless CPU. grep maxDuration across src and vercel.json: zero hits.
W1-167.fixDirection: Set an explicit `export const maxDuration` (e.g. 300) on /api/upload/finalize and confirm Fluid compute is enabled on the Vercel project (owner dashboard check); for contributePhotoDirect consider capping the display encode at a saner dimension (e.g. 8192px) or quality 82, and reuse the display decode for the thumb (resize from the decoded pipeline, not a second decode of the original).
W1-167.gateOrTest: Live timing test on production with a ~95MP, ~19MB PNG through the Collection contribute flow (test account), recording wall time; a comment/doc pinning the project's actual duration default.
W1-167.reproPlan: Test-account write via the app UI: contribute a synthetic 19MB ~95MP PNG to the Collection on production and time it; if it 504s, the finding is confirmed.

W1-168.title: Account export is unbounded (no take on any of the ten queries) and pretty-printed; a prolific member's export can exceed Vercel's 4.5MB response cap and 500
W1-168.expected: The GDPR export succeeds for the most prolific member the site can produce, or is chunked/streamed.
W1-168.actual: All ten findMany calls (posts, comments, likes, photos, catchupEntries, adminMessages, reportsFiled, contributions, places) have no `take`, everything is buffered into one object, and `JSON.stringify(body, null, 2)` roughly doubles the byte count with indentation before returning it as a single NextResponse. Vercel caps function response bodies at ~4.5MB; a member with years of letters (posts.content is the full text of every letter) plus hundreds of comments and catch-up answers can cross it, at which point the export 500s (FUNCTION_RESPONSE_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE) with no fallback — and the rate limit (3/day) means three failed attempts lock them out until tomorrow. Unlikely at launch, increasingly plausible over years toward the 2,000-member ceiling.
W1-168.evidence: export/route.ts:87-91 `prisma.post.findMany({ where: { authorId: userId }, orderBy: { createdAt: "asc" }, select: { ... content: true ... } })` — no take; line 164 `return new NextResponse(JSON.stringify(body, null, 2), ...)` — fully buffered, indented.
W1-168.fixDirection: Drop the pretty-printing (JSON.stringify(body)) to roughly halve the size now; longer-term, stream the JSON or split the export into sections. Optionally count bytes and, over a threshold, return a smaller non-indented body.
W1-168.gateOrTest: A unit test asserting the export uses compact JSON; a synthetic-data measurement of bytes-per-1000-posts to pin the real headroom.
W1-168.reproPlan: code-argument-only at current data volumes (fabricating a >4.5MB member on production would mean mass-writing real rows).

W1-169.title: Email case/whitespace never normalized at signup or login, but IS normalized at password reset: mixed-case signups can never reset their password (silently), one mailbox can register twice, and exact-case login lockouts
W1-169.expected: One canonical form of an email address across signup, login, and reset: 'Ananya@Gmail.com ' and 'ananya@gmail.com' are the same account everywhere.
W1-169.actual: Signup stores the address exactly as typed; login looks it up exactly as typed; ONLY the reset flow lowercases+trims before lookup. A member whose stored email contains any uppercase (or who types a stray trailing space at login) gets 'Invalid email or password', and their password-reset request silently sends nothing — the anti-oracle design returns the identical { ok: true } either way, so there is no signal to anyone that it failed.
W1-169.evidence: registerUser stores raw: `const existing = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: parsed.data.email } })` (actions.ts:103-105) and `email: parsed.data.email` in the create (actions.ts:149); signupSchema uses plain `z.email(...)` with no transform (validators.ts:18). authorize() lowercases ONLY the rate-limit key: `const acctKey = email.trim().toLowerCase();` (auth.ts:62) but queries raw: `const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email } });` (auth.ts:102-104) — no trim, no lowercase. The reset flow does the opposite: `const raw = ((formData.get("email") as string) ?? "").trim().toLowerCase();` then `findUnique({ where: { email: raw } })` (email-actions.ts:160-166), and by design 'ALWAYS returns the same bare { ok: true }' (comment at 138-143), so the miss is invisible. Schema: `email String @unique` (schema.prisma:13) — a case-SENSITIVE Postgres unique, and no lower(email) index or citext exists anywhere in prisma/ (grep confirmed). Neither login-client.tsx nor signup-form.tsx lowercases before submit (grep confirmed). Consequences chain: (1) signup 'Sanan@Gmail.com' → reset typed any way except that exact casing finds no row → no mail, forever, silently; (2) 'sanan@gmail.com' and 'Sanan@Gmail.com' can both register (case-sensitive unique allows both) — one human, two accounts, the exact duplicate problem adminMergeUsers exists to clean up; (3) login requires byte-exact case match of whatever was stored at signup.
W1-169.fixDirection: Normalize (trim + toLowerCase) at every boundary: in registerUser before the findUnique/create, in authorize() before the findUnique (keep acctKey as-is), and keep the reset flow as the reference. Then a one-time data migration: lowercase every existing User.email, first checking `SELECT lower(email), count(*) FROM "User" GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1` for collisions to merge by hand. Optionally add a unique index on lower(email) in a migrations-manual file as the structural backstop.
W1-169.gateOrTest: New unit test in the security-regressions suite: register with 'MiXeD@Case.Com', assert authorize() succeeds with 'mixed@case.com' and that requestPasswordReset('mixed@case.com') enqueues a row. A second assert that registering the lowercase twin of an existing mixed-case address is refused.
W1-169.reproPlan: code-argument-only (a live proof would write a real user row into the shared production database)

W1-170.title: Clicking a superseded verification link shows 'Already confirmed — nothing left to do' (happy bird, no resend button) to a member who is NOT confirmed
W1-170.expected: A verify link that was invalidated by a newer 'resend' should say 'this link was replaced, use the newest email' (or offer a resend) — never claim the address is confirmed when it is not.
W1-170.actual: mintToken burns ALL outstanding tokens of a kind on every new mint, setting usedAt on tokens that were never redeemed. readToken cannot distinguish 'redeemed' from 'superseded' — both come back reason 'used' — and confirmEmailToken maps 'used' straight to 'already', which the page renders as 'Already confirmed / This address was confirmed earlier. Nothing left to do.' with the celebrating bird and, because 'already' is in the GOOD set, the resend button is suppressed (canResend = signedIn && !alreadyVerified && !good). The member walks away believing they are done; every Stage-1/Stage-2 gate stays closed.

The mapping: `if (read.reason === "used") { // Used token: if the address really is confirmed, say so plainly. return "already"; }` (email-actions.ts:106-110) — the comment claims a check ('if the address really is confirmed') that the code does not perform. The rendering: COPY.already = 'Already confirmed / This address was confirmed earlier. Nothing left to do.' (verify-client.tsx:31-34), GOOD includes 'already' (line 55), so `canResend = signedIn && !alreadyVerified && !good` (line 76) is false — no way forward is offered. Trigger sequence a launch member will hit: signup sends mail 1 (token A); mail is slow, member presses Resend on the banner; the first row is already status 'sent' so enqueueMail's fold does not apply (fold only matches status queued/sending, email-queue.ts:308-317) → new row → token B minted, token A burned; member opens the OLDER mail in their inbox → 'Already confirmed', false.
W1-170.fixDirection: In confirmEmailToken, when readToken returns 'used', load the user via the token row (rows are kept 7 days past expiry precisely to answer this kind of question — auth-tokens.ts:102-106; readToken already selects userId before consuming) and return 'already' only when user.emailVerified != null; otherwise return a new 'superseded' outcome (or reuse 'expired') whose copy says a newer link replaced this one, with the resend button enabled. Alternatively store a distinct supersededAt instead of writing usedAt at mint time.
W1-170.gateOrTest: Unit test on the flow: mint token A, mint token B (burning A), then confirmEmailToken(A) for a user whose emailVerified is null must NOT return 'already'.
W1-170.reproPlan: code-argument-only (proving it live requires registering a real account and sending real mail from the shared production domain)

W1-171.title: R2 delete failures are swallowed with no log anywhere (delImageByKey empty catch), and purgeUserAccount reports delete ATTEMPTS as deletions — a GDPR purge can leave every image publicly fetchable forever while the audit log says 'N stored image(s) removed'
W1-171.expected: Deleting a member's stored images either succeeds, or the failure is at least logged with the failed keys and reflected in the audit entry so it can be retried — especially in the purge path, where the code itself documents that after the row cascade 'nothing can enumerate the objects' ever again.
W1-171.actual: delImageByKey's catch block is completely empty — not even the repo's own 'loud in dev' rule is honoured, making it the one catch site in the codebase that violates the stated contract. purgeUserAccount then counts `deleted += 1` for every URL regardless of outcome, and both the retention sweep and adminDeleteUser write that count into the audit log as fact. If R2 has a bad minute (or credentials rotate, or the bucket name env var drifts) during a purge, zero objects are deleted, the rows that pointed at them are already gone, the images stay live at their public pub-*.r2.dev URLs forever, and every record says the purge removed them.
W1-171.evidence: storage.ts:218-228: `export async function delImageByKey(key: string): Promise<void> { try { ... } catch { // best-effort cleanup } }` — empty catch, no console.error even in development. account-purge.ts:108-113: `let deleted = 0; for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); deleted += 1; } return { ok: true, imagesDeleted: deleted };` — the counter increments unconditionally because delImage never throws. The header comment on purgeUserAccount even says 'the audit entry the CALLER writes records how many objects were actually removed' (account-purge.ts:85-86) — which this makes untrue. Consumed as fact at retention.ts:127-133 (`detail: "...${purged.imagesDeleted} stored image(s) removed"`) and admin-actions.ts:64-73. The irreversibility is documented in the same file: 'URLs are collected FIRST, because the cascade takes the pointing rows with it and afterwards nothing can enumerate the objects' (account-purge.ts:80-82). Every other delete caller (deletePost, declinePhoto, adminRemovePhoto, updateAvatar) shares the same invisible-failure property, but the purge is where it becomes unrecoverable.
W1-171.fixDirection: Make delImageByKey return a boolean (or throw-and-let-callers-decide) and log the key on failure in ALL environments (this is a moderation/GDPR path, not per-page telemetry). In purgeUserAccount, count real successes, include failures (count + keys) in PurgeResult, and have the retention sweep/adminDeleteUser record failures in the audit detail and errors[]. For durability, consider writing failed keys to a small table the next sweep retries — the row cascade means these keys exist nowhere else.
W1-171.gateOrTest: Unit test with a stubbed R2 client that rejects DeleteObjectCommand: purgeUserAccount must return imagesDeleted: 0 and surface the failed keys; the retention sweep result must carry the failure.
W1-171.reproPlan: code-argument-only (any live proof would delete real objects or real rows in the shared production bucket/database)

W1-172.title: Feed 'Today / This week / This month / This year' filters compute day boundaries in server-local (UTC) time — wrong post sets for every IST member; server-rendered letter/photo dates shift a day before 05:30 IST
W1-172.expected: 'Today' for a member in India means the IST calendar day (the codebase already knows this rule: wordle.ts keys on Asia/Kolkata, admin-analytics.ts uses AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata').
W1-172.actual: getTimeFilterDate builds boundaries from the server clock, which is UTC on Vercel: `new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate())` (feed/actions.ts:748-749). UTC midnight is 05:30 IST, so a member filtering 'Today' at 02:00 IST gets a window that starts at 05:30 IST YESTERDAY (posts from a different day counted as today), and between 05:30 IST and midnight the window silently excludes anything posted 00:00-05:30 IST. 'This week' compounds it with `d.setDate(d.getDate() - d.getDay())` (Sunday-start in UTC, line 751-752); month and year shift the same way. Separately, server components render date-only stamps with no timeZone: letters/[id]/page.tsx:165 `new Date(letter.createdAt).toLocaleDateString("en-GB", ...)` and collection/[id]/page.tsx:145 — a letter published at 01:00 IST on the 15th displays 'the 14th' to everyone, since server-side toLocaleDateString defaults to UTC.
W1-172.evidence: feed/actions.ts:742-760 — the whole switch runs on the server inside the loadPosts server action (all four cases quoted above); nothing passes a timezone. Contrast with the codebase's own correct handling: wordle.ts:20-22 `date.toLocaleDateString("en-CA", { timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata" })` and admin-analytics.ts:584-585 `EXTRACT(HOUR FROM "endedAt" AT TIME ZONE 'Asia/Kolkata')` — the rule exists, these surfaces missed it. Members are stated IST (+5:30) in the brief; servers UTC.
W1-172.fixDirection: Compute filter boundaries in Asia/Kolkata: derive the IST calendar date (the en-CA/timeZone trick already used in wordle.ts, or Intl.DateTimeFormat parts), then construct the UTC instant for IST midnight (IST date minus 5h30m). For the rendered dates, pass timeZone: 'Asia/Kolkata' to every server-side toLocaleDateString of a member-facing date (letters, collection detail, catchup masthead/console/archive where those render on the server), or move formatting into client components where the browser's zone is correct.
W1-172.gateOrTest: Unit test getTimeFilterDate (extract it to a pure lib file): with a mocked now of 21:00 UTC (02:30 IST next day), 'today' must start at 18:30 UTC, not 00:00 UTC.
W1-172.reproPlan: Read-only live proof: sign in via dev-login, post nothing; at any time between 05:30 IST and midnight IST call loadPosts({timeFilter:'today'}) and compare its boundary against an IST-midnight query — or simply evaluate getTimeFilterDate on the server and read the returned instant.

W1-173.title: All five feed/collection toggle actions (toggleLike, toggleCommentLike, toggleBookmark, togglePhotoLove, votePoll) have no P2002/P2025 handler and no client pending-guard: a double-tap throws an unhandled server-action error and desyncs the optimistic heart
W1-173.expected: The DB @@unique constraints (Like [userId,postId] schema:465, CommentLike:627, Bookmark:428, PhotoLove:188, PollVote:616) are the real guard, so the second racer's P2002/P2025 must be caught and treated as 'already done', the way report-action.ts:189-192 and catchups' runAction already do.
W1-173.actual: Every toggle is check-then-write with no try/catch: `const existing = await prisma.like.findUnique(...); if (existing) { await prisma.like.delete({ where: { id: existing.id } }); } else { await prisma.like.create(...) }` (feed/actions.ts:477-495). Two overlapping requests (the heart has NO disabled state — handleLike in post-card.tsx:134-144 fires the action on every click with only optimistic setState) both read existing=null → the loser's create throws P2002 → the server action throws → on the client `await toggleLike(post.id)` REJECTS, `result.error` handling never runs, the rejection is unhandled, and the optimistic state is left inverted relative to the database (two clicks flipped the UI twice; the server recorded one like). The delete side throws P2025 the same way. votePoll's switch branch (`update({ where: { id: existing.id } })`, feed/actions.ts:295-297) throws P2025 if the vote row vanished between read and write. Catch-ups' toggleEntryLove is wrapped by runAction so it degrades to a friendly error (catchups/actions.ts:162-172) — the feed and collection toggles have no such wrapper.
W1-173.evidence: post-card.tsx:134-144: `async function handleLike() { const next = !liked; setLiked(next); setLikeCount(...); if (demo) return; const result = await toggleLike(post.id); if (result.error) { ... } }` — no busy flag, no try/catch, so a rejected action promise never reverts state or toasts. Same shape in comments-section.tsx and letter-engagement.tsx. Schema constraints confirmed present (the brief's required check): Like schema.prisma:465, CommentLike:627, Bookmark:428, PollVote:616, PhotoLove:188, CatchupEntryLove:801 — every one-per-user rule has its unique; only the handlers are missing.
W1-173.fixDirection: Two cheap layers: (a) in each toggle action, catch P2002 on create → return { success: true, liked: true } (it IS liked), and P2025 on delete/update → return the current truth instead of throwing; (b) in the client handlers, add a busy ref (or useTransition isPending) and a try/catch that reverts optimistic state and toasts on rejection.
W1-173.gateOrTest: Unit-test the action against a stubbed prisma that throws {code:'P2002'} on create: toggleLike must resolve with success, not reject. Playwright: double-click the heart, expect.poll the like count settles at 1 with no console error.
W1-173.reproPlan: Live: sign in via dev-login on localhost, open a post, fire two toggleLike calls concurrently from the console (Promise.all of two fetches to the action endpoint) and observe one rejection; harmless (a like on your own test post) but the shared-DB rule argues for code-argument-only unless done on the owner's own row.

W1-174.title: deletePost / deleteDraft / declinePhoto delete the R2 bytes BEFORE the database row: a failed row-delete leaves live content with permanently dead images
W1-174.expected: The ordering purgeUserAccount documents and follows: 'bytes are deleted only AFTER the row delete succeeds, because if the delete throws and rolls back, the member still exists and their images must keep rendering' (account-purge.ts:83-86).
W1-174.actual: deletePost runs `await deletePostImages(post.images); await prisma.post.delete({ where: { id: postId } });` (feed/actions.ts:336-339) — bytes first. If post.delete throws (DB blip, pooler timeout, or any future FK RESTRICT), the action errors, the post remains fully visible in the feed, and its images are 404s forever; retrying the delete works, but a member who gives up after the error leaves a broken post standing. deleteDraft (feed/actions.ts:250-252) and declinePhoto (collection/actions.ts:544-549: three delImage calls, then photo.delete) have the same inverted order. adminRemovePhoto does it correctly (hide row first, then bytes, collection/actions.ts:585-592).
W1-174.evidence: Quoted lines above; contrast with the explicitly-reasoned correct order in account-purge.ts:74-86. delImage never throws (storage.ts:267-271), so the images are already gone by the time the row delete runs — there is no rollback for object storage.
W1-174.fixDirection: Swap the order in all three: delete the row first, then best-effort delete the bytes (collect URLs before the row delete, as purgeUserAccount does). For declinePhoto also move the row delete ahead of the three delImage calls.
W1-174.gateOrTest: Unit test with a prisma stub whose post.delete rejects: assert delImage was not yet called.
W1-174.reproPlan: code-argument-only (forcing a row-delete failure against the shared production database is not safe)

W1-175.title: sendMail has no timeout, and verificationMailState performs the Resend send synchronously inside the (main) layout's render Promise.all: a hanging Resend blocks every page for every unconfirmed member, and a verificationMailState throw 500s their layout
W1-175.expected: Third-party calls on a render path carry a timeout (the codebase's own pattern: turnstile.ts:98 `AbortSignal.timeout(5000)`, razorpay.ts:84 `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)`, catchups.ts resolveSpotify 3s), and a mail-state read that fails must degrade, not take the page down.
W1-175.actual: email.ts:181-187 calls `await api.emails.send({...})` with no AbortSignal and the Resend SDK sets no default timeout of its own — a Resend endpoint that hangs (as opposed to erroring, which IS handled at email.ts:197) holds the caller until the function's 60s ceiling. verificationMailState is 'the sender, not just the reader': for an unconfirmed member with a queued row and budget available it awaits claimAndSend → sendMail inside the layout's `const [unreadCount, mailState] = await Promise.all([...])` (layout.tsx:34-51), i.e. inside first-byte render of EVERY authenticated page for that member. Additionally, verificationMailState can itself throw (e.g. the DB hiccups between claimAndSend's claim and its catch-block bookkeeping update at email-queue.ts:228-235 — a catch that performs another awaited DB write and rethrows on its failure), and because it sits in the same Promise.all as the notification count, one rejection fails the whole layout (the Promise.all sibling-abort class): the unconfirmed member gets an error page instead of a page with a degraded banner.
W1-175.evidence: email.ts:180-187 (fetch-based SDK call, no signal, no timeout option); the design note email-queue.ts:552-562 ('Sending from the read path makes the invariant structural... one Resend call inside one page load'); layout.tsx:41-45 `session.user.emailConfirmed ? Promise.resolve(null) : verificationMailState(session.user.id)` awaited in the render Promise.all; claimAndSend's catch block itself awaits prisma.outboundEmail.update (email-queue.ts:227-237) so a second failure there propagates out of verificationMailState.
W1-175.fixDirection: Give sendMail an AbortSignal.timeout (10-15s) mapped to { ok: false, error: 'timeout' } — the queue's retry machinery already handles that outcome cleanly. Wrap the verificationMailState call in the layout with its own .catch(() => null) (banner degrades to nothing) so it can never reject the layout's Promise.all; and wrap claimAndSend's catch-block update in its own try/catch that logs instead of rethrowing.
W1-175.gateOrTest: Unit test sendMail against a fetch stub that never resolves: must reject/return within the timeout. Test verificationMailState with a throwing prisma stub: must not propagate.
W1-175.reproPlan: code-argument-only (requires simulating a hung Resend endpoint; not reproducible safely against the live key)

W1-176.title: A bounce or spam-complaint webhook rewrites OutboundEmail.status 'sent'→'failed', which silently removes that send from dailyBudget's count — the queue can then overrun Resend's real 100/day cap on exactly the high-bounce launch day the queue was built for
W1-176.expected: dailyBudget counts what Resend actually accepted today (its own comment: 'Counted off sentAt rather than a counter column, so it cannot drift out of step with what actually went out').
W1-176.actual: dailyBudget counts `where: { status: "sent", sentAt: { gte: startOfUtcDay() } }` (email-queue.ts:258-260) — it requires status 'sent'. The Resend webhook deliberately flips bounced/complained rows to status 'failed' so they surface on the admin worklist (webhook route.ts:118 `status: "failed"` for bounces, :128 for complaints) but leaves sentAt set. Every same-UTC-day bounce therefore subtracts one from 'used', the drain believes it has more budget than Resend does, and sends past the provider's real 100/day — those late sends fail, burn retry attempts, and can consume the RESET_RESERVE arithmetic that exists to keep password resets deliverable. The 5-message safety margin (DAILY_CAP=95, email-queue.ts:73-80) absorbs five bounces; a launch-day address list stale enough to matter blows past five — the exact scenario the webhook's own header comment describes ('a few hundred invitations... half of them bouncing off stale addresses').
W1-176.evidence: Quoted both sides above; bounced rows keep sentAt (the webhook patch at route.ts:99-133 never touches sentAt), so the fix is purely a filter change. The interaction is invisible today because nothing has bounced; it activates precisely under launch load.
W1-176.fixDirection: Count budget by sentAt alone: `where: { sentAt: { gte: startOfUtcDay() } }` (a row with sentAt set was accepted by Resend regardless of its later delivery status), or `status: { in: ["sent", "failed"] }, sentAt: { gte: ... }`. One-line change in dailyBudget plus the mirror count in mailHealth (email-queue.ts:502-505) if the admin number should match.
W1-176.gateOrTest: Unit test: create a row with status 'failed' but sentAt today (the bounce shape); dailyBudget().used must include it.
W1-176.reproPlan: code-argument-only (proving it live requires generating a real bounce from the production sending domain)

W1-177.title: joinBatchGroup find-or-create has no unique backstop (Group.name is not unique): two same-batch members signing up concurrently create two 'Batch of YYYY' groups and the batch splits
W1-177.expected: Exactly one 'Batch of 2010' group ever exists; concurrent first-signups from one batch race safely (the codebase's own standard elsewhere: catchup creation catches P2002 on the unique Catchup.groupId, catchups/actions.ts:366-372).
W1-177.actual: `let group = await prisma.group.findFirst({ where: { name } }); if (!group) { group = await prisma.group.create({...}) }` (actions.ts:215-230) with the code's own admission one line up: 'Group.name is not unique in the schema, so match by exact name' (schema.prisma:191-208 confirms — only @@index([visibility, createdAt])). Two members of a new batch submitting within the same window both see null and both create. Members of the batch are then split across two identical-looking groups (later signups land in whichever findFirst returns first), group feeds diverge, and any batch-group Catch-up can only attach to one of them (Catchup.groupId unique). Launch day — many same-batch signups in the same hour — is the exact concurrency profile.
W1-177.evidence: Quoted above. The catch around joinBatchGroup (actions.ts:176-181) logs and continues, so even the loser of a hypothetical unique constraint would today be silently dropped from the group rather than upserted into the winner.
W1-177.fixDirection: Add a partial/functional unique backstop in migrations-manual (e.g. UNIQUE index on name for the batch groups, or a dedicated batchYear column on Group with a unique index), then rewrite joinBatchGroup as create-catch-P2002-then-findFirst-and-upsert-membership. A cleanup query for any already-duplicated batch groups belongs in the same change.
W1-177.gateOrTest: Unit test the race: stub findFirst to return null twice, assert the second create path recovers via the constraint instead of inserting a duplicate.
W1-177.reproPlan: code-argument-only (would create real Group rows in the shared production database)

W1-178.title: Two live write endpoints skip validation caps entirely: updateUserPlaces (settings) accepts unbounded label/city strings and unvalidated placeId/lat/lng, and the legacy onboarding updateProfile writes bio/city/workplace/socials with no length limit at all
W1-178.expected: Every server action Zod-validates everything including shapes and lengths (the repo standard: onboarding's own placeSchema caps label/city at 160 and validates placeId as int, components/onboarding/actions.ts:22-28; profileSchema caps bio at 1000).

The legacy (auth)/onboarding updateProfile — still live, imported by onboarding/page.tsx:16 — loops seven fields (`bio, currentCity, workplace, jobTitle, phone, instagram, linkedin`) and writes any non-empty string straight to prisma.user.update with no cap (actions.ts:12-27), bypassing every limit profileSchema enforces on the same columns elsewhere (bio 1000, phone 24, instagram 100...).

(auth)/onboarding/actions.ts:15-27 quoted in full: `for (const field of fields) { const value = formData.get(field) as string | null; if (value && value.trim()) { data[field] = value.trim(); } } ... await prisma.user.update({...data})`. Both are 'use server' exports, i.e. public POST endpoints regardless of what UI calls them. adminUpdatePlaces (admin/people/actions.ts:132-148) shares updateUserPlaces' shape but is admin-gated, lower risk.
W1-178.fixDirection: Give updateUserPlaces the exact placeSchema onboarding already has (z.array(placeSchema).max(30)) and let adminUpdatePlaces share it. For the legacy updateProfile, either delete it and move the onboarding page onto the validated components/onboarding actions, or bolt profileSchema's field caps onto it.
W1-178.gateOrTest: Unit test: updateUserPlaces with a 100k-char label and with placeId: 'x' must return a validation error, not throw or write.

W1-179.title: Directory numeric URL params reach Prisma as NaN: /directory?year=1a (or yearFrom/yearTo) throws inside render and the page errors
W1-179.expected: A malformed filter value in the URL degrades to 'filter ignored' (or empty results), never to an error page.

W1-180.title: Abandoned presigned uploads are never cleaned up: staging/ and collection/*-o originals (the EXIF/GPS-bearing files) accumulate forever at public URLs with no lifecycle sweep
W1-180.expected: A staged object whose finalize never arrives (tab closed, network drop, browser crash between the PUT and the finalize call) is eventually deleted — by an R2 lifecycle rule on the staging/ prefix or a sweep.
W1-180.actual: The presign route mints keys under `staging/<userId>/...` (kind 'post') and `collection/<userId>/...-o.<ext>` (kind 'collection') (presign route.ts:102-106); deletion happens ONLY in the finalize route's finally (finalize:121-124) and in contributePhotoDirect's success/error paths (collection/actions.ts:366-372). For the collection kind this is worse than cost: the staged file is the raw original whose EXIF/GPS the whole M12 re-encode exists to strip, sitting at a public R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL/collection/... URL (unguessable cuid, but public and permanent). Related orphan paths in the same class: /api/upload's multi-file loop returns 422 after file 1 already hit R2 (upload/route.ts:128-136 — file 1's object is never referenced or deleted), and contributePhotoDirect orphans its two freshly-put webp objects if the subsequent prisma.photo.create throws (collection/actions.ts:361-364 vs 377).

W1-180.fixDirection: Cheapest and most robust: an R2 lifecycle rule (dashboard, owner action) expiring `staging/` after 1 day and unreferenced `collection/*-o.*` after 7 days. Code-side alternative: a step in the nightly retention sweep listing the staging/ prefix and deleting objects older than 24h; and in contributePhotoDirect, delete the two put objects in the catch around photo.create.
W1-180.gateOrTest: After the lifecycle rule exists, docs/OPERATIONS.md records it; a unit test pins contributePhotoDirect deleting its puts when the row insert fails (stubbed prisma).
W1-180.reproPlan: code-argument-only (verifying live would write real objects into the production bucket)

W1-181.title: Collection fallback upload path (used whenever presign/CORS fails) dies at Vercel's ~4.5MB platform body cap for full-resolution photos, with an opaque failure the 25mb bodySizeLimit cannot fix
W1-181.expected: When the direct-to-R2 path is unavailable (new domain not in the bucket's CORS allowlist, presign hiccup), a >4.5MB Collection photo either still uploads or fails with a message that names the size problem.

Members on any future domain/preview deployment uploading real photos hit an unexplained failure.

W1-181.fixDirection: In the contribute dialog's fallback branch, check file.size > ~4MB BEFORE attempting the proxied upload and show a specific message ('this photo is too large to upload from this connection right now — try again later or a smaller export'); optionally catch the failed action invocation and map it to the same sentence. W1-183.title: Retention sweep is one serverless invocation doing every table's delete plus every due account purge sequentially — approaching the 60s ceiling as purges with many images stack up, and a timeout loses the sweep's own audit entry
W1-183.expected: The nightly sweep completes comfortably inside the function duration limit at realistic scale, or degrades in a resumable way.
W1-183.actual: The purge step loops due accounts serially (`for (const row of rows) { const purged = await purgeUserAccount(row.id); ... }`, retention.ts:120-134), and each purge deletes R2 objects one-by-one (`for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); }`, account-purge.ts:109-112). A member with hundreds of Collection photos means hundreds of sequential DeleteObject round trips (~100-200ms each from a Vercel function to R2); two or three heavy accounts falling due the same night plus the seven deleteMany steps can plausibly cross 60s. Because each step IS idempotent, a timeout mostly self-heals tomorrow — but the sweep's closing writeAudit (retention.ts:151-155) and the route's JSON result are lost, so the owner's 'is retention actually running' answer (the stated purpose of that audit entry) goes dark for that night, and a heavy account could conceivably time out mid-purge-loop repeatedly (its own purge is transactional and completes or not; the loop position is what's lost).
W1-183.evidence: Quoted loops above; no batching (delImage calls are not Promise.all'd in the purge, unlike deletePostImages), no maxDuration export on the route, no chunking of due accounts.
W1-183.fixDirection: Batch object deletes (Promise.allSettled in groups of ~20, or S3 DeleteObjects batch API), cap accounts purged per sweep (e.g. 10 oldest-due per night — idempotence makes the rest tomorrow's work), and write the audit entry per-purge rather than only at the end (it already does per-purge entries; keep the summary but make it best-effort early).
W1-183.gateOrTest: A timing assertion is impractical; pin the batching with a unit test that purgeUserAccount issues grouped deletes, and log sweep duration in the result JSON so the GitHub Action can alert past 30s.
W1-183.reproPlan: code-argument-only (cannot run the sweep against production data)

W1-187.title: Demo reset leaves the world half-written for its whole duration and can sign every concurrent visitor out to a dead /login page; nothing bounds two resets running at once, which can interleave and 500 or strip tables until the next reset
W1-187.expected: A reset pressed by one visitor (the Reset button is on every demo page, unauthenticated at the API) should not break another visitor's session or leave a corrupted world; ideally the rewrite is transactional or at least serialized.
W1-187.actual: Three connected defects. (1) seedDemo is ~40 sequential statements with no transaction (seed.ts:72-95 deletes 21 tables one by one, then recreates); for the several seconds it runs, concurrent visitors see an empty/partial feed, missing posts, and FK failures (P2003) on any in-flight comment/like against rows being deleted; a visitor's server action throws an unhandled Prisma error -> generic error UI. (2) In the window between `prisma.user.deleteMany({})` (seed.ts:95) and the user createMany (seed.ts:99), demoSession's findUnique on DEMO_USER_ID returns null (auth.ts:339-358 "if (!user) return null") and the (main) layout redirects that visitor to /login (layout.tsx:24-26) — a real credentials form on a deployment with no accounts and no way back except manually navigating away. (3) The 20s throttle is module state on ONE serverless instance ("serverless instances do not share memory... bounds one instance rather than the fleet", route.ts:35-42), and the cron GET path never touches lastReset at all — so two resets can genuinely run concurrently (two instances, or cron + button at 20:00 UTC). Both write the SAME fixed ids (demo-post-*, demo-u-*, demo-notif-*), so run B's createMany can hit P2002 against run A's rows and die mid-seed AFTER having deleted tables A had already filled — e.g. B's comment.deleteMany runs after A wrote comments, then B dies on post P2002: the demo serves a feed with zero comments until the next successful reset (nightly).
W1-187.evidence: seed.ts:66-71 comment admits the order is "spelled out so that a failure halfway through leaves a diagnosable state" — i.e. explicitly not atomic. route.ts:42-43: `const MIN_GAP_MS = 20_000; let lastReset = 0;` (module scope, per instance); GET handler (route.ts:86-112) has no throttle interaction. auth.ts:354-358: "An unseeded demo database is a deployment mistake... returning null sends the visitor to /login" — but the same null fires mid-reset, which is a routine nightly runtime state, not a deployment mistake. demo-bar.tsx:67-71 awaits the POST before navigating, so the presser is safe; every OTHER concurrent visitor is not. seedDemo's ids are deterministic constants (`pid = (slug) => \`demo-post-${slug}\``), so concurrent runs collide on primary keys by construction.
W1-187.fixDirection: Wrap seedDemo's body in one `prisma.$transaction` (a single-database rewrite of ~1,600 rows is well within Postgres limits; raise the interactive-transaction timeout for this call) so visitors read either the old world or the new, never the half-world, and the user row never vanishes; alternatively delete users LAST and upsert the visitor row first. Serialize resets with a Postgres advisory lock taken via the reset's own DIRECT client (it is its own session; do this on the unguarded client, not the pooled app client) or a cheap `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a one-row lock table, so a second concurrent reset waits or no-ops. Consider `export const maxDuration = 60` on the route so a slow cold start cannot be killed mid-rewrite.
W1-187.gateOrTest: A demo-DB integration test (verify-guard style) that fires two seedDemo calls concurrently and asserts final counts equal one clean seed; and one that queries the demo mid-seed asserting the visitor row exists throughout (after the transactional fix, a concurrent read can never see it absent).
W1-187.reproPlan: Against the demo deployment: open two browsers, press Reset in one, navigate in the other within ~2s; observe the second browser bounced to /login or an empty feed. Concurrency half: fire two POST /api/demo/reset from two IPs in parallel and check the response of the loser plus post-state row counts. Demo DB only.

W1-196.title: places/search runs a sequential scan of all 234,934 Place rows on every keystroke of 4 or more characters (the altNames ILIKE arm defeats both expression indexes), with no cap on query length
W1-196.expected: The type-ahead stays on the indexed prefix path; per-keystroke cost is an index range scan plus a small sort.
W1-196.actual: For queries of 4+ characters (i.e. most of the keystrokes of any real city name), the WHERE becomes `lower(asciiName) LIKE 'q%' OR lower(name) LIKE 'q%' OR altNames ILIKE '%q%'`. Because the third arm has no index (altNames has none, and '%q%' is unindexable by btree anyway), Postgres cannot BitmapOr the clause and must sequential-scan the whole 234k-row table, running three pattern matches per row (altNames is a long comma list). Typing "bengaluru" fires ~6 such scans. The route's own comment (lines 20-23) claims the 4-char gate stops short queries from forcing a seq scan, but every long query forces one. On the shared Supabase instance (one DB for prod AND local dev) a launch-day burst of members filling in their cities stacks 50-150ms scans; q is also unbounded in length (route.ts:89 only checks `raw.length < 1`), so a pathological 10KB query multiplies per-row match cost. Rate limit is 120/min/user (rate-limit.ts:94) and fail-open.
W1-196.evidence: route.ts:99-102: `const altNamesClause = raw.length >= 4 ? Prisma.sql`OR "altNames" ILIKE ${containsPattern} ESCAPE '\\'` : Prisma.empty;` spliced into the WHERE at route.ts:104-109. The only indexes on Place are the two lower() text_pattern_ops expression indexes (round6.sql:30-31), which serve the two prefix arms but nothing serves altNames. An OR with one unindexable arm forces a full table scan in Postgres. Secondary: even prefix-only queries of 1 char sort every match ('a%' is tens of thousands of rows) before LIMIT 8 (route.ts:110-119), a top-N sort per keystroke.
W1-196.fixDirection: Add a pg_trgm GIN index on altNames (manual migration, consistent with the existing hand-applied index policy) so the ILIKE arm is indexable, or restructure as UNION ALL of the two indexed prefix arms LIMIT 8 plus a separately LIMITed altNames arm only when the prefix arms return nothing. Independently cap raw query length (e.g. slice to 80 chars) and consider raising the minimum length for the altNames arm.
W1-196.gateOrTest: EXPLAIN (via a read-only run-sql inspection by the fix session) showing no Seq Scan on Place for a 6-char query; a regression note in the route comment. Optionally a timing assertion in a script hitting /api/places/search.
W1-196.reproPlan: Read-only: EXPLAIN SELECT with the exact quoted WHERE against the live Place table (read-only query), compare plans with and without the altNames arm.

W1-198.title: Load more race: a late page-2 response fetched under the OLD filters is appended into the NEW filter's results and clobbers the new cursor

W1-198.fixDirection: Add a generation counter ref incremented both in the props-reset effect and at the start of handleLoadMore; discard the response if the generation moved (same pattern as usePlaceSearch's requestIdRef).

W1-198.reproPlan: Live: chrome-devtools MCP with network throttling; filter to a city, click Load more, immediately switch filters, observe foreign rows appended.

W1-200.title: "Batch: newest first" sort lists every member with NO batch year first (Postgres DESC = NULLS FIRST), and keyset Load more over the null sort key risks silent truncation

The pagination in actions.ts:65-71 cursors on `{ id: cursor }` while ordering by the nullable batchYear. batchYear is nullable by design (schema.prisma:37 `batchYear Int?`, null for teachers and mid-school leavers) and teacher rows exist (facultyCount tile renders).

W1-201.title: Hard-deleted cursor row (retention purge or admin delete between pages) makes Load more return empty and silently ends the directory list early
W1-201.expected: Pagination survives a row disappearing between pages: the next page continues from the surviving neighbours.
W1-201.actual: The cursor is the raw id of the last displayed row (`cursor: { id: cursor }, skip: 1`). Prisma cursor pagination resolves the cursor row by unique id to anchor the sort position; when that row no longer exists (the 60-day deletion sweep purges User rows outright; admin deletes too), Prisma's documented behaviour is to return no rows, so the member's Load more yields `{ users: [], nextCursor: null }` and the tail of the result set is unreachable until they reload with fresh filters. Marked suspected only because Prisma 7's exact empty-result behaviour for a missing cursor row should be confirmed once in dev before the rework.
W1-201.gateOrTest: A seeded test: fetch page 1, delete the boundary row, fetch page 2, assert the remaining rows still arrive.
W1-201.reproPlan: code-argument-only against production data; provable in dev only with a disposable row, which is a write -- leave to the fix session.

W1-205.reproPlan: Live: chrome-devtools MCP, type in the search box and immediately click a result; watch the URL bounce back.

W1-206.title: Search telemetry (logSearch) is fire-and-forget with no after()/waitUntil: on Vercel the write can be frozen with the function and lost
W1-206.expected: Work that must outlive the response is scheduled via next/server after() (or waitUntil), per taxonomy 6f; the owner's "most common searches" question depends on these rows actually landing.
W1-206.actual: Both routes call `void logSearch({...})` immediately before returning the response. logSearch performs up to two sequential Prisma round trips (dedupe findFirst, then create/update); once the response is returned Vercel may freeze the lambda before those complete, so an unknown fraction of searches (biased toward fast responses, i.e. most of them) is silently never recorded. The in-code "fire-and-forget" comment covers swallowing errors, not serverless suspension.
W1-206.evidence: places route.ts:127-133: `void logSearch({ scope: "places", query: raw, userId: session?.user?.id, results: results.length }); return NextResponse.json(results);` (identical shape at users/search route.ts:72-79). grep confirms neither file references after( anywhere. search-log.ts:50-79 shows the two-query write that must survive the response.
W1-206.fixDirection: Wrap the call in `after(() => logSearch({...}))` from next/server in both routes (and audit the feed's logSearch call site for the same shape while there).
W1-206.gateOrTest: A grep-style regression check (the repo already pins patterns in security-regressions.test.mjs) asserting logSearch call sites are inside after(); observable fix: SearchLog rows appear reliably in production.
W1-206.reproPlan: code-argument-only (loss is probabilistic on the platform; locally the process never freezes).

W1-207.title: A batch-tile year filter is silently overridden by the batch-range facet while both render as active filter tokens
