W1-308.fixDirection: Persist dimensions at upload time (sharp already decodes every image server-side; store w/h alongside the URL in the images JSON) and emit them on the img tags, or apply a CSS aspect-ratio placeholder per slot as an interim.
W1-308.gateOrTest: Lighthouse CLS on /feed via the existing chrome-devtools audit; visual suite masks won't catch this (it is transient), so pin with a CLS budget check.
W1-308.reproPlan: Read-only: chrome-devtools performance trace on /feed with cache disabled; read the layout-shift events attributed to post images.

W1-309.title: Purging any user who is a Group creator cascade-deletes the whole group, everyone's posts in it, and the entire Catch-up (all rounds, prompts, entries) attached to it
W1-309.expected: Deleting one member (self-requested purge after the 60-day grace, adminDeleteUser, or adminMergeUsers of a duplicate) removes THAT member's data. Shared containers they happened to create survive, the way Catchup.createdById is SetNull precisely so 'the Catch-up survives if they leave' (schema.prisma:702).
W1-309.actual: Group.creatorId is `onDelete: Cascade` (schema.prisma:201: `creator User @relation(fields: [creatorId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)`). `prisma.user.delete` inside purgeUserAccount therefore deletes every Group the member created, which cascades: Post.groupId Cascade (schema.prisma:406) deletes every OTHER member's posts in the group; Catchup.groupId Cascade (schema.prisma:717) deletes the Catch-up, then CatchupEdition -> CatchupPrompt -> CatchupEntry -> CatchupEntryLove all Cascade, destroying every member's answers. Two creation paths make this near-certain to fire: (1) signup auto-creates 'Batch of {year}' groups with `creatorId: userId` for whoever signs up first from a batch — the code itself says the creator exists 'only to satisfy the required FK' (src/components/auth/actions.ts:212-227); (2) starting a Catch-up sets `creatorId` on its private group (catchups/actions.ts:446). None of the three deletion paths handles createdGroups: purgeUserAccount only clears filed reports then `prisma.user.delete` (account-purge.ts:99-102); adminDeleteUser delegates to it (admin-actions.ts:59); adminMergeUsers re-points posts/comments/photos/entries but never groups, then deletes the source (admin/people/actions.ts — no occurrence of 'group' in the file), so merging a duplicate can also destroy a batch group while the just-re-pointed posts die with it. The retention sweep runs this UNATTENDED (retention.ts:121), so 60 days after the first-of-their-batch member requests deletion, their entire batch group and every classmate's group posts and catch-up history silently vanish overnight. Additionally, the cascaded rows of OTHER authors carry R2 image URLs (Post.images, CatchupEntry.images) that nothing deletes — collectImageUrls only reads the purged user's own rows (account-purge.ts:38-46) — so those bytes are orphaned in R2 forever on top of the row loss.
W1-309.evidence: schema.prisma:201 `creator  User          @relation(fields: [creatorId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)`; schema.prisma:406 `group       Group?       @relation(fields: [groupId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)` on Post; schema.prisma:717 `group     Group            @relation(fields: [groupId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)` on Catchup, whose editions/prompts/entries are all Cascade (744, 764-765, 784-786). auth/actions.ts:220-227: `if (!group) { group = await prisma.group.create({ data: { name, description: ..., visibility: "public", creatorId: userId } ... }` with the comment 'they become its creator only to satisfy the required FK'. account-purge.ts:99-102: `await prisma.$transaction([ prisma.report.deleteMany({ where: { reporterId: userId } }), prisma.user.delete({ where: { id: userId } }) ]);` — no group handling. retention.ts:120-121 runs it nightly per due account. The schema's own SetNull on Catchup.createdById ('nullable so the Catch-up survives if they leave', schema.prisma:702) proves the survival intent that the Group cascade defeats.
W1-309.fixDirection: Break the ownership cascade: make Group.creatorId nullable with onDelete: SetNull (matching Catchup.createdById), via a dated file in prisma/migrations-manual/ (ALTER the FK constraint + DROP NOT NULL), plus `npx prisma generate`. Audit the few readers of group.creatorId for null-handling. Alternatively (weaker) purgeUserAccount/adminMergeUsers could re-point or explicitly guard createdGroups before user.delete, but SetNull at the schema level is the only version that protects every future delete path. Decide separately whether a purged sole-member private group should be garbage-collected deliberately rather than by FK accident.
W1-309.gateOrTest: New unit/integration test: create user A, have A's signup mint a batch group, add user B with a post in it and a catch-up entry; purge A; assert the group, B's post, and B's entry all survive. Pin in src/lib/security-regressions.test.mjs style, plus a schema assertion that Group.creatorId is not Cascade.
W1-309.reproPlan: code-argument-only (proving it live would destroy real shared rows in the ONE shared database; the cascade chain is fully visible in schema.prisma)

W1-310.title: Account purge deletes DB rows first and R2 bytes best-effort afterwards with the URL list held only in memory: any failure, crash or timeout mid-loop orphans the member's images in R2 permanently, while the audit entry claims they were removed
W1-310.expected: A purge (GDPR Art. 17, audits H9/M35) reliably removes the member's R2 objects, or at minimum leaves a durable record of what still needs removing so a retry can finish the job; the audit trail reports what actually happened.
W1-310.actual: purgeUserAccount collects URLs in a local array, deletes the rows in a transaction, then loops `for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); deleted += 1; }` (account-purge.ts:109-112). Three defects compound: (1) delImageByKey swallows every error (`catch { /* best-effort cleanup */ }`, storage.ts:225-227), so a transient R2 429/500 during the loop silently skips the object — and because the pointing rows are already gone, the file's own comment admits 'afterwards nothing can enumerate the objects' (account-purge.ts:79-81): the miss is permanent and the bytes stay publicly fetchable at pub-*.r2.dev, which is exactly the pre-H9 failure this module exists to close. (2) `deleted` counts loop iterations, not successes, and flows into the audit detail `${purged.imagesDeleted} stored image(s) removed` (retention.ts:132, admin-actions.ts:70), so the compliance record can state images were removed when none were. (3) If the serverless function crashes or hits its duration ceiling between the row transaction and the end of the loop (see the unbounded-sweep finding), every remaining URL is lost with the process. There is no persisted work list, no retry, and no orphan-reconciliation sweep on the R2 side.
W1-310.evidence: account-purge.ts:108-113: `let deleted = 0; for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); deleted += 1; } return { ok: true, imagesDeleted: deleted };` — increment is unconditional. storage.ts:218-228: `export async function delImageByKey(key: string): Promise<void> { try { ... DeleteObjectCommand ... } catch { // best-effort cleanup } }` — void return, error swallowed, caller cannot know. account-purge.ts:77-81 comment: 'URLs are collected FIRST, because the cascade takes the pointing rows with it and afterwards nothing can enumerate the objects' — i.e. the in-memory array is the last copy. retention.ts:131-132 writes `"${purged.imagesDeleted} stored image(s) removed"` into the account.purge audit row.
W1-310.fixDirection: Make the object list durable before the row delete: either (a) delete R2 objects keyed by prefix instead of by collected URLs — all app-minted uploads live under `uploads/<userId>/...` and `avatars/<userId>/...` (see ownedUploadUrls and the merge's avatar note in admin/people/actions.ts:322-330), so a ListObjectsV2+delete over those two prefixes AFTER the row delete is re-runnable and misses nothing even on crash; or (b) persist the collected URLs into a small PendingImagePurge table in the same transaction as user.delete, drain it in the loop, and let the nightly sweep retry leftovers. Also make delImageByKey return success/failure and count only true successes in imagesDeleted.
W1-310.gateOrTest: Unit test with a stubbed storage layer: make delImage fail for one of three URLs, assert imagesDeleted reports 2 (not 3) and that the failed key remains discoverable (pending row or prefix listing) for a retry; a second run must remove it.
W1-310.reproPlan: code-argument-only (a live proof would require deleting a real account; the swallow-and-count-anyway path is fully visible in the two quoted functions)

W1-311.title: Admin-message screenshots (AdminMessage.imageUrl) are never deleted from R2 by any path: account purge misses them and the retention sweep's 2-year deleteMany orphans them
W1-311.expected: purgeUserAccount is 'the ONE meaning of gone' (SECURITY.md): every R2 object class a member created — avatar, post images, catch-up entry images, Collection photos, admin-message screenshots — is removed at purge. And when the retention sweep expires AdminMessage rows at 730 days, the bytes those rows point at go with them.
W1-311.actual: AdminMessage has `imageUrl String? // one optional screenshot (WebP via /api/upload)` (schema.prisma:587), written by the member-facing messages actions (`create: { authorId: session.user.id, fromAdmin: false, body, imageUrl }`, messages/actions.ts:94). collectImageUrls queries only User.photoUrl, Post.images, Photo thumb/url/original, and CatchupEntry.images (account-purge.ts:38-46) — AdminMessage is absent, so on purge the member's screenshots (bug reports and admin conversations, which routinely contain personal data) survive in R2, publicly fetchable, with the pointing rows cascade-deleted (AdminThread.memberId Cascade -> AdminMessage.threadId Cascade) so nothing can ever find them again — the exact H9 failure mode, via a model added after H9 was closed. Independently, the sweep's `prisma.adminMessage.deleteMany({ where: { createdAt: { lt: cutoff(730) } } })` (retention.ts:73-77) deletes rows without touching imageUrl bytes, so every screenshot older than two years becomes an untracked orphan on the normal nightly path too. A repo-wide grep of delImage callers (upload/finalize, collection, admin/people, feed, settings, storage, account-purge) confirms no code path anywhere deletes an AdminMessage image.
W1-311.evidence: account-purge.ts:37-46: `const [user, posts, photos, entries] = await Promise.all([ prisma.user.findUnique(...photoUrl...), prisma.post.findMany(...images...), prisma.photo.findMany(...), prisma.catchupEntry.findMany(...images...) ]);` — four sources, no adminMessage. retention.ts:73-77: `(await prisma.adminMessage.deleteMany({ where: { createdAt: { lt: cutoff(KEEP_DAYS.adminMessages) } } })).count` — pure row delete. schema.prisma:590 `thread AdminThread @relation(fields: [threadId], references: [id], onDelete: Cascade)` plus schema.prisma:568 AdminThread.member Cascade completes the purge-time row cascade.
W1-311.fixDirection: Add `prisma.adminMessage.findMany({ where: { authorId: userId, imageUrl: { not: null } }, select: { imageUrl: true } })` to collectImageUrls (or supersede the whole collector with the uploads/<userId>/ prefix delete from the previous finding, which covers this class automatically). For the sweep, select imageUrl of the about-to-expire rows and delImage each before/after the deleteMany.
W1-311.gateOrTest: Extend the purge test: member sends an admin message with a screenshot; purge; assert the object is gone from storage (local-fs mode makes this assertable in a unit test). Second test for the sweep path with a backdated AdminMessage row.
W1-311.reproPlan: code-argument-only (live proof would require purging a real account; the absent query in collectImageUrls is definitive)

W1-312.title: Visit and SearchLog have no retention mechanism at all: absent from the sweep, absent from prune.mjs, absent from the SECURITY.md retention table — Visit alone can consume the 500MB database tier within roughly a year at 2,000 members
W1-312.expected: Every table that grows with traffic has something bounding it (the sweep, a prune, or a by-design cap), and the owner's retention table covers all personal-data tables. The project's own standard: prune.mjs exists because one unbounded table 'can actually exhaust' the 500MB free tier.
W1-312.actual: runRetentionSweep deletes from exactly seven tables (adminMessages, reports, contributions, notifications, loginAttempts, auditLogs, outboundEmails — retention.ts:73-107) plus due accounts; prune.mjs touches only Notification. Nothing anywhere deletes Visit or SearchLog rows (repo-wide grep for visit/searchLog deleteMany: zero hits outside generated code; the only non-telemetry readers are admin-analytics SELECTs). Both tables were added 2026-08-19, AFTER prune.mjs was written, whose header still claims 'Nothing else here grows unbounded' (prune.mjs:9-10) — that claim is now false. Arithmetic: a Visit row is one per member-sitting and carries ~20 columns including two path strings, referrer, four geo strings, UA-derived strings and coordinates (~300-450 bytes with tuple overhead) plus three indexes (PK, endedAt, [userId,endedAt]). 2,000 members at the schema's own engagement assumption (last-seen.ts:23 uses '2,000 members at 30 views a day') is 1,500-3,000 visits/day = 0.5-1.1M rows/year, roughly 250-600MB/year — on the same 500MB Supabase free tier that prune.mjs cites, this is the largest and fastest-growing table in the schema and it is unbounded. SearchLog is smaller (60s per-user dedupe, all three scopes require auth so userId is always set) but also unbounded and additionally pays a full btree on the raw query text (@@index([query]), schema.prisma:1003). Neither table appears in the SECURITY.md retention table (docs/SECURITY.md:82-90 lists only the seven swept classes), so the published policy has no answer for how long presence/search personal data is kept — a GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) gap in exactly the framework the sweep was built to satisfy (retention.ts:6).
W1-312.evidence: retention.ts:23-40 KEEP_DAYS has keys only for adminMessages, reports, contributions, notifications, securityLogs, sentEmailLog — no visits, no searches. prune.mjs:5-10: 'notifications are ~0.8KB each and accumulate forever... the ONE thing in this schema that can actually exhaust it. Nothing else here grows unbounded' — written before Visit/SearchLog existed. Grep across src/ and scripts/ for `visit.deleteMany|searchLog.deleteMany|DELETE FROM "Visit"|DELETE FROM "SearchLog"`: no matches. schema.prisma:1013-1016 (ContentView comment) shows the team already did this arithmetic for views ('2,000 members at twenty views a day is 14M rows a year, which is gigabytes on a 500MB plan') and chose a bounded counter — the identical reasoning was never applied to Visit.
W1-312.fixDirection: Pick retention windows with the owner (e.g. Visit 90-180 days — the analytics room's questions are about recent behaviour; SearchLog 180-365 days) and add two deleteMany steps to runRetentionSweep (both tables need a createdAt/endedAt-leading index for the sweep predicate: Visit already has @@index([endedAt]); SearchLog has @@index([scope, createdAt]) which does not lead on createdAt — add @@index([createdAt]) or sweep per-scope). Record both in the SECURITY.md retention table and in the KEEP_DAYS comment block.
W1-312.gateOrTest: Extend the sweep's result type and any sweep test to include visits/searches counts; a schema-coverage assertion (every model with a traffic-driven insert path appears either in KEEP_DAYS, in prune.mjs, or on an explicit bounded-by-design list) would catch the next telemetry table added without a policy.
W1-312.reproPlan: Read-only live proof: `SELECT count(*), pg_total_relation_size('"Visit"') FROM "Visit"` via the admin analytics room or a read-only query; growth rate over a week extrapolates the arithmetic.

W1-313.title: Two contradictory Notification retention policies ship simultaneously: prune.mjs deletes at 30 days while retention.ts and the published SECURITY.md policy say 1 year — the effective behavior is 30 days and the sweep's notification step is dead code
W1-313.expected: One owner decision, one mechanism. The documented policy (SECURITY.md retention table: 'Notifications | 1 year', mirrored in retention.ts:32-33 'Notifications: 1 year. Purely transient by design') is what members experience.
W1-313.actual: snapshot.yml runs `node scripts/ops/prune.mjs --days 30` nightly (snapshot.yml:75), and prune.mjs's comment claims its own owner mandate: 'the owner asked for a flat 30 days' (prune.mjs:47-49). So notifications are actually destroyed at 30 days — a member returning from a two-month absence finds an empty bell, 11 months earlier than the published policy promises. Meanwhile runRetentionSweep's `notification.deleteMany({ createdAt: { lt: cutoff(365) } })` (retention.ts:88-92) can never match a row, because prune removed everything older than 30 days long before it turns 365 — the step is permanently a no-op that still reports a reassuring 0 in the nightly audit JSON. Both files cite the owner for different numbers; at least one record of his decision is wrong, and the schema comment at Notification (schema.prisma:534-536, 'the 100-per-user prune') references a third mechanism that does not exist anywhere in the codebase (no such code; grep finds only the flat-30-days prune).
W1-313.evidence: prune.mjs:23 `const DAYS = args.includes("--days") ? Number(...) : 30;` and :47-49 'A notification nobody opened in a month is not going to be opened; the owner asked for a flat 30 days.' vs retention.ts:32-33 `/** Notifications: 1 year. Purely transient by design. */ notifications: 365,` vs docs/SECURITY.md retention table row '| Notifications | 1 year |' captioned '(owner, 2026-08-19)'. snapshot.yml:72-75 wires prune into the nightly run.
W1-313.fixDirection: Ask the owner which number is the decision; then delete the losing mechanism entirely (if 30 days: remove the notifications step from KEEP_DAYS/retention.ts and fix the SECURITY.md table; if 1 year: remove the prune step from snapshot.yml or point prune.mjs at 365). Also fix the stale '100-per-user prune' comment at schema.prisma:534-536 and prune.mjs's now-false 'nothing else grows unbounded' header.
W1-313.gateOrTest: A one-line assertion tying the two constants together is impossible across .mjs/.ts, so pin the surviving policy in the sweep's unit test and delete the other code path; docs check in the audit-status tracker.
W1-313.reproPlan: Read-only live proof: `SELECT min("createdAt") FROM "Notification"` — if the oldest row is ~30 days old, prune is winning and the 1-year policy is fiction.

W1-314.title: Retention-sweep step failures are invisible to the nightly alarm: every step's error is caught, the route answers HTTP 200, and retention.yml only fails on HTTP status — a permanently failing account purge (a member's legal deletion request never finalising) shows green forever
W1-314.expected: The workflow's own design note: a failure 'fails loudly, which is the correct symptom' (retention.yml:14). A night where a table's delete or an account's purge failed should turn the GitHub run red, because that run is the only automated observer.
W1-314.actual: `step()` swallows every exception (`catch (err) { console.error(...); errors.push(name); return 0; }`, retention.ts:66-70) and per-account purge failures merely push `purge:${row.id}` (retention.ts:122-125); the route then returns `NextResponse.json(result)` — always 200 (route.ts:34-35). retention.yml's guard is `curl -sS -f` (retention.yml:41-45), which reacts only to the HTTP status, so a night where EVERY step failed (DB hiccup, a new FK blocking user.delete, R2 credentials rotated) still produces a green Actions run. The only trace is the errors array inside the retention.sweep audit-row JSON — and if the DB is the thing failing, that final writeAudit fails silently too (audit.ts:67-71 catches everything, logging only outside production), leaving zero trace anywhere. The console.error lines go to Vercel function logs, which nobody reads nightly and the Hobby plan retains only briefly. The worst concrete case: a deletion-requested account whose purge fails repeatedly (e.g. a future RESTRICT FK, the H8 pattern) is never erased, with a green tick every morning.
W1-314.evidence: retention.ts:63-71: `const step = async (name, fn) => { try { return await fn(); } catch (err) { console.error(...); errors.push(name); return 0; } };` route.ts:34-35: `const result = await runRetentionSweep(); return NextResponse.json(result);` — no status branching on result.errors. retention.yml:41-45: `# -f turns an HTTP error (401, 500) into a job failure ... curl -sS -f ...` — the mechanism exists but nothing ever produces the 500.
W1-314.fixDirection: Return a non-2xx (e.g. 500) from the route when `result.errors.length > 0` — the deleteMany steps are idempotent so the workflow's retry-by-rerun costs nothing — or keep 200 and have retention.yml parse the JSON body and `exit 1` on a non-empty errors array (jq is available on ubuntu-latest). Either way the audit row should still be written first.
W1-314.gateOrTest: Unit test on runRetentionSweep with one step forced to throw: assert errors non-empty; route-level test asserting the HTTP status reflects it.
W1-314.reproPlan: code-argument-only (forcing a step failure against the shared production database is not acceptable)

W1-315.title: The sweep's account-purge loop is unbounded (findMany with no take, sequential per-URL R2 deletes) against the serverless duration ceiling: a backlog of due accounts or one photo-heavy member can kill the run mid-purge, amplifying the orphaned-bytes defect
W1-315.expected: A nightly job on a Vercel function bounds its work per invocation so it cannot hit the platform duration ceiling, and anything it must finish (R2 cleanup after row deletion) is not in the killable tail.
W1-315.actual: `prisma.user.findMany({ where: { deletionRequestedAt: { lt: cutoff(DELETION_GRACE_DAYS) } }, ... })` has no `take` (retention.ts:116-119), and each due account then runs collectImageUrls (4 queries) + a transaction + `for (const url of urls) await delImage(url)` — one sequential R2 round trip per object (account-purge.ts:109-112). A member with a large Collection contribution can alone mean hundreds of serial DeleteObject calls; several accounts falling due the same night (or accumulating behind a stretch of failed runs — see the invisible-failure finding) multiplies it. Neither the route nor vercel.json exports/configures `maxDuration` (route.ts has no segment config; vercel.json contains only regions/framework/crons), so the function runs under whatever the plan's default ceiling is (60s classic Hobby; up to 300s under Fluid) and is killed at it. Because R2 deletion happens after row deletion per account, the kill lands exactly in the window that orphans bytes permanently (see the purge-ordering finding); the run's final audit entry and result are also never written, and the GH job records a bare curl failure with no partial-result JSON. The seven deleteMany steps are single fast statements and are fine; the purge loop is the unbounded part.
W1-315.evidence: retention.ts:115-136: `const rows = await prisma.user.findMany({ where: { deletionRequestedAt: { lt: cutoff(DELETION_GRACE_DAYS) } }, select: {...} }); for (const row of rows) { const purged = await purgeUserAccount(row.id); ... }` — no take, no time budget. account-purge.ts:109-111: `for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); ... }` — serial. vercel.json (whole file quoted in audit notes) has no functions/maxDuration block; sweep/route.ts exports only GET.
W1-315.fixDirection: Cap the nightly batch (`take: 10`, oldest deletionRequestedAt first) — leftovers are naturally picked up tomorrow since the predicate re-derives; export `maxDuration` explicitly on the route at the plan's maximum; batch the R2 deletes (DeleteObjects supports 1000 keys per call, or Promise.allSettled in chunks of ~10). The prefix-delete redesign from the purge-ordering finding removes the per-URL serial loop entirely.
W1-315.gateOrTest: Unit test asserting the sweep processes at most N accounts per run; the existing sweep-idempotency reasoning (retention.ts:14-16) already covers the resume-next-night behavior.
W1-315.reproPlan: code-argument-only (cannot stage a purge backlog against the shared database)

W1-316.title: Every fire-and-forget telemetry write (recordLoginAttempt, logSearch x3, recordView x4, the AuthToken opportunistic sweep) is a bare void'ed promise with no after()/waitUntil: on Vercel its completion after the response is not guaranteed, so login-attempt/search/view data is silently and intermittently lost
W1-316.expected: Work that must outlive the response on a serverless platform is registered with `after()`/`waitUntil` — the codebase itself does exactly this for the mail-queue drain ('it must run AFTER the response has been streamed', layout.tsx:58-69) — or is awaited before the response is produced.
W1-316.actual: recordLoginAttempt internally detaches its write (`void prisma.loginAttempt.create({...}).catch(...)`, login-attempt.ts:46-59) and is invoked from authorize() in src/lib/auth.ts at 7 call sites; the failed-login paths return to the client almost immediately after, so the create races the function freeze. logSearch is `void`-ed in two API routes immediately before `return NextResponse.json(...)` (users/search/route.ts:72-78 then :80 return; places/search/route.ts:127-134) — and logSearch is itself two sequential DB round trips (dedupe findFirst then create/update, search-log.ts:50-79), widening the race window. recordView is `void`-ed in four RSC pages that finish rendering right after. None uses `after()`. Vercel's execution model freezes the instance once the response completes; a pending promise may resume on a later invocation or never, so under real traffic some fraction of LoginAttempt/SearchLog/ContentView writes silently vanish — undermining precisely the surfaces they were built for: 'who cannot sign in' (login-attempt.ts:20-27 says an invisible locked-out member is the failure this exists to prevent) and the zero-result search list. The loss is unobservable because every one of these writers deliberately logs failures only outside production. touchLastSeen is NOT affected (awaited in the layout's Promise.all, layout.tsx:35-52). The auth-tokens.ts:107 void'ed deleteMany is the benign end of the same pattern (self-heals on next mint).
W1-316.evidence: login-attempt.ts:44-46: 'Deliberately not awaited by the caller...' `void prisma.loginAttempt.create({...})`. places/search/route.ts:127-135: `void logSearch({ scope: "places", ... }); return NextResponse.json(results);`. layout.tsx:63 shows the codebase's own correct pattern for post-response work: `after(async () => { ... await drainMailQueue(); ... })`. search-log.ts:50-72 shows logSearch performs findFirst + create — two awaits inside the detached promise.
W1-316.fixDirection: Wrap each detached call in `after(() => ...)` from next/server (route handlers and RSC pages both support it in Next 16), or simply await them — each is one-to-two fast same-region round trips and the routes already await a rateLimit check. For recordLoginAttempt, have it return the promise and register it via after() in auth.ts, or accept the await (~5ms in bom1). Keep the never-throws contract either way.
W1-316.gateOrTest: Grep-style regression check: no `void logSearch|void recordView` outside an after() callback (a small unit test over source text, in the spirit of security-regressions.test.mjs). Live: compare LoginAttempt row counts against Vercel function invocation counts for /login over a week.
W1-316.reproPlan: Live-but-safe partial proof: sign in with a wrong password on production a few times in quick succession, then count matching LoginAttempt rows in /admin (owner-visible) — a shortfall confirms drops; absence of shortfall does not disprove (timing-dependent).

W1-317.title: retention.yml and snapshot.yml both fire at 21:00 UTC despite retention.yml's comment claiming it avoids simultaneity: the sweep's Notification deleteMany and prune.mjs's batched Notification DELETEs run concurrently, and the night's metric counts are taken mid-sweep
W1-317.expected: The nightly jobs are staggered, as their own comments intend: backup 20:30 UTC, then non-overlapping successors ('inside the same quiet-hours window as the backup ... but not simultaneous with either', retention.yml:18-20; 'half an hour after backup.yml, so the two never contend', snapshot.yml:11-12).
W1-317.actual: Both schedules are literally `- cron: '0 21 * * *'` (retention.yml:21, snapshot.yml:16). retention.yml's 'not simultaneous with either' enumerates only backup and the catchups cron; snapshot was never added to the claim. Consequences, mild but real: (1) snapshot's collectDb counts (mail_sent, notifications-adjacent aggregates, members_total during a purge night) run while the sweep is deleting from the same tables, so the recorded history for a purge night is off by the sweep's deletions depending on statement interleaving; (2) the sweep's `notification.deleteMany` (retention.ts:88-92) and prune.mjs's loop of `DELETE FROM "Notification" WHERE id IN (SELECT ... LIMIT 5000)` (prune.mjs:63-72) target overlapping row sets concurrently on two different poolers (app transaction pooler vs DIRECT_URL session pooler) — ordinary row-lock waits, with a small deadlock surface between an unbounded single-statement delete and a batched one. GitHub's cron jitter means they usually won't start the same second, but nothing orders them.
W1-317.evidence: retention.yml:17-21: `schedule: # 21:00 UTC == 02:30 IST: ... but not simultaneous with either. - cron: '0 21 * * *'`. snapshot.yml:14-16: `schedule: - cron: '0 21 * * *'`. Both claim 02:30 IST in their own comments.
W1-317.fixDirection: Move snapshot.yml to 21:30 UTC (03:00 IST) or retention to 21:30; update both comments. (Resolving the Notification double-policy finding removes half the contention on its own.)
W1-317.gateOrTest: None needed beyond the cron lines themselves; a comment-accuracy fix travels with the schedule change.
W1-317.reproPlan: code-argument-only (schedule facts are in the two files)

W1-318.title: snapshot.mjs runs at 21:00 UTC but queries PostHog for 'today's UTC date', so the 21:00-24:00 UTC window (02:30-05:30 IST) is never counted on any day — a permanent 3-hour hole in the one metrics history built to outlive the vendors
W1-318.expected: Each day's posthog.events/people/pageviews row eventually reflects the full day: either the job snapshots the *previous* completed day, or a later run overwrites today's partial numbers with final ones.
W1-318.actual: `DAY = startOfUtcToday()` (snapshot.mjs:28-33) and the HogQL filter is `WHERE toDate(timestamp) = toDate('${iso}')` with iso = DAY (snapshot.mjs:196-203). Running at 21:00 UTC, the query covers 00:00-21:00 of the current UTC day; events from 21:00-24:00 UTC are attributed to a date the job will never query again (tomorrow's run asks about tomorrow). The upsert `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` (snapshot.mjs:282-283) would heal it if a run ever re-asked about a past day, but none does. Sentry's `statsPeriod=24h` (snapshot.mjs:168) has the mirror-image quirk: a rolling window labelled with the run day, overlapping 3h of the prior day's row. Small in absolute terms (02:30-05:30 IST is deep night for an IST membership) but it is a systematic bias in the exact artifact whose stated purpose is to 'say in 2028 what the site looked like in 2026' (snapshot.mjs:7-9).
W1-318.evidence: snapshot.mjs:27-28: `const DAY = args.includes("--day") ? new Date(`${dayArg}T00:00:00Z`) : startOfUtcToday();` snapshot.mjs:196-203: HogQL `WHERE toDate(timestamp) = toDate('${iso}')` with `const iso = DAY.toISOString().slice(0, 10)`.
W1-318.fixDirection: Have the PostHog (and Sentry) collectors snapshot YESTERDAY's completed UTC day (`daysAgo(1)`) instead of today, keeping db/github collectors on 'now' semantics; or add a second small upsert for yesterday's posthog metrics in the same run. Label which metrics are point-in-time vs completed-day in the admin room.
W1-318.gateOrTest: A --dry run comparison across two consecutive days would show the gap; after the fix, posthog.pageviews for day N should match PostHog's own UI for day N.
W1-318.reproPlan: Read-only: compare a stored posthog.pageviews row against the PostHog dashboard's figure for the same date; the stored one will be consistently lower.

W1-319.title: snapshot.mjs --day backfill records TODAY's live database, Sentry and GitHub values under the requested past date, silently corrupting the historical series it claims to backfill
W1-319.expected: The workflow_dispatch input advertises 'Backfill a specific day (YYYY-MM-DD)' (snapshot.yml:19-21): running it for 2026-08-01 writes numbers that describe 2026-08-01.
W1-319.actual: Only the PostHog collector actually uses DAY as a data filter. collectDb computes `count(*) FROM "User"` etc. — the CURRENT totals — and its windows are `daysAgo(7)/daysAgo(30)` relative to the requested day but evaluated against present-day lastSeenAt values (snapshot.mjs:60-104); collectSentry always queries `statsPeriod=24h` from now (snapshot.mjs:168); collectGithub reads the latest backup runs (snapshot.mjs:228-241). All of these rows are then upserted under the past `day` (snapshot.mjs:277-285), overwriting whatever genuine numbers that day's original run captured. So using the advertised backfill after, say, a missed night writes today's member/post/mail totals into the missing date — and if run for a date that already has data, it destroys correct history. The header comment even acknowledges the tension ('the only source that can be asked about the past', snapshot.mjs:56-58) without acting on it.
W1-319.evidence: snapshot.mjs:73-104: the big SELECT has no reference to DAY except `d7/d30` lower bounds on lastSeenAt — `(SELECT count(*) FROM "User") AS members_total` is unconditionally current. snapshot.mjs:277-284: `const day = DAY.toISOString().slice(0, 10); await db.query(`INSERT INTO "MetricSnapshot" ... ON CONFLICT ("day","source","metric") DO UPDATE SET value = EXCLUDED.value ...`)` — current values keyed under the past day. Also snapshot.mjs:27: `--day` with a missing/malformed value yields Invalid Date and the run fails with an unhelpful throw.
W1-319.fixDirection: Restrict --day to the posthog source (skip db/sentry/github collectors when backfilling, since their numbers cannot be recovered for the past), or rename/re-document the input as 'PostHog-only backfill'. Validate dayArg (exists, matches YYYY-MM-DD, produces a valid Date) before connecting.
W1-319.gateOrTest: A --dry --day run should list only posthog.* metrics after the fix.
W1-319.reproPlan: Safe live proof with --dry: `node scripts/ops/snapshot.mjs --day 2026-01-01 --dry` prints db.members.total equal to today's count under the 2026-01-01 label (writes nothing).

W1-320.title: snapshot.mjs backup.ok reads workflow_runs[0], which can be an in-progress or manually-dispatched run with conclusion null, recording a false backup failure for the day
W1-320.expected: github.backup.ok = 1 whenever the most recent COMPLETED backup succeeded; the metric exists to answer 'did last night's backup run, and did it pass' (snapshot.mjs:222-224).
W1-320.actual: `const last = runs[0]; add("github", "backup.ok", last?.conclusion === "success" ? 1 : 0);` (snapshot.mjs:235-236) takes the newest run regardless of status. GitHub scheduled workflows routinely start late by 10-40 minutes; backup fires at 20:30 UTC (backup.yml:34) and snapshot at 21:00, so on a night where backup's start slipped past ~20:58 (or the dump is slow), runs[0] is `in_progress` with `conclusion: null` and backup.ok is recorded 0 even though the backup then succeeds. A manual `workflow_dispatch` of backup near the snapshot time produces the same false negative, and `backup.age_hours` (snapshot.mjs:237-239) similarly uses the possibly-running run. The stored history then shows phantom backup failures that never happened.
W1-320.evidence: snapshot.mjs:228-241: fetches `/actions/workflows/backup.yml/runs?per_page=10` with no `status=completed` filter; `add("github", "backup.ok", last?.conclusion === "success" ? 1 : 0)`. backup.yml:34: `- cron: '30 20 * * *'`; snapshot.yml:16: `- cron: '0 21 * * *'` — a 30-minute nominal gap against GitHub's documented multi-minute cron jitter.
W1-320.fixDirection: Add `&status=completed` to the runs query (the API supports it), or take the first run whose conclusion is non-null. Keep failures_last_10 over completed runs only for consistency.
W1-320.gateOrTest: After the fix, manually dispatch backup and immediately run snapshot --dry: backup.ok must reflect the previous completed run, not 0.
W1-320.reproPlan: Safe live proof: trigger backup via workflow_dispatch, run `node scripts/ops/snapshot.mjs --dry` while it is in progress, observe `github.backup.ok = 0` printed despite the last completed backup having succeeded.

W1-321.title: After a purge, other members' User.coverPhoto (and Group.coverImage) strings still point at the purged uploader's deleted Collection photo bytes, leaving broken cover images with no cleanup or fallback path in the purge
W1-321.expected: When a purge deletes a contributor's Photo rows (uploaderId Cascade) and their R2 bytes, surfaces that reused those photos degrade gracefully — the referencing field is cleared or the renderer falls back.
W1-321.actual: User.coverPhoto is 'a Collection photo url reused as profile cover' (schema.prisma:104) — a plain string with no FK. purgeUserAccount deletes the uploader's Photo rows via the user.delete cascade (Photo.uploaderId Cascade, schema.prisma:172) and then deletes the bytes those rows pointed at (collectImageUrls gathers thumbUrl/url/originalUrl, account-purge.ts:41-44). Nothing updates other members whose coverPhoto equals one of those URLs (grep: no coverPhoto handling in account-purge.ts or admin actions), so their profiles are left requesting a now-404 object. The purge comment explicitly reasons about whose bytes they are (account-purge.ts:33-35) but not about the dangling reuse references. Whether members see a broken-image glyph or an acceptable empty state depends on the profile renderer, which is why this is 'suspected': the dangling pointer is certain, the visual severity needs one render check.
W1-321.evidence: account-purge.ts:33-35: '`coverPhoto` is deliberately absent: it is a Collection photo REUSED as a profile cover, so its bytes belong to whoever contributed it' — the reasoning covers whose bytes to delete, not who still points at them. schema.prisma:104: `coverPhoto String? // a Collection photo url reused as profile cover` — no relation, so no cascade or SetNull can fire.
W1-321.fixDirection: In purgeUserAccount, after collecting the URL set, `prisma.user.updateMany({ where: { coverPhoto: { in: urls } }, data: { coverPhoto: null } })` (and the same for Group.coverImage if groups resurface) inside the delete transaction; independently, make the cover renderer tolerate a failed image load.
W1-321.gateOrTest: Purge test: member B sets member A's photo as cover; purge A; assert B.coverPhoto is null (or the profile renders the no-cover state).
W1-321.reproPlan: Live proof possible on the demo deployment only (set a cover from a seeded photo, delete the uploader via admin, view the profile); do not run on production.

W1-322.title: Server-rendered display dates show the UTC calendar day, not the IST day: formatDisplayDate and formatTimeAgo have no timeZone, so every letter/photo written between 00:00 and 05:30 IST reads as the previous day forever
W1-322.expected: A letter published at 00:30 IST on 15 June shows "15 Jun 2026" — the valley's day is an IST day (the codebase already states this rule in src/lib/wordle.ts: "we ask for the IST date, because the valley's day is an IST day").
W1-322.actual: formatDisplayDate is `new Date(date).toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { day: "numeric", month: "short", year: "numeric" })` with no timeZone option, and formatTimeAgo's >4-week fallback is `date.toLocaleDateString("en-IN", {...})` with no timeZone. Both are called from genuine React Server Components running in UTC on Vercel: letters/page.tsx line 163 `metaLine(batchLine(l.author), formatDisplayDate(l.createdAt))` and letters/[id]/page.tsx line 188 `date={formatDisplayDate(letter.createdAt)}` (neither file is "use client"). A letter created at 00:30 IST 15 June is 19:00 UTC 14 June, so the server renders "14 Jun 2026" for every viewer, permanently. 00:00–05:30 IST is ~23% of the clock and includes India's late-night posting hours. The same helpers are also used server-side across admin pages (admin/page.tsx, admin/audit, admin/support, admin/catchups) and messages/thread-list.tsx (no "use client" directive; whether it inherits a client boundary needs one check).
W1-322.evidence: src/lib/utils.ts:151-157: `export function formatDisplayDate(date: Date | string): string { return new Date(date).toLocaleDateString("en-GB", { day: "numeric", month: "short", year: "numeric" }) }` — no timeZone. utils.ts:21-25 (formatTimeAgo fallback): `return date.toLocaleDateString("en-IN", { day: "numeric", month: "short", year: "numeric" })` — no timeZone. Contrast with src/lib/wordle.ts:18-21 which does it right: `return date.toLocaleDateString("en-CA", { timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata" })`. Server call sites quoted above; the letters pages import from "@/lib/utils" at src/app/(main)/letters/page.tsx:11 and are async server components with prisma calls, so this string is computed in the server's UTC zone, not the member's browser.
W1-322.fixDirection: Add `timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata"` to the toLocaleDateString options in formatDisplayDate and in formatTimeAgo's date fallback in src/lib/utils.ts (matching the site-wide IST-day convention wordle.ts already documents). W1-323.title: normalizeHouse resolves alias lookups through the prototype chain: typing "constructor", "toString", "valueOf" (etc.) into the free-text "Other house" box returns a Function/Object instead of a string, crashing the picker or silently losing the entry

W1-323.actual: For inputs that collide with Object.prototype members, `HOUSE_ALIASES[lower]` returns an inherited value: "constructor" → the Object constructor function (truthy → returned), "toString"/"valueOf"/"hasOwnProperty" → functions, "__proto__" → Object.prototype. Client path: house-picker.tsx addOther() does `const name = normalizeHouse(otherText); if (!name) return; ... onChange([...value, name])` — a Function is truthy, lands in the string[] state, and the trigger renders it via `<MetaDots parts={value.map(...)}>`, so React throws "Functions are not valid as a React child" and the onboarding/settings page falls to the error boundary. Server path: saveOnboardingHouses maps `house: normalizeHouse(r.house)` then `.filter((r) => r.house.length > 0)` — a Function's .length is its arity (Object has length 1, passes), and `JSON.stringify` OMITS function-valued properties, so `[{"year":2020}]` is stored with the house silently gone (parseHouseYearEntries later filters the malformed row out, so the member's entry just vanishes).

The codebase already fixed exactly this class once, in src/lib/city-coords.ts:140-144: "Object.hasOwn, not a bare `CITY_COORDS[key]`: a filter value like 'constructor' or '__proto__' ... would otherwise return an inherited member ... turning a member's `/directory?city=...` into an uncaught 500." houses.ts has no such guard. Downstream: src/components/common/house-picker.tsx:129-131 and src/components/onboarding/actions.ts:146-148 as quoted in "actual".
W1-323.fixDirection: In normalizeHouse, replace `if (HOUSE_ALIASES[lower]) return HOUSE_ALIASES[lower]` with an `Object.hasOwn(HOUSE_ALIASES, lower)` guard, exactly mirroring the city-coords.ts fix. Also check src/components/profile/house-chain-editor.tsx:236, the third call site with the same free-text path.
W1-323.gateOrTest: Unit test (new houses.test.mjs, same pattern as the existing *.test.mjs files): for every key of Object.prototype ('constructor', 'toString', 'valueOf', 'hasOwnProperty', '__proto__', 'isPrototypeOf', 'propertyIsEnumerable', 'toLocaleString'), assert typeof normalizeHouse(k) === "string" and it equals the title-cased input.

W1-324.title: PostHog identify never fires on a full page load into a (main) route: the child's effect runs before the provider's init effect, the __loaded guard returns, and its deps never change — so member sessions are counted anonymous and person-based funnels are empty
W1-324.expected: Every signed-in session calls posthog.identify(userId, ...) so `person_profiles: "identified_only"` builds profiles and cross-page funnels can follow one member — the stated purpose of the component.
W1-324.actual: PostHogProvider (root layout) calls posthog.init() inside its own useEffect. PostHogIdentify is rendered by the nested (main) layout — a descendant — and its effect body is `if (!posthog.__loaded) return; posthog.identify(...)`. React flushes effects bottom-up (children before parents) within a commit, and both components hydrate in the same commit on a full page load (neither is inside a Suspense boundary — both are layout-level). So on every hard load of /feed (which is how essentially every authenticated session starts: login performs a full redirect to /feed, and proxy.ts 302s "/" to /feed for cookie-holders), the identify effect sees __loaded === false and returns. Its dependency array [userId, accountType, batchYear, isOwner] never changes during the session and the (main) layout persists across client navigations, so the effect never re-runs: the session is never identified. Identify only works in the rare path where posthog was already initialised in this JS context before (main) layout mounts (e.g. client-side navigation from the signed-out landing page into the app without a full load — which the login flow does not do).
W1-324.evidence: src/components/analytics/posthog-identify.tsx:31-39: `useEffect(() => { if (!posthog.__loaded) return; posthog.identify(userId, { accountType, batchYear, isOwner }); ... }, [userId, accountType, batchYear, isOwner]);` — a guard with no retry and constant deps. src/components/analytics/posthog-provider.tsx:32-35: `useEffect(() => { if (!KEY) return; posthog.init(KEY, {...` — init happens in the PARENT's effect, which React runs after all descendants' effects in the same commit. posthog-js sets __loaded synchronously inside init(), so the ordering is the entire question, and the ordering is child-first.
W1-324.fixDirection: Make identify resilient to init order: either call posthog.identify unconditionally (posthog-js queues calls made before init via its stub array — verify with the pinned posthog-js 1.418.1; if the imported instance queues, the __loaded guard can simply be dropped), or pass a `loaded` callback from the provider through context/state so PostHogIdentify re-renders and re-runs its effect once init completes, or move posthog.init to module scope of the provider file (guarded by typeof window) so it precedes all effects. Add the identified call to any manual verification checklist for analytics.
W1-324.gateOrTest: A Playwright spec that hard-loads /feed signed in and asserts a `/ingest` request whose body contains "$identify" (network assertion, written after the live confirmation per the repo's MCP-then-Playwright rule).
W1-324.reproPlan: Read-only live proof: sign in on production (or dev with NEXT_PUBLIC_POSTHOG_DEV=1), hard-reload /feed with the network panel filtered to /ingest, and observe that no $identify event is sent for the whole session; PostHog's Persons page showing (near-)zero identified members despite 49 active accounts corroborates.

W1-325.title: Fire-and-forget telemetry writes (void logSearch / void recordView) run after the response on Vercel with no after()/waitUntil, so search logging and view counters silently under-record in production
W1-325.expected: Every search a member makes and every profile/letter/photo/round view is recorded — these features exist because the owner explicitly asked "what are people failing to find" and "who looked at what" (the files' own headers).
W1-325.actual: All seven call sites use bare `void logSearch({...})` / `void recordView(...)` with no await and no next/server after()/waitUntil. On Vercel, execution after the response completes is not guaranteed: whenever the enclosing render/route finishes before the DB round-trip resolves (fast pages, warm caches, slow pooler moments), the write is frozen with the lambda and may never land — or lands unpredictably when the instance thaws for the next request. The API routes are worst: `void logSearch(...)` immediately precedes `return NextResponse.json(...)`, so the promise races the response by design. Dev always works (process stays alive), which is exactly why this class ships unnoticed; both helpers also swallow errors silently in production (`if (NODE_ENV !== "production") console.error`), so there is no signal when loss happens.
W1-325.evidence: src/app/api/users/search/route.ts:72: `void logSearch({ ... })` followed directly by the JSON return. src/app/(main)/feed/page.tsx:31: `void logSearch({ scope: "feed", query: q, userId: s?.user?.id });` inside an RSC render. src/lib/search-log.ts and content-view.ts are plain async Prisma writers with no after() anywhere (`grep -rn "after(" src/lib/search-log.ts src/lib/content-view.ts` is empty). The audit brief's 6f row states the platform contract: nothing runs after the response without after()/waitUntil.
W1-325.fixDirection: Wrap each fire-and-forget call in `after(() => logSearch(...))` / `after(() => recordView(...))` from next/server (stable in Next 16), which keeps the non-blocking behaviour while guaranteeing completion. Since the sites are few, a repo-wide grep for `void logSearch|void recordView` in the check script would pin the pattern.
W1-325.gateOrTest: Add a security-regressions-style static test asserting no bare `void logSearch(`/`void recordView(` remains outside an after() wrapper (grep-based, like src/lib/security-regressions.test.mjs pins the deleted admin-login route).
W1-325.reproPlan: code-argument-only (loss is probabilistic under production timing; proving it live would need production load). Corroborating read-only check: compare SearchLog row counts against PostHog search-box autocapture counts for the same window.

W1-327.title: Code-unit truncation and initials split surrogate pairs: plainExcerpt, letterTitle and getInitials cut strings with .slice()/[0] on UTF-16 units, rendering U+FFFD when an emoji or non-BMP character sits at the boundary
W1-327.expected: A teaser truncated at its cap ends cleanly ("..." after a whole character); initials of a name are whole characters.
W1-327.actual: plainExcerpt: `return plain.slice(0, maxLen).trimEnd() + "..."` — if code unit 160 falls between the halves of a surrogate pair (any emoji, many Indic-adjacent and historic scripts), the teaser ends in a lone surrogate the browser paints as � before the ellipsis. letterTitle line 356 has the identical `firstLine.slice(0, maxLen).trimEnd() + "..."`. getInitials lines 41-42 take `parts[0][0]` / `parts[parts.length-1][0]` — for a name beginning with an emoji or non-BMP letter this is half a surrogate pair, so the avatar fallback shows �; additionally a whitespace-only name would make parts[0][0] undefined and `.toUpperCase()` throw, though current validators (firstName/lastName trim().min(1), profile name min 2) make an all-whitespace stored name unlikely rather than impossible (profileSchema's name has no .trim() before min(2), so "  " passes min(2) — two spaces — and getInitials("  ") then throws: `"  ".trim().split(/\s+/)` → [""] → parts[0][0] undefined → TypeError).
W1-327.evidence: src/lib/utils.ts:388-389: `if (plain.length <= maxLen) return plain; return plain.slice(0, maxLen).trimEnd() + "..."`. utils.ts:356: `return firstLine.length > maxLen ? firstLine.slice(0, maxLen).trimEnd() + "..." : firstLine`. utils.ts:38-43: `const parts = name.trim().split(/\s+/); if (parts.length === 0) return "?"; if (parts.length === 1) return parts[0][0].toUpperCase();` — the length-0 branch is unreachable (split of "" yields [""]) and parts[0][0] is a bare code unit. profileSchema (validators.ts:54) is `name: z.string().min(2).max(100)` with no .trim(), so a two-space name passes validation.
W1-327.fixDirection: Truncate with Array.from (code points) or Intl.Segmenter (graphemes): `[...plain].slice(0, maxLen).join("")`; take initials via `[...parts[0]][0] ?? "?"`; add .trim() to profileSchema.name so whitespace-only names cannot be stored.
W1-327.gateOrTest: Unit tests: plainExcerpt of a string whose 160th code unit is inside an emoji ends without a lone surrogate; getInitials("🦜 Ravi") returns whole characters; getInitials("  ") does not throw; profileSchema rejects "  ".
W1-327.reproPlan: code-argument-only; trivially demonstrable in a local node REPL with the quoted expressions.

W1-328.title: Year validators evaluate new Date().getFullYear() in UTC at module scope: for 5.5 hours every New Year (and for as long as a warm lambda survives past it), the current year is rejected as "hasn't happened yet"

From 00:00 to 05:30 IST on 1 January the server year is still last year, so `photoYear: max(getFullYear(), "That year hasn't happened yet")` rejects the member's true current year; worse, because the value is captured at module scope, a Vercel lambda instance imported in December and kept warm into January keeps the stale cap for its entire lifetime, extending the window arbitrarily. computeBatchFromSchooling (utils.ts:294) re-reads the clock per call (no staleness) but is still UTC, giving the same 5.5-hour window for `yearJoined > thisYear` rejections.

Same pattern at 104-109 (profileSchema batchYear/yearJoined/yearLeft/taughtFrom/taughtUntil) and 186-189 (photoSchema.photoYear). src/lib/utils.ts:294: `const thisYear = new Date().getFullYear()` inside computeBatchFromSchooling, UTC on the server.
W1-328.fixDirection: Compute the cap per validation rather than per import — Zod supports a function via .refine, or use a helper `currentISTYear()` (mirror wordle.ts's Asia/Kolkata rendering) and call it inside a .superRefine/.refine on each year field. Alternatively accept +1 headroom on every "this year" cap (as yearLeft already does), which makes both the timezone and the warm-lambda staleness harmless.
W1-328.gateOrTest: Unit test constructing the schemas with a faked clock (or refactored to accept a now() injection) asserting the cap tracks the IST year across the 31 Dec 18:30 UTC boundary.
W1-328.reproPlan: code-argument-only (the failing window is New Year's morning).

W1-330.title: batchTypeFromLeaving silently returns "ISC" for impossible input (batchYear earlier than yearLeft), so a swapped-fields typo at signup or settings stores a nonsense batch with a confident board credential and no error

W1-331.title: Email case is never normalized at signup/login while password reset lowercases: any account registered with an uppercase letter in its email can NEVER receive a reset link (silent, permanent lockout), and one mailbox can register twice
W1-331.expected: One mailbox = one account, findable by any casing: signup, login and reset should agree on a canonical (lowercased) form of the address, per taxonomy 6e.
W1-331.actual: Signup stores the address exactly as typed; login looks it up exactly as typed; but the forgot-password flow lowercases before lookup. A member who signed up as 'Amy@Gmail.com' gets 'check your inbox' from the reset form and no mail ever arrives, forever, with no signal anywhere (the identical-answer anti-oracle design hides the miss). Two rows for one mailbox ('Amy@x.com' + 'amy@x.com') are also possible since the unique index is case-sensitive.
W1-331.evidence: registerUser stores raw case: `email: parsed.data.email` (actions.ts:149) — signupSchema uses `z.email(...)` (validators.ts:18) which validates format but applies no lowercase transform, and prisma/schema.prisma:13 is `email String @unique` (Postgres btree, case-sensitive). authorize() looks up raw: `const user = await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email } })` (auth.ts:102) — note it builds `const acctKey = email.trim().toLowerCase()` (auth.ts:62) for rate-limit keys and the human-pass, but NOT for the DB lookup. requestPasswordReset destroys the case first: `const raw = ((formData.get("email") as string) ?? "").trim().toLowerCase();` then `prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: raw } })` (email-actions.ts:160,165) and on a miss returns the identical `{ ok: true }` (by design, line 174), so the mixed-case member sees the 'A reset link is on its way to …' screen (forgot-client.tsx:194) and nothing is ever enqueued. The doomed loop the login comment warns about (login-client.tsx:386-390 'telling someone their password is wrong when it isn't sends them into a doomed reset loop') is exactly what ships for these accounts: wrong-case login says 'Invalid email or password', and the reset path is a black hole. signHumanPass already lowercases (human-pass-rule.ts:16 `email.toLowerCase()`), so the codebase is internally split on the convention.
W1-331.fixDirection: Pick lowercase as canonical: (1) lowercase in signupSchema (z.email().transform or .toLowerCase() in registerUser before findUnique/create); (2) lowercase in authorize() before the findUnique (use acctKey, which already exists); (3) run a one-time idempotent SQL migration lowercasing existing User.email rows (guard: check for case-only duplicate pairs first and resolve manually — count today is likely zero); (4) optionally add a functional unique index on lower(email) via migrations-manual to make the invariant structural. Keep requestPasswordReset as-is once the store is canonical.
W1-331.reproPlan: Read-only proof against prod data: `SELECT email FROM "User" WHERE email <> lower(email);` — any row returned is a member already locked out of reset. Behavioral proof on a test account: sign up via the UI with 'RvAuditTest@example.com', then submit forgot-password for 'rvaudittest@example.com' (lowercased is what the server does anyway) and observe OutboundEmail: no reset row is created.
W1-331.gateOrTest: Unit test on a shared normalizeEmail() used by all three flows; plus a security-regressions-style test asserting registerUser and authorize both lowercase before hitting the User table.

W1-333.title: Avatar upload (onboarding photo step + settings) promises 15MB but ships the raw file through a server action, which Vercel hard-caps at ~4.5MB — typical phone photos fail, and the photo step's missing try/catch turns that failure into a permanently stuck spinner

W1-333.evidence: Client gate: `if (file.size > 15 * 1024 * 1024) { toast.error("Photo must be under 15MB") }` (photo-step.tsx:42-44) then `fd.set("file", file); const result = await updateAvatar(fd);` — bytes through the action. Server gate agrees: `const MAX_AVATAR_INPUT = 15 * 1024 * 1024;` (settings/actions.ts:20) and `if (file.size > MAX_AVATAR_INPUT) return { error: "Photo must be under 15MB" }` (line 215). The repo itself documents the platform cap: upload-client.ts:14-16 — 'The caller then falls back to its classic server-proxied upload, which is capped at ~4.5MB on Vercel'. next.config.ts `serverActions: { bodySizeLimit: "25mb" }` lifts only Next's own limit (and proxyClientMaxBodySize only matters self-hosted); Vercel's serverless request-body ceiling is a platform constant the config cannot raise. Avatars have NO presigned direct-to-R2 path — directUploadPut supports only `kind: "post" | "collection"` (upload-client.ts:19-21). The same platform cap likely also bites the Collection contribute server action (contributePhoto — the config comment at next.config.ts:106-110 expects 20MB photos through it), flagged here for the collection-territory investigator.
W1-333.fixDirection: Route avatars through the existing presign path (add kind "avatar" to /api/upload/presign + directUploadPut, then pass the staged key to updateAvatar for the sharp/512px pass server-side reading from R2), or downscale client-side before posting (src/lib/image-downscale.ts exists) so the wire size stays under ~4MB. Independently, wrap the photo-step await in try/catch/finally so busy always resets and a real message shows.
W1-333.reproPlan: Against the production deployment with a test account: attempt an avatar upload with a 6MB JPEG on the /welcome photo step; observe the network tab 413 and the spinner never resolving. (Local dev will NOT reproduce — no platform cap — which is why it survived QA.)
W1-333.gateOrTest: E2e spec uploading a >4.5MB fixture through the avatar path once the fix lands; unit-level assertion that every FormData file path either presigns or client-downscales below 4MB.

W1-334.title: Nine auth/onboarding client call sites await server actions with no try/catch: any transient failure (network blip, deploy mid-session, cold-start timeout, 413) leaves the button permanently disabled in its busy label with no error shown
W1-334.expected: Every awaited server action mirrors login-client.tsx:364-409 and signup-form.tsx:391-444, which wrap in try/catch/finally so the pending flag always resets and the member gets 'Something went wrong. Please try again.'
W1-334.actual: A rejected action promise escapes the handler: the busy state set before the await never resets (button stuck on 'Sending...'/'Saving...'), and the rejection is unhandled. Chaos cases from the brief (DB slow/down mid-request, session/deployment skew) all land here.
W1-334.evidence: forgot-client.tsx:67+82: `setSending(true); ... const result = await requestPasswordReset(formData);` — no try, no finally; a throw exits with sending=true (button disabled at line 156 `disabled={sending}`, label 'Sending...'). reset-client.tsx:116-117: `setBusy(true); const result = await resetPassword({ token, password });` same shape ('Saving...' forever, the typed password stranded); and after success, line 135 `const signedIn = await signIn(...)` — a throw there strands the member on the 'we are signing you in now' screen with the redirect setTimeout never scheduled (password IS changed, so at least manual login works). verify-client.tsx:103-105: `setBusy(true); ... const result = await resendVerification();`. trivia-gate.tsx:45: `getTriviaQuestion().then(setQuestion)` with no .catch — a rejection leaves the question '...' and the Check button disabled forever (line 202 `disabled={!question ...}`), and swapQuestion (line 60) has the same hole. register-step.tsx:81-83, houses-step.tsx:66-72 (`handleSave`) and its mount effect (line 56, `await getOnboardingHouses()` — loading stuck true), photo-step (covered in the 4.5MB finding), and legacy onboarding/page.tsx:26 (`await updateProfile(formData)` then router.push with no error branch at all).
W1-334.fixDirection: Mechanical: wrap each await in try/catch with the shared generic sentence and move the busy-reset into finally, exactly as login-client/signup-form already do. For trivia-gate's fetch, add .catch that sets an inline error with a retry button (a failed question fetch currently has no recovery but reload).
W1-334.reproPlan: Local: load /forgot-password, stop the dev server, submit — button sticks on 'Sending...' with a console unhandled-rejection; same probe per site.
W1-334.gateOrTest: ESLint discipline or a small unit test greping auth/onboarding clients for awaited actions outside try (same pattern as security-regressions.test.mjs); or per-form Playwright specs with route interception returning 500.

W1-335.title: Turnstile widget's `dead` latch is permanent: one challenge error-callback bricks every subsequent sign-in/signup/reset submit in that tab (server fails closed on the missing token), and only a full page reload recovers
W1-335.expected: The widget's own header comment promises 'a broken third party never bricks sign-in' — after a transient challenge error, a later submit should re-attempt the challenge (Turnstile supports reset()) rather than permanently give up.
W1-335.actual: After `error-callback` fires once (transient network loss while the challenge brews, an extension interfering, a Cloudflare hiccup after retries are exhausted), `dead.current = true` forever. Every later getToken() resolves null instantly, the form submits tokenless, and the server refuses: verifyTurnstile has `if (!token) return false;` when a secret is configured, so authorize() throws BotCheckFailed and the member sees the bot-check message on every attempt with correct credentials, with no hint that reloading fixes it. The fail-open posture only covers the SERVER side (siteverify unreachable / key unset); the client-side failure modes (script blocked, challenge error, 12s timeout) all fail closed.
W1-335.evidence: turnstile-widget.tsx:107-110: `"error-callback": () => { dead.current = true; waiters.current.splice(0).forEach((w) => w(null)); }` — no `window.turnstile.reset(...)`, no un-latching, unlike "expired-callback" (105) which does reset. Line 136: `if (dead.current) return Promise.resolve(null);`. turnstile.ts:86: `if (!token) return false;` (after the secret-configured check), and auth.ts:91-94: `if (!human) { ... throw new BotCheckFailed(); }`. registerUser and requestPasswordReset share the same fate via verifyHumanFromForm (turnstile.ts:130-135).
W1-335.fixDirection: In error-callback, reset the widget and clear the latch (optionally after a short backoff, and only latch dead after N consecutive errors); alternatively have getToken(), when it finds dead=true, attempt one re-render/reset before resolving null. Also worth an explicit user-facing sentence for the tokenless-refusal case suggesting a reload, since the server cannot distinguish it from a bot.
W1-335.reproPlan: Local with TURNSTILE_DEV_REAL=1: load /login, use DevTools request blocking on challenges.cloudflare.com AFTER the script loads to force the challenge to error, then unblock and submit repeatedly — every attempt returns bot-check until reload.
W1-335.gateOrTest: Unit test on a widget harness: simulate error-callback then assert a later getToken() attempts a reset rather than resolving null.

W1-336.title: Trivia pass expiry (30-min TTL) or cookies-blocked leaves the signup register step unrecoverable: registerUser demands the entry question but the UI has no way back to the trivia step, so the filled form dead-ends (cookie-blocked browsers loop forever)
W1-336.expected: If the server refuses because the gate pass is missing/expired, the flow returns the person to the trivia step (keeping their typed form state), or the pass is refreshed transparently.
W1-336.actual: registerUser returns { error: "Please answer the entry question before signing up." } which renders as a red line under the form; the step state machine only ever moves trivia→register (onPass at signup-client.tsx:392) — there is no setStep("trivia") anywhere after that, so the only recovery is a full reload, which discards every field. A visitor with cookies disabled passes the client-side gate (checkTrivia returns ok regardless of whether the browser stored rv_trivia_pass) and then hits this error on every submit, indefinitely, with an instruction they cannot follow.
W1-336.evidence: actions.ts:17-21: `if (!(await hasPassedTrivia())) { return { error: "Please answer the entry question before signing up." }; }`. TTL: trivia-actions.ts:83 `const TOKEN_TTL_MS = 30 * 60 * 1000;` and hasPassedTrivia (226-242) requires BOTH rv_trivia_pass and rv_trivia_id cookies (231: `if (!token || !browserId) return false;`). Note also the id cookie's maxAge is set at FIRST attempt (line 182-190), so someone whose first wrong attempt was 29 minutes before their pass loses the id cookie a minute later and the still-valid pass stops verifying. signup-client.tsx: `const [step, setStep] = useState<Step>("trivia")` (line 30) and the only transition is `onPass={() => setStep("register")}` (392).
W1-336.fixDirection: Map that specific server error to setStep("trivia") in SignupForm's error branch (lift the trivia error into a callback prop so signup-client can flip back while React state preserves the form fields, since the component stays mounted under AnimatePresence), and refresh the rv_trivia_id maxAge whenever the pass is minted. Optionally detect document.cookie-disabled up front and show a plain 'this site needs cookies to sign up' notice.
W1-336.reproPlan: Local: pass trivia, delete the rv_trivia_pass cookie in DevTools, submit the filled form — observe the dead-end error with no route back; or block all cookies in a fresh profile and walk the flow.
W1-336.gateOrTest: Playwright: clear the pass cookie between steps, submit, expect the trivia step to return with the form state intact.

W1-337.title: joinBatchGroup is find-then-create with no unique constraint on Group.name: two same-batch signups racing (launch day is exactly when this happens) create duplicate 'Batch of {year}' groups and permanently split the batch membership
W1-337.expected: One group per batch year, however many members register concurrently — per taxonomy 6d, the DB constraint is the only real guard for find-or-create.
W1-337.actual: Both concurrent registrations findFirst → null → both create → two rows named 'Batch of 2019'; each member lands in a different one, and every later member joins whichever findFirst returns first (nondeterministic order — no orderBy). Catch-ups and batch fan-outs built on the group then address half the batch. No cleanup path exists.
W1-337.evidence: actions.ts:215-230: `let group = await prisma.group.findFirst({ where: { name }, select: { id: true } }); if (!group) { group = await prisma.group.create({ ... }) }` — the code's own comment concedes 'Group.name is not unique in the schema, so match by exact name'. The membership upsert below it (232-236) is protected by `@@unique` on (groupId,userId), so the pattern was known — it just wasn't applied to the group row itself. Launch is the high-risk window: a WhatsApp-batch-group of classmates signing up within the same minute is the expected adoption pattern, and signup rate limits are per-IP so they do not serialize this.
W1-337.fixDirection: Add a unique constraint (e.g. a partial/functional unique on name for batch groups, or a dedicated batchYear column with @@unique) via a dated migrations-manual file, switch joinBatchGroup to upsert/`create...catch P2002 then findFirst`, and add a one-time dedupe query merging any existing duplicates' members before the constraint lands.
W1-337.reproPlan: code-argument-only (provoking it live means racing two real signups against the shared production DB). A read-only check for prior occurrences: `SELECT name, count(*) FROM "Group" WHERE name LIKE 'Batch of %' GROUP BY name HAVING count(*) > 1;`
W1-337.gateOrTest: Unit test firing two concurrent joinBatchGroup calls against a transaction-wrapped test double; the schema constraint is the real gate.

W1-338.title: Legacy /onboarding page is orphaned but live, and its updateProfile action writes bio/currentCity/workplace/jobTitle/phone/instagram/linkedin with NO validation — no length caps, no phone normalization — bypassing every rule profileSchema enforces on the same columns
W1-338.expected: Every write path to a column enforces the same rules (the codebase's own M18 principle, validators.ts:113-120: 'this is the second write path to them, so it gets the same gate').
W1-338.actual: A signed-in member navigating to /onboarding (it resolves; it is only absent from nav) can submit a multi-hundred-KB bio (server-action bodies accept up to 25MB per next.config), an unnormalized phone, uncapped instagram/linkedin — values profileSchema caps at 1000/24/100/200. Oversized text then flows into every surface that renders these columns (directory cards, profile), the exact over-fetch/rendering weight 6j warns about.
W1-338.evidence: onboarding/actions.ts:12-20: `const fields = ["bio", "currentCity", "workplace", "jobTitle", "phone", "instagram", "linkedin"]; for (const field of fields) { const value = formData.get(field) as string | null; if (value && value.trim()) { data[field] = value.trim(); } }` then `prisma.user.update({ ... data })` — no Zod, no max, no normalizePhone (compare profileSchema: bio max(1000), phone max(24), instagram max(100), linkedin max(200), validators.ts:56-76). The page is reachable: it sits in (auth)/onboarding, is NOT in proxy publicPaths (so it needs a session — fine), and welcome/page.tsx:13-18 itself calls it 'dead code today ... not linked from anywhere'. Dead-but-routable plus unvalidated write = the gap.
W1-338.fixDirection: Delete the legacy page and action outright (the /welcome wizard superseded it; welcome/page.tsx's comment says only file-deletion scope stopped it), or if kept, run its input through profileSchema.pick(...) + normalizePhone like settings does. Deletion is the simplification the pre-release audit wants anyway.
W1-338.reproPlan: Signed in as a test account locally, visit /onboarding, paste a 100KB string into Bio, save; read the row length back via prisma studio (read-only confirm).
W1-338.gateOrTest: security-regressions.test.mjs-style assertion that (auth)/onboarding/actions.ts no longer exists, or a unit test that its action rejects >1000-char bio.

W1-339.title: The landing page (and every route) is dynamically rendered because the root layout awaits cookies() for the theme — the 'landing stays statically rendered' claim in proxy.ts is false in shipped code
W1-339.expected: The signed-in '/'→/feed redirect was deliberately placed in the proxy 'so the landing page stays statically rendered for logged-out visitors' (proxy.ts comment) — i.e. '/' served from CDN with static TTFB, the stated reason auth() was kept out of page.tsx.
W1-339.actual: RootLayout awaits getThemeCookie() → cookies(), a dynamic API, which opts every route under it — including '/', /login, /signup — into per-request SSR (no ppr/cacheComponents in next.config to give a static shell). The architectural care taken in page.tsx and proxy.ts is silently void: every anonymous landing hit pays a function invocation and cold-start latency, and at 2,000 members' worth of shared-link traffic that is the TTFB profile of the front door.
W1-339.evidence: layout.tsx:69 (in RootLayout, an async server component): `const theme = (await getThemeCookie()) ?? "light";`; theme.ts:23-25: `export async function getThemeCookie() { const value = (await cookies()).get(THEME_COOKIE)?.value; ... }`. proxy.ts:150-154: 'Handled here rather than in `app/page.tsx` so the landing page stays statically rendered for logged-out visitors: calling `auth()` in the page would opt the whole route into dynamic rendering for everyone.' — cookies() has identical dynamic-rendering semantics to auth(). next.config.ts experimental block contains only optimizePackageImports/serverActions/proxyClientMaxBodySize — no PPR.
W1-339.fixDirection: Signed-out pages are always light-theme (dark is only entered via settings), so move the theme-cookie read out of the root layout into the (main) layout (or a client-side <ThemeScript> reading document.cookie before paint), letting '/', /login, /signup and the policy pages go static. Verify with `next build` output: '/' should list as prerendered.
W1-339.reproPlan: Read-only: run a curl against production '/' twice and compare x-vercel-cache headers (MISS/expected dynamic today), or inspect the deployed build output page in the Vercel dashboard — orchestrator-level check.
W1-339.gateOrTest: A build-output assertion in CI that '/' is static (grep the build manifest), so a future layout edit cannot silently re-dynamify the front door.

W1-340.title: Signup Join button re-enables during the 1400ms celebration window: a double-click after success fires registerUser again, painting 'An account with this email already exists' over the welcome toast before navigating anyway
W1-340.expected: After a successful registration the form stays inert for the celebration beat; the one unrepeatable success moment is not interruptible by its own submit button.

A second press re-runs the whole submit: fresh Turnstile getToken, registerUser returns the already-exists error (the P2002/pre-check path), setError paints the red line and hoopoe.react("error") fires mid-celebration; navigation to /welcome still happens at 1400ms, so the member's final frames of signup are a success toast, an error line, and an error-shaking bird at once.
W1-340.evidence: signup-form.tsx:429-437: `hoopoe.celebrate(3); toast.success("Welcome to the jungle!"); ... setTimeout(onSuccess, 1400);` inside try; lines 442-444: `} finally { setLoading(false); }` — unconditional. Button: line 680 `disabled={loading}`.
